📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss. The online unit still lost money, and the results came with another delayed quarterly filing after a going-concern warning in August.

Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter. It is still not profitable. North America Interactive groups the company’s sports betting and iGaming businesses in both countries. The unit lost less money than a year earlier, but it stayed in the red.

Industry observers note that the pace stands out against the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, according to Citizens JMP Securities. That was down from 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. Bally’s online growth ran well ahead of that slowing trend.

Industry observers note that the quarter was not a clean step up, though. North America Interactive posted $66.1 million in second-quarter revenue, up 16.9% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales were therefore lower than the quarter before. First-quarter revenue was $60.5 million, a 35.9% increase.

Industry observers note that for the first nine months of 2026, the unit had preliminary revenue of $189.2 million. That compares with $134.0 million for February 8 to September 30, 2025, and $16.9 million for January 1 to February 7, 2025.

Sources indicate that A narrower loss points to progress. Yet the unit has not reached break-even, even while growing faster than the market. For a smaller US operator, online scale is still not translating into profit.

Sources indicate that all third-quarter figures are preliminary. Bally’s has not finished closing its books for the period ended September 30, 2026, and the numbers could change. It filed a late-filing notice dated November 10 because it needed more time to finish reviewing its third-quarter financial statements.

According to recent reports, that makes three late quarterly reports in 2026. Bally’s notified the SEC in May that its first-quarter report would be late. It did the same in August for the second quarter. Both notices cited more time needed to review financial statements.

It has been revealed that in the first-quarter 10-Q, management concluded that disclosure controls were not effective. The cause was a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, first disclosed in the 2025 annual report.

According to recent reports, the second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 14, went further. Two tests tied to the company’s revolver, a net leverage covenant and a liquidity requirement, were expected to be missed during the coming year. That same filing carried a going-concern warning, questioning whether Bally’s could keep operating. The shares fell more than 25% in one trading session afterward.

It has been revealed that bally’s reports strong revenue growth in Q3 2026. Data and info: https://t.co/ekSd5Ngu0Q.

• Group revenue increased 22% to USD 807.6m, while North America Interactive revenue rose 26% to USD 62.7m.

CEO Robeson Reeves said development projects remain on track and market conditions are stable going into the fourth quarter and 2027. The Bronx casino resort is expected to cost $4.0 billion and open by 2030. Bally’s closed a financing package led by WhiteHawk Capital Partners that provided $400 million in term loans for the project. Another $160 million in delayed-draw commitments remains available. The term loans come due 18 months after they are first funded.

The delayed third-quarter 10-Q comes next. The company has stated it should arrive before its five-day SEC grace period runs out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier.
  • MotorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier.
  • Across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier. Retail sports betting also rebounded sharply from September, adding to the month's gains.

MotorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier. Its rivals both lost ground. MGM Grand Detroit slipped 2.7% to $51.3 million. Hollywood Casino at Greektown fell 5.0% to $21.6 million.

Across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million. That was up 2.1% from October 2025 and 5.2% from September 2026. Year-to-date revenue from January through October was up 2.3%.

CDC Gaming Reports put October 2025 table and slot revenue at $105.9 million.

Sources indicate that MGM still holds the largest piece of the market. It took 47% of Detroit’s October revenue. MotorCity held 33%, and Hollywood Casino at Greektown held 20%.

The October split continues a pattern from late summer. In August, MotorCity rose 8.3% to $33.8 million and MGM grew 2.3% to $52.9 million, while Greektown fell 2.6% to $22.2 million, InterGame reported. Detroit’s August total was $109.7 million.

Recent findings suggest that greektown’s slide deepened in September, when its revenue fell 8.8% year over year to $21.34 million. October’s decline was smaller. MGM, by contrast, moved from growth in August to a decline in October.

Recent findings suggest that the citywide trend has been uneven. September table and slot revenue was 4.7% higher than a year earlier but 5.6% lower than in August. October’s rebound lifted aggregate revenue above September’s $103.55 million.

According to recent reports, retail sports betting produced $2.4 million in October. That compares with $769,771 in retail QAGR in September. Handle at the Detroit casinos was $12.87 million for the month.

AI code editors like Cursor make it quick to produce a polished static page. Describe a hero section, an about block and a contact form, and you'll have working HTML, CSS and JavaScript in an afternoon. The trouble starts when that page needs to live inside WordPress. WordPress doesn't serve a folder of HTML files; it builds pages from PHP templates, a theme hierarchy and its own content system.

This tutorial shows a lightweight way to bridge that gap: wrap your generated front end in a child theme of an existing parent theme, then deploy it with nothing more than a ZIP upload. It's the approach SEO specialist Shumaila Asghar used to build her portfolio website, and it works well for small sites where you want full control of the design without building a theme from scratch.

You could paste your HTML into a page builder block or edit the parent theme's files directly. Both approaches cause problems later. Page builders often strip or rewrite markup, and any edits made to a parent theme are overwritten the next time it updates.

It has been revealed that A child theme inherits everything from its parent, including templates, styles and features, and lets you override only what you need. For this workflow, a lightweight, well-maintained parent such as Kadence works well: it handles the essentials like menus, accessibility features and responsive defaults, while your child theme supplies the custom design.

Before touching WordPress, finish the front end as a static page. Blueprint each section up front (for a portfolio, that might be hero, about, skills, services, experience, projects and contact), then generate and refine the code in your editor.

Test it locally on desktop and mobile. Check navigation, spacing, button states and readability. It's much easier to fix layout bugs now, when you're dealing with plain HTML and CSS, than after the code is split across PHP templates.

One habit worth forming: read the code the AI produces rather than accepting it wholesale. You'll need to understand its structure in the next step.

#149463. Tech Report: TRL v1.0: Post-Training Library Built to Move with the Field

Tech Report: TRL v1.0: Post-Training Library Built to Move with the Field

📅 31 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is.
  • Sources indicate that TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods.
  • In a recent development, TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is. What started as a research codebase has become a dependable library people build on, with clearer expectations around stability. This isn't just a version bump. It reflects the reality that TRL now powers production systems, and embraces that responsibility.

Sources indicate that TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods. But coverage isn’t the goal by itself. What matters is making these methods easy to try, compare, and actually use in practice. The design of the library wasn’t decided upfront. It is the result of years of iteration — the first commit goes back more than six years — and it has been shaped by everything the field threw at it: new algorithms, new models, shifting paradigms. Over time, this pressure forced the codebase toward a very specific design. Parts of it might look unusual at first, but like in many evolutionary codebases, they exist for a reason.

In a recent development, TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still. So the question is not how to design the perfect abstraction. It is how to make stable software in a domain that keeps invalidating its own assumptions. This is what we tried to solve in TRL v1.0, and this post explains how.

Post-training has not evolved as a smooth refinement of one recipe. It has moved through successive centers of gravity, each changing not just the objective, but the shape of the stack.

PPO [Schulman et al., (2017); Ziegler et al., (2019)] made one architecture look canonical: a policy, a reference model, a learned reward model, sampled rollouts, and an RL loop.

Then DPO-style methods such as the original DPO [Rafailov et al., (2023)], ORPO [Hong et al., (2024)], and KTO [Ethayarajh et al., (2024)] cut through that stack: preference optimization could work without a separate reward model, value model, or any online RL. Components that had looked fundamental suddenly looked optional.

RLVR-style methods such as GRPO [Shao et al., (2024)] shifted the center again. On tasks like math, code, and tool use, rewards often come from verifiers or deterministic checks rather than learned reward models. Sampling and rollouts matter again, but the objects in the loop are no longer quite the ones PPO libraries were designed around.

The lesson is not just that methods change. The definition of the core keeps changing with them. Strong assumptions here have a short half-life. This is probably why no post-training library is really stable yet.

So what does it mean to build a library for a field that won't sit still? The answer is counterintuitive: don't try to capture the essence of what's stable today. Instead, design around what could change. Reward models illustrate why: they looked essential in PPO, became optional in DPO, and came back as verifiers in RLVR methods — structures that could be deterministic functions rather than learned models. Any abstraction built around their original form would have been obsolete twice over by now. The library survives by recognizing that strong assumptions have a short life, and by making that changeability central to how the codebase is organized.

Industry observers note that this is the environment in which TRL is downloaded 3 million times a month, and in which major downstream projects treat it as stable infrastructure. The field keeps shifting the ground, and at the same time, those users need things not to break.

TRL didn’t make a deliberate decision to become a library. It found out it already was one. Projects like Unsloth and Axolotl — with thousands of owners between them — had built directly on top of TRL’s trainers and APIs. A breaking change in TRL propagated instantly into their stacks. A renamed argument, a shifted default, a restructured output — any of these became someone else’s incident. The shift had already happened. v1.0 is the moment TRL acknowledged it explicitly.

Industry observers note that the unusual thing about TRL’s stability model is not what it guarantees, it is what it tolerates alongside those guarantees. Stable and experimental coexist within the same package, with explicitly different contracts. The stable core follows semantic versioning. The experimental layer makes no such promises — it is where fresh methods land while they are still being evaluated, and where the API can move fast to keep up with the field.

In a recent development, this isn’t a compromise. It’s a response to a specific constraint: the field produces newly introduced methods faster than any of them can earn stability. Refusing to add immature methods would make TRL irrelevant within months. Adding them all to stable would break every downstream project every time an algorithm turned out not to work as expected.

Industry observers note that promotion from experimental to stable isn’t automatic. What matters is the ratio between maintenance cost and actual usage. Some methods earn their place because the community uses them heavily. Others become viable because we can make them cheap enough to maintain — and the design of the codebase is what makes that possible.

Industry observers note that in practice, the stable surface includes trainers for SFT, DPO, Reward modeling, RLOO, and GRPO, along with their close variants. The experimental surface is broader and moves faster; for an up-to-date view, the best reference is the TRL documentation.

The breaking changes needed to reach v1.0 were distributed deliberately across the 0.x releases. Migration from the last 0.x version is minimal — see the migration guide.

In a domain where patterns keep changing, the temptation is to build flexible abstractions that can accommodate anything. Our answer was the opposite: limit abstractions to the strict minimum — while recognizing that this “minimum” is almost always overestimated.

In practice, this translates into a very local approach to code:.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is not to eliminate structure altogether — shared utilities still exist — but to avoid imposing abstractions where the domain itself is not yet stable. For instance, rather than defining a common base class for offline trainers, we prefer independent implementations when their future evolution is uncertain.

According to recent reports, judges are a good example of what happens when we don’t follow this principle. Early on, we introduced a Judge abstraction to unify the various ways of evaluating model outputs. It looked reasonable at the time. In practice, it was never really used — the abstraction didn’t match how people actually approached evaluation, and it added indirection without adding value. It still lives in the repo, mostly as legacy. In hindsight, shipping the concrete implementations without the unifying abstraction would have served users better.

Sources indicate that this approach favors explicit and modifiable usage over rigid frameworks: less magic, but more control. It comes with an obvious cost: code duplication. While often seen as an anti-pattern, in this context it has proven not only acceptable, but effective. Contrary to intuition, it remains manageable in practice with a small but consistent discipline: keeping deltas between implementations minimal and avoiding unnecessary divergence. Like in the Transformers design philosophy, we accept duplication and local explicitness by design. The motivations largely coincide, with some nuance in focus.

It has been revealed that this is easier to see than to describe. Compare RLOO and GRPO: large parts of their implementation are duplicated almost line for line. That is not accidental, and it is not dead weight. These methods are close enough that keeping their code paths aligned makes them easier to read, easier to evolve, and cheaper to maintain.

The goal of this comparison is not to argue that TRL should be judged as best on every axis. It should not. Some systems are built for maximum throughput (like PipelineRL), some are optimized for a narrower slice of the problem (like LLaMA-Factory), and some offer a more opinionated development experience in a specific environment (like Tinker). TRL occupies a different place in the ecosystem: it is a general-purpose post-training library that tries to keep the API and the code as simple as the domain allows, while combining broad method coverage, deep Hugging Face integration, a relatively low infrastructure burden, and an explicit stability contract.

Libraries like Unsloth and Axolotl are not included here because they build on top of TRL rather than sitting beside it in the comparison; in that sense, many of their customers are also TRL users indirectly.

Some rows are factual (GitHub stars, Last release, Last commit), others are qualitative judgments (Semver stability).

Recent findings suggest that taken together, these comparisons point to a clear role for TRL: a general-purpose library designed to keep breadth, simplicity, integration, and stability in the same place. Its full downstream footprint is hard to measure, since most deployments are private and reverse dependencies are largely invisible, but the available signals already show that TRL operates at a distinctly different scale.

By now, the logic of v1.0 should be clear: it is not a claim that post-training has stabilized. On the contrary, it is an acknowledgment that the field will keep shifting, and that we're confident that the library has the right shape to absorb whatever comes next. The question is not what comes after v1.0, but what’s next for v1.0.

In a recent development, today, GRPO in TRL is primarily used through a synchronous loop: generate rollouts, score them, then step the optimizer. That shape is simple and dependable, but it ties throughput to the slowest stage and leaves performance on the table at scale.

The fix is conceptually simple: generation and training don't need to be lock-stepped. We already have an early asynchronous GRPO design, and the next step is to harden it. The core idea is to decouple generation and training, letting generation run continuously on dedicated inference resources while training consumes a steady stream of scored trajectories, with buffering, backpressure, and clear policy-version accounting. This improves utilization and scales across GPUs and nodes. Other libraries already offer forms of asynchronous RL, but bringing it to TRL would make this style of training available through broader integrations, simpler APIs, and a much lower barrier to adoption.

The next candidates include KTO and newer distillation trainers such as SDFT, SDPO, and possibly GOLD or GKD. As discussed in Section 2, before moving them to stable, the goal is to minimize code differences across implementations and monitor sustained community interest relative to maintenance cost.

TRL supports large-scale training, including multi-node runs and larger models; the next step is to make this path significantly more robust and easier to operate in production. That includes stronger guarantees around distributed stability, clearer scaling defaults, and deeper support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), especially expert parallelism, where routing, load balancing, and memory behavior become critical.

Training is still too often driven by vibes. Loss curves go down, reward curves go up, a few samples look better than before, and people convince themselves the run is working. When it fails, they scroll through logs, compare runs by eye, and guess. That is already a weak interface for humans. For agents, it is worse: it is barely an interface at all.

One of the most important directions for TRL is to make training legible to software, not just to people. That means going beyond dashboards and raw metrics to produce explicit signals: is the policy improving, collapsing, over-optimizing the verifier, drifting off-distribution, or plateauing? The goal is for TRL to surface these patterns automatically, explain them clearly, and turn them into actions.

The proposal is to embed heuristics directly into the training loop and emit structured, actionable warnings — the kind a beginner can act on immediately and an agent can parse:.

Not just logging what happened — reasoning about what it means and what to do next. Useful for beginners who need guardrails, and for agents that need a training stack they can actually automate.

Post-training doesn't converge. It shifts, and the next shift is already coming.

In a recent development, v1.0 is not a claim that things have settled. It's an acknowledgment that they haven't yet, and a commitment that the library can be relied on anyway. Six years of evolving alongside the field — and alongside the hundreds of contributors who made it possible — shaped a design we're confident is ready for what comes next, whatever that turns out to be. The community and the downstream projects had already assumed that stability — v1.0 makes it real.

Migration from the last 0.x release is minimal, and the migration guide covers everything. If you're new, now is a good time to start.

West Virginia's online casinos posted record monthly revenue in October 2026, the second full month with bet365 live in the state. The result pushed 2026 revenue past the total for all of 2025, while a bill to raise the iGaming tax remains pending.

Industry observers note that the revenue measure is adjusted gross interactive wagering receipts. State law defines it as an operator’s gross online wagering receipts minus winnings paid to players. Under 2019’s House Bill 2934, the privilege tax on those receipts goes into the Interactive Wagering Fund each week, and every licensed racetrack and historic resort pays it.

bet365 launched online sports betting and casino in the state on Aug. 27, 2026. West Virginia is its fourth U.S. online casino state. In its other 14 states, bet365 offers sports betting only.

According to recent reports, lottery licensing documents show bet365 received an interim license in January 2026. It was approved for a full annual license on July 29. West Virginia was the firm’s sixth North American launch in 13 months, Yogonet reported. The earlier rolls out were Kansas and Maryland in August 2025, Missouri in December 2025, Michigan in April 2026 and Alberta in July 2026.

According to recent reports, west Virginia’s market has a fixed structure. The Interactive Wagering Act allows no more than five gaming facility licenses with online wagering. Every online game counts as a state-owned lottery game. October’s record is consistent with bet365 adding to that market, but the operator split has yet to be shown.

In a recent development, two months of 2026 remain to be reported. The comparison months set a high bar. Adjusted gross interactive gaming receipts were $37,198,210 in November 2025. Receipts for the fiscal year to date through Nov. 30, 2025, were $169,425,990.

Industry observers note that the broader lottery picture also demonstrates growth. The Lottery took in more than $1.33 billion in gross revenue in fiscal 2026, which ended June 30. It sent $582.9 million to the state. Revenue was $58 million higher than in fiscal 2025. In its fiscal 2026 wrap-up, the Lottery named iLottery and iGaming as its biggest growth areas, and said iGaming was following national gaming trends.

Higher revenue also raises the stakes of a pending tax change. Introduced on Jan. 16, 2026, House Bill 4397 would increase the iGaming privilege tax. The bill is still listed as pending in the House Local Governments Committee.

According to recent reports, the next detail to watch is the operator breakdown. The Lottery publishes a file that splits interactive wagering data by skin and casino. That file will show how much of October’s record came from bet365.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma,’ he indicates.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products.

In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “upcoming form of medieval obscurantism.”.

“Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed.

“He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.”.

In a recent development, leCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models.

Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models.

Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year.

The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse.

“Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read.

Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post.

Amodei has also called for measures, such as stricter export controls on the export of high-end accelerators to China; a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation operations, for which his company has previously accused Alibaba and other Chinese model devs; and mandating safety testing for sufficiently advanced open-weights models.

In other words, Anthropic doesn’t want all freely downloadable models banned, just the ones that Amodei thinks aren’t playing fair or are powerful enough to compete with its own.

LeCun isn’t the only one who has pushed back against anti-open-weights rhetoric in recent memory.

Earlier this summer, a cadre of tech titans, including Meta, Microsoft, IBM, Dell, and Nvidia, wrote an open letter [PDF] in support of open-weights models.

Open models “strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang mentioned at the time. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.”.

It has been revealed that as we previously reported, Nvidia’s future depends on its ability to sell to a diverse set of customers ranging from the major model houses like Anthropic and OpenAI to public clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises. And while many of these companies are perfectly happy to get their AI through Claude or ChatGPT, others, whether it be for regulatory or cost reasons, are not.

Earlier this month, we reported how British neobank Revolut cut their vibe coding tab by 10x by moving its roughly 2,000 employees from Claude to Z.AI’s GLM 5.1 running on a cluster of 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs.

The problem for Anthropic, and OpenAI for that matter, is the more enterprises that embrace open-weights models, the less likely they are to spring for Claude or ChatGPT.

In a recent development, the Register reached out to Anthropic for comment, but had not heard back at the time of publication. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that imagine going from a therapeutic protein concept to a synthesis-ready, codon-optimized DNA sequence in an afternoon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OpenMed, Open-Source Agentic AI for Healthcare & Life Sciences.

TL;DR: We built an end-to-end protein AI pipeline covering structure prediction, sequence design, and codon optimization. After comparing multiple transformer architectures for codon-level language modeling, CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 emerged as the clear winner with a perplexity of 4.10 and a Spearman CAI correlation of 0.40, significantly outperforming ModernBERT. We then scaled to 25 species, trained 4 production models in 55 GPU-hours, and built a species-conditioned system that no other open-source project offers. Complete results, architectural decisions, and runnable code below.

Sources indicate that imagine going from a therapeutic protein concept to a synthesis-ready, codon-optimized DNA sequence in an afternoon. That is the pipeline OpenMed set out to build, and this post documents the process from start to finish.

In Part I, we mapped the landscape of protein AI: the architectures powering structure prediction, the open-source tools available for protein design, and the ecosystem of models from AlphaFold to ESMFold. That was a survey. This is the build.

At OpenMed, we set out to build a complete pipeline that takes a protein idea from concept to expression-ready DNA. That means three stages: predict the 3D structure of a protein, design amino acid sequences that fold into that structure, and optimize the underlying DNA codons so the protein actually expresses in the target organism. Along the way, we ran extensive experiments comparing transformer architectures for codon optimization, scaled our best model to 25 species, and built tooling that ties it all together.

In a recent development, this is not a polished success story. It is a transparent account of what worked, what surprised us, and what we would do differently, with runnable code and full results at every step.

Industry observers note that the pipeline has three components, each addressing a different stage of the protein engineering workflow described in Part I. Structure prediction determines what shape a protein takes. Sequence design determines which amino acids will produce that shape. Codon optimization determines which DNA will produce those amino acids efficiently in a living cell.

Recent findings suggest that the mRNA optimization work is where we invested the most effort, and where we have the most to share. The folding and design components use established tools (ESMFold from Meta, ProteinMPNN from the Baker Lab, both covered in depth in Part I). The codon optimization component is entirely ours: new models, new training infrastructure, new evaluation metrics.

In Part I, we surveyed the protein AI landscape and noted that most biological language models are adaptations of NLP architectures. The open question was which architecture. BERT variants dominate protein modeling (ESM-2, ProtTrans), but codon sequences have different statistical properties than both natural language and amino acid sequences. Codons are triplets drawn from a small 64-token alphabet, with strong positional dependencies and species-specific usage biases. We needed to find out what works from first principles.

The core question: which transformer architecture works best for codon-level language modeling?

This matters because codon optimization is crucial for therapeutic mRNA, vaccines, and recombinant protein production. The genetic code is degenerate: the same protein can be encoded by astronomically many different DNA sequences, but some codon arrangements express 100x better than others. The Pfizer-BioNTech COVID vaccine, for example, was codon-optimized for human expression. We wanted to build a model that could learn these preferences directly from natural coding sequences, rather than relying on hand-crafted frequency tables.

We started with a small CodonBERT baseline (6M params, following Sanofi's published architecture) and scaled up through two families: ModernBERT, which represented the latest efficiency innovations from the NLP community, and RoBERTa, the proven workhorse behind Meta's ESM protein language models.

According to recent reports, the choice of RoBERTa was deliberate. As we discussed in Part I, Meta's ESM-2 (which powers ESMFold) is itself a RoBERTa variant trained on protein sequences. We hypothesized that the same architecture family that learned amino acid patterns might also learn codon patterns. ModernBERT was the counterpoint: a 2024 architecture with RoPE embeddings, Flash Attention, and alternating local/global attention layers, representing everything the NLP community had learned since RoBERTa's 2019 release.

Recent findings suggest that to ensure a fair comparison, every model was trained on identical data with the same evaluation protocol. We used 250,000 coding sequences (CDS) from E. coli RefSeq, covering chromosome and complete assembly accessions. This is a clean, well-annotated dataset where codon usage patterns are well-characterized in the literature, giving us ground truth to validate against.

It has been revealed that our tokenizer maps each codon to a single token: 64 codons plus 5 special tokens (PAD, UNK, CLS, SEP, MASK) for a 69-token vocabulary. This is intentionally minimal. Unlike BPE tokenizers used in NLP, where subword boundaries are statistically learned, codon boundaries are biologically defined. Every three nucleotides encode one amino acid. Our tokenizer respects this.

It has been revealed that training ran on 4 A100 GPUs (80GB) with FSDP sharding, using 15,000 to 25,000 steps depending on model size. All models used masked language modeling (MLM) with 15% masking rate, the same objective used by ESM-2 for protein sequences.

The result was unambiguous: RoBERTa outperformed ModernBERT by 6x on perplexity (4.01 vs 26.24). This was not a marginal difference. ModernBERT, despite its modern attention patterns and efficient architecture, fundamentally underperformed the classic RoBERTa design on codon sequences.

Sources indicate that 1. Pre-trained NLP weights do not transfer to biology.

We initialized ModernBERT from its published English-language checkpoint, expecting the learned attention patterns to provide a useful starting point. They did not. Our best explanation: ModernBERT's pre-training on English text instilled inductive biases (subword frequency distributions, positional attention patterns) that actively interfere with learning codon statistics. RoBERTa, initialized randomly and trained purely on biological data, had no such baggage. This aligns with what the field has seen more broadly: ESM-2 and ProtTrans both train from scratch on biological data rather than fine-tuning from NLP checkpoints.

2. Hyperparameter tuning unlocked biological alignment.

This was the most surprising and practically notable finding of the exploration. Compare CodonRoBERTa-large v1 and v2:.

Sources indicate that same architecture. Same data. Same number of parameters. The only differences: half the learning rate and a longer warmup (2,000 steps vs 1,000). Yet v2's predicted codon likelihoods are 16x better correlated with real biological codon preferences, as measured by Codon Adaptation Index.

The perplexity actually got slightly worse (4.10 vs 4.01), which means v2 is marginally less accurate at predicting the exact masked codon. But it is dramatically better at predicting codons that biology actually uses. The slower training schedule let the model settle into representations that capture genuine biological signal rather than overfitting to surface statistics.

According to recent reports, this is a crucial insight for anyone training biological language models: MLM loss alone does not measure biological relevance. Domain-specific metrics are essential. In our case, CAI correlation turned out to be the metric that separates a useful model from a technically impressive but biologically meaningless one.

3. The base model is remarkably efficient.

Sources indicate that codonRoBERTa-base (92M params) achieved nearly identical perplexity to the large model (4.01 vs 4.10) with 3.4x fewer parameters and proportionally less training time. Its CAI correlation (0.219) is lower than v2's (0.404), but still well above the baseline and ModernBERT. For teams without access to multi-GPU clusters, the base model is a practical choice that captures most of the codon modeling performance at a fraction of the cost.

Recent findings suggest that in Part I, we described the three-stage workflow that most computational protein engineering projects follow: predict structure, design sequences, optimize codons. Here we run each stage with real data and report what we actually got.

Industry observers note that ESMFold architecture. The model parses a single amino acid sequence through the ESM-2 encoder, then predicts 3D coordinates via a folding trunk and structure module. Figure from Bertoline et al., Biomolecules 2024, CC-BY 4.0.

As covered in Part I, ESMFold is Meta's single-sequence structure predictor. It uses ESM-2, a 15-billion-parameter protein language model trained on 65 million UniRef sequences, as its backbone. The key advantage over AlphaFold 2 is speed: ESMFold skips the computationally expensive multiple sequence alignment (MSA) step and predicts structures directly from a single amino acid sequence. That makes it seconds per protein instead of hours.

According to recent reports, the tradeoff is accuracy. ESMFold achieves ~0.87 TM-score on CASP14 targets vs. AlphaFold's ~0.92. For rapid prototyping and candidate screening, that gap is acceptable. When a pipeline generates 100 designed sequences and needs to refold all of them to check viability, speed matters more than the last few percentage points of accuracy.

We ran ESMFold on 30 protein chains sourced from the Protein Data Bank. These are real experimental structures with known ground truth, spanning sequence lengths from 211 to 519 residues. The set deliberately includes both easy targets (single-domain proteins) and challenging ones (chains from a multi-chain ribosomal complex, PDB 7K00) to stress-test the model.

Industry observers note that the PTM scores are solid: anything above 0.5 suggests the model has the overall topology correct, and our average of 0.79 indicates high confidence in the predicted folds. The pLDDT scores are lower than published ESMFold benchmarks, which initially concerned us. The explanation turned out to be our test set composition: the ribosomal chains from 7K00 are part of a large multi-chain complex, and ESMFold (which predicts single chains in isolation) cannot model the inter-chain contacts that stabilize these structures. For single-domain proteins in our set, pLDDT scores were consistently above 70.

It has been revealed that each prediction takes ~10-30 seconds on an A100. The output includes:.

It has been revealed that proteinMPNN architecture. (A) The encoder processes backbone atom distances; the decoder autoregressively generates amino acid sequences. (B) Random decoding order improves diversity. (C) Tied positions enable symmetric and multi-state design. Figure from Dauparas et al., Science 2022, CC-BY 4.0.

In a recent development, as we described in Part I, protein design is the inverse of protein folding. Folding goes sequence to structure: given amino acids, predict the 3D shape. Inverse folding goes the other way: given a target 3D shape, find amino acid sequences that will fold into it.

Sources indicate that proteinMPNN, from David Baker's lab at the University of Washington, is the current gold standard for this task. It was published in Science in 2022 and has since been validated experimentally: designed sequences fold into their target structures at rates far exceeding random or earlier computational methods. The architecture treats the protein backbone as a graph, where nodes are amino acid positions and edges connect spatially proximate residues (K-nearest neighbors in 3D). A message-passing neural network propagates information through this graph, then autoregressively generates a sequence one residue at a time.

We ran ProteinMPNN on PDB structure 7K00 (a large multi-chain ribosomal complex):.

Here's what the output looks like:.

The first line is the native (natural) sequence extracted from the crystal structure. Subsequent lines are ProteinMPNN's designed variants. At temperature 0.1 (low randomness), the model recovers ~42% of the original amino acids, purely from 3D geometry. This is a strong result: it means the model independently rediscovered nearly half the residues that evolution selected, using only the backbone coordinates as input.

In a recent development, several practical notes from running ProteinMPNN. Scores are negative log-likelihoods, so lower is better. The 42% recovery rate is typical for well-resolved structures and consistent with the original paper's benchmarks. Higher sampling temperatures produce more diverse but riskier sequences. For real design work, the most powerful feature is partial design: catalytic residues, binding site amino acids, or any positions with known functional importance can be fixed in place, while ProteinMPNN redesigns only the scaffold around them. This is the standard approach for engineering a more stable version of an enzyme without disrupting its active site.

It has been revealed that this is where the pipeline transitions from existing tools to our own models. ESMFold and ProteinMPNN are established, well-validated software that we integrated. Codon optimization is where we built something upcoming.

Codon usage frequencies vary dramatically between organisms. These heatmaps compare codon preferences across E. coli, yeast, and CHO cells, the three expression hosts covered by our multi-species models. Figure from Kim et al., J. Microbiol. Biotechnol. 2025, CC-BY 4.0.

The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are encoded by multiple codons. Leucine, for example, has six: TTA, TTG, CTT, CTC, CTA, and CTG. All six produce the same amino acid in the final protein. Methionine and tryptophan are the exceptions, with only one codon each.

This redundancy means that for any given protein, there are astronomically many DNA sequences that encode it. A typical 300-amino-acid protein has roughly 10^150 possible codon combinations. They all produce the same amino acid chain, but they do not all produce the same amount of protein. Codon choice affects translation speed (because tRNA molecules are not equally abundant for all codons), mRNA stability (because the nucleotide sequence affects how swiftly the transcript degrades), co-translational folding (because translation pauses at rare codons give the protein time to fold), and immune recognition (because the innate immune system in mammalian cells can distinguish native from foreign mRNA patterns). In practice, bad codon choices can reduce protein expression by 100x. This is why every mRNA vaccine, every recombinant protein therapeutic, and every gene therapy vector goes through codon optimization.

In a recent development, the scale of the codon optimization problem. For a typical mRNA, there are over 10^600 possible codon sequences encoding the same protein. The challenge is finding the arrangement that maximizes expression. Figure from Zhang et al. (LinearDesign), Nature 2023, CC-BY 4.0.

The classical method is simple: measure which codons appear most frequently in highly-expressed genes of the target organism, then replace every codon with the most frequent synonym. This is codified as the Codon Adaptation Index (CAI), a per-sequence score that measures how closely the codon usage matches the organism's preferred distribution.

In a recent development, CAI-based optimization works, but it is crude. It treats each codon position independently, ignoring the sequence context. It produces repetitive sequences (the same "optimal" codon used everywhere for a given amino acid), which can cause ribosome stalling and mRNA secondary structure problems. And it misses complex dependencies: the optimal codon at position 50 might depend on what codons are at positions 48 and 52, which a frequency table cannot capture.

In a recent development, we reframe codon optimization as a language modeling problem. Instead of looking up frequencies in a table, we train a transformer on hundreds of thousands of natural coding sequences using masked language modeling (MLM), the same pre-training objective used by BERT, RoBERTa, and Meta's ESM protein models. The model sees a codon sequence with 15% of positions masked and learns to predict the missing codons from context.

Recent findings suggest that what the model learns, implicitly, is the grammar of codon usage: which codon patterns appear in nature, which codons tend to co-occur, and how preferences shift depending on the surrounding sequence context. This is fundamentally richer than a frequency table because the model captures long-range dependencies across the entire coding sequence.

After our architecture exploration (see above), CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 emerged as the winner:.

In a recent development, evaluating a codon language model is not straightforward. As we learned from the v1/v2 comparison above, a model can have excellent perplexity (accurately predicting masked codons) while having poor biological alignment (predicting codons that nature does not actually prefer). We evaluate on three complementary axes:.

According to recent reports, 1. Perplexity measures how well the model predicts masked codons, computed as the exponentiated cross-entropy loss. A perplexity of 4.10 means the model is, on average, choosing between ~4 equally likely codons at each masked position. Given that most amino acids have 2-6 synonymous codons, this indicates the model has learned meaningful preferences rather than guessing uniformly. Lower is better. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 4.10.

Industry observers note that 2. CAI Correlation (Spearman) measures whether a model's predicted codon likelihoods align with known biological codon usage preferences. We compute the Codon Adaptation Index for each test sequence, then correlate it with the model's pseudo-log-likelihood score. A positive correlation means the model assigns higher probability to sequences that biology actually uses. This is the metric that matters most for practical codon optimization, because it directly measures whether the model has learned biologically relevant patterns vs. just statistical ones. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 0.404 (p < 10^-20).

Sources indicate that 3. Synonymous Recovery asks: when the model predicts a codon for a masked position, does it at least get the amino acid right? Even if it picks the wrong synonym (e.g., CTT instead of CTC for leucine), predicting the correct amino acid demonstrates the model understands the protein-level constraint. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 12.1% top-1 synonymous.

Putting it all together across our model variants:.

According to recent reports, the RoBERTa family dominates across the board. For production use, CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 is the clear choice: it has the strongest biological alignment (CAI 0.404) while maintaining competitive perplexity. For teams with limited compute, CodonRoBERTa-base delivers nearly the same perplexity at 3.4x fewer parameters. ModernBERT underperformed substantially, which we attribute to its NLP-pretrained weights interfering with codon pattern learning.

Single-species codon optimization is useful, but limited. Every organism has its own codon usage biases shaped by millions of years of evolution. E. coli favors different codons than human cells, which favor different codons than yeast. A model trained only on E. coli data will not produce optimal codons for human expression.

The industry standard is to use separate CAI tables for each organism. We wanted something better: a single model that understands codon usage across organisms, can be conditioned on a target species, and can transfer knowledge from data-rich organisms (human, with 145k annotated coding sequences) to data-poor ones (E. coli, with 9k). After establishing CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 as our best architecture on single-species data, we built this system.

In a recent development, assembling a multi-species codon dataset is not as simple as downloading a few genomes. Each organism lives in a different NCBI RefSeq assembly, with different annotation quality, different CDS boundaries, and different sequence conventions. We wrote an automated pipeline that downloads CDS sequences from 25 organisms, validates them (checking for proper start/stop codons, length divisible by 3, no internal stops), labels each sequence with a species token, and splits into train/test sets with stratification by species.

The final dataset spans three domains of biotechnology relevance:.

In a recent development, the coverage is deliberate: bacteria are the workhorse of recombinant protein production, yeast dominates industrial biomanufacturing, and mammalian cells (especially CHO and human) are required for therapeutic proteins and mRNA vaccines. These 25 organisms collectively cover the vast majority of real-world codon optimization use cases.

A model that sees sequences from 25 different organisms needs to know which organism it is looking at. We solved this by extending our 69-token codon vocabulary with 25 species tokens, creating a 94-token system. Each sequence is prepended with its species token (e.g., [HUMAN], [ECOLI], [YEAST]), so the model learns species-specific codon preferences within a single shared architecture.

In a recent development, this design has three advantages. First, it enables species-conditioned generation: the same model produces human-optimal or E. coli-optimal codons depending on which species token is prepended. Second, it enables cross-species transfer learning: universal codon patterns (like avoiding certain dinucleotides, or preferring GC-rich codons in GC-rich genomes) are shared across all species, while species-specific preferences are captured by conditioning on the species token. Third, the 94-token vocabulary is backward-compatible with our 69-token single-species models, since the first 69 tokens are identical.

The universal base model is a 311.9M-parameter RoBERTa-large, identical in architecture to our single-species v2 but with the expanded 94-token vocabulary. It was trained for 48 hours on 4 A100 GPUs using the full 362k-sequence multispecies dataset.

The test perplexity of 24.9 is higher than our single-species model's 4.01, which might look like a regression. It is not. The multispecies model must learn distinct codon preferences for 25 different organisms, each with its own evolutionary history and tRNA pools. A bacterium like M. tuberculosis (65% GC content) uses completely different codons than human cells (41% GC). The model is solving a fundamentally harder problem, and the perplexity reflects that. What matters is whether species-specific fine-tuning can recover performance, and it does.

Recent findings suggest that the universal base model is a generalist. For production use, specialists perform better. OpenMed's fine-tuning strategy starts from the multispecies checkpoint and trains further on a single species at a lower learning rate (2e-5 vs 5e-5), preserving cross-species knowledge while specializing the model's predictions for one organism.

Training all three priority species:.

It has been revealed that the most key result here is the HUMAN model: at 24.3 perplexity, it is the only specialist that beats the universal base, making it our production model for therapeutic mRNA applications. But the ECOLI result is arguably more interesting from a research perspective. With only 8,547 training sequences (compared to 131k for human), the E. coli specialist still improved over the multispecies base. This validates the transfer learning hypothesis: training on 25 species first, then fine-tuning on a small species-specific dataset, works better than training on the small dataset alone. For the many organisms where annotated CDS data is scarce, this approach opens the door to reasonable codon optimization without needing tens of thousands of species-specific sequences.

The CHO model showed slight degradation (25.5 vs 24.9), which we attribute to insufficient training steps. ECOLI got 5,000 steps for 8.5k sequences (0.59 steps per sequence), while CHO got 10,000 steps for 42.5k sequences (0.24 steps per sequence). A rerun with 15,000 steps should close this gap. All three specialists fine-tuned in just 7 hours total, leveraging the 48-hour investment in the multispecies base.

After 55 hours of training, we have:.

For therapeutic mRNA (Moderna, BioNTech-style vaccines):.

For industrial protein production:.

According to recent reports, the multi-species suite covers the three pillars of applied codon optimization. For therapeutic mRNA, the HUMAN specialist model optimizes codons for expression in human cells, directly applicable to vaccine design (Moderna and BioNTech both codon-optimize their mRNA constructs) and gene therapy vectors. For recombinant protein production, the ECOLI specialist handles the most common bacterial expression host, while the CHO specialist covers the mammalian cell line used to produce most monoclonal antibodies and biopharmaceuticals. For organisms not covered by a specialist, the multispecies base model accepts any of the 25 species tokens and generates organism-appropriate codons.

According to recent reports, the transfer learning result is particularly relevant for the broader community. Many industrially important organisms (non-model bacteria, insect cells, plant cells) have limited annotated CDS data. Our results with E. coli (8.5k sequences, improved over base) suggest that multispecies pre-training followed by small-scale fine-tuning is a viable path for these organisms, without requiring the tens or hundreds of thousands of sequences that training from scratch demands.

According to recent reports, the full project consumed 55 GPU-hours on 4 A100 80GB GPUs (~$165 at AWS spot pricing), produced ~150 GB of models and checkpoints across 4 training runs, and covers 381,283 CDS sequences from 25 species downloaded from NCBI RefSeq. All models use the same 311.9M-parameter architecture, are saved in safetensors format for fast loading, and run inference on a single GPU with 16GB+ VRAM. Everything is released under Apache 2.0.

The modern computational protein design workflow. Structure generation (top) produces backbone coordinates; sequence optimization (bottom) finds amino acid sequences that fold into the target shape. Our pipeline adds a third step: codon optimization for expression. Figure from Kortemme, Cell 2024, CC-BY 4.0.

It has been revealed that in Part I, we described the protein engineering loop as a cycle of prediction, design, and optimization. Here is what that looks like in practice with OpenMed's pipeline. Each step feeds into the next, and the entire computational phase runs in an afternoon on a single GPU.

Consider a concrete scenario: engineering a more stable version of a therapeutic enzyme that degrades too quickly in the bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that step 1: Fold (ESMFold). Predict the structure of the starting sequence to understand its active site and identify regions that might be destabilized. ESMFold returns a 3D structure in PDB format, per-residue confidence scores (pLDDT) highlighting uncertain regions, and an overall topology confidence metric (PTM).

In a recent development, step 2: Design (ProteinMPNN). Keep the active site fixed but redesign the scaffold for improved stability. ProteinMPNN takes the backbone coordinates, a list of immutable positions (catalytic residues), and generates 100 diverse candidate sequences, each predicted to fold into the target shape.

It has been revealed that step 3: Verify (ESMFold). Refold all 100 candidates with ESMFold to confirm they still adopt the correct shape. Filter for high mean pLDDT (>80), correct topology (RMSD to original), and low clash scores.

Step 4: Optimize (CodonRoBERTa). Take the best amino acid sequences and use CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 to generate optimal DNA sequences for expression in the target organism (E. coli, yeast, or mammalian cells). The model scores synonymous codon choices based on learned biological preferences, identifies contextually optimal codons rather than just globally frequent ones, and produces sequences with high CAI correlation.

Recent findings suggest that step 5: Synthesize and Test. Order the DNA from a synthesis company, clone it into an expression vector, and test expression and activity in the lab.

This loop, from hypothesis to synthesis-ready DNA, replaces what once took months of iterative wet-lab trial and error. A researcher arrives at the bench with 5-10 computationally vetted candidates instead of one or two educated guesses. The success rate improves, the cost drops, and the design cycle compresses from months to days.

For a full ecosystem overview, tool selection guide, and license reference, see Part I.

OpenMed is not working in isolation. Two recent models push the codon/mRNA modeling frontier further:.

In a recent development, mRNABERT (Xiong et al., Nature Communications 2025): 86M-param BERT with a dual tokenization scheme (single nucleotides for UTRs, codons for CDS) and cross-modality contrastive learning against frozen ProtT5-XL protein embeddings. Trained on 18M sequences. Achieves R^2 = 0.66 on full-length mRNA translation efficiency, a 1.6-10x improvement over prior RNA models. Code and weights available (Apache 2.0).

NUWA (Zhong et al., bioRxiv 2026): Three domain-specific RoBERTa encoders (Bacteria, Eukaryota, Archaea) with curriculum MLM and supervised contrastive learning. Trained on 115M sequences across ~25,000 species. Beats CodonBERT on 11/13 BEACON benchmark tasks. No code or weights released.

Sources indicate that both models train on 50-300x more data than OpenMed used. That is the primary gap, and we are transparent about it.

Here is what OpenMed does that neither of them offers:.

In a recent development, species-conditioned single model. mRNABERT has no species conditioning at all. NUWA trains three separate models (one per domain of life). We put 25 species tokens into one 94-token vocabulary and train a single model that can be prompted for any organism. More parameter-efficient, more flexible.

According to recent reports, transfer learning to low-resource organisms, validated. We showed that fine-tuning the multispecies base on just 8.5k E. coli sequences improves over the base model. Neither mRNABERT nor NUWA demonstrates this.

Full open-source pipeline. ESMFold + ProteinMPNN + CodonRoBERTa, end to end, with training code, configs, eval scripts, and model weights. All Apache 2.0. mRNABERT releases code but not the pipeline. NUWA releases nothing.

OpenMed is running a proof-of-concept for a fundamentally different approach: Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for codon sequences.

According to recent reports, standard MLM predicts masked tokens. JEPA predicts masked embeddings. The hypothesis: if the model is forced to predict in embedding space rather than token space, it should learn that synonymous codons (different DNA, same amino acid) are functionally equivalent. MLM cannot achieve this because it is trained to distinguish every token.

According to recent reports, early results from our evaluation suite (JEPA vs. MLM baseline, same data, same hyperparameters, 15k steps each):.

Industry observers note that the synonymous robustness result is the one that matters most for our hypothesis. JEPA embeddings are nearly identical (99.97% cosine similarity) for sequences that differ only in synonymous codon choices. MLM embeddings shift significantly (94.14%). This means JEPA does learn that synonymous codons are interchangeable, exactly as predicted.

The open challenge: JEPA right now suffers from dimensional collapse (91.78% of variance concentrated in one component). This is a known failure mode for self-supervised methods and suggests the VICReg regularization weights need tuning. The architecture works; the training dynamics need more iteration.

It has been revealed that this is early-stage research, not production-ready. But if the collapse problem can be solved, JEPA could produce codon embeddings that are inherently amino-acid-aware, something that MLM, by its token-level prediction objective, fundamentally cannot achieve.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A 3D model that looks smooth in a desktop modeling application can become a very different experience inside a web page. The browser must download the asset, decode its geometry and textures, upload resources to the GPU, compile materials and render the scene while the rest of the page stays responsive.

In a recent development, consider an ecommerce team adding a rotatable chair model to a product page. The asset works well on a developer's laptop, but the first mobile test highlights a long blank interval, a sharp increase in memory use and uneven rotation. The problem is not necessarily the JavaScript viewer. The model itself may contain more data than the page can comfortably deliver.

A preflight process catches these problems before the asset is connected to production code. This checklist walks through it, and includes a small, tested script that audits a GLB file against a budget. Tool details change, so check each project's documentation for current behavior.

For the chair, rotation may help shoppers inspect the rear frame, arm shape and the relationship between the seat and legs. That is a clear use. Adding the same model as a moving background behind the product description would add download and rendering costs without equivalent value.

Define the purpose before setting a performance budget. A featured product viewer may justify more detail than a small decorative object. The decision also affects whether the model should load immediately, wait until the user scrolls near it or appear only after someone selects "View in 3D.".

Editable authoring files often contain information a browser does not need, so web delivery should use an asset prepared for runtime rather than the original scene from a modeling application.

The Khronos glTF specification describes glTF as a format designed for efficient transmission and loading of 3D scenes and models. A .gltf asset can reference separate buffers and images, while a binary .glb file can package the scene and its resources into one file.

GLB is convenient when a team wants a single deployable asset, but a single container does not guarantee a small payload. Large textures, dense geometry, unused animations and unnecessary scene objects can still make the file expensive. Document the format decision along with supported materials, texture limits, coordinate conventions and animation requirements.

Before debugging React components, shaders or loading logic, confirm that the file itself behaves as expected. Several free viewers can open a model in the browser for a quick visual check:.

It has been revealed that whichever you use, rotate the chair, zoom in and inspect it from above, below and behind. This check can reveal obvious problems:.

In a recent development, A viewer is useful for visual inspection, but it is not a performance profiler or automatic repair tool. A model can display correctly while still being too heavy for the intended page. Viewers also differ in lighting and material handling, so confirm the final look in your own renderer.

Recent findings suggest that open the model in an appropriate inspection or editing tool and review what it contains. A product model should not carry unused lights, cameras, hidden prototypes, duplicate meshes or animation clips left over from production. These elements can increase file size, complicate traversal or create confusing behavior after import.

Check the object hierarchy as well. Hundreds of separately transformed parts can increase CPU work and draw-call overhead even if the total polygon count looks reasonable. At the same time, combining every surface into one mesh can make material changes or interaction difficult. If owners can change the chair's upholstery and frame independently, those areas need useful separation. Decorative components that never change may not.

Sources indicate that triangle count matters, but it is only one part of the cost. A model with moderate geometry and several large uncompressed textures may use more memory than a denser mesh with efficient textures. Transparent materials, multiple lights, shadows and many separate materials can also affect rendering performance.

Establish budgets by device class and use case rather than copying one universal limit. A hero asset viewed full-screen has different requirements from twelve models displayed in a product grid.

Several of those numbers can be read straight from the file. The Node.js script below reads a GLB's JSON chunk, counts triangles, meshes, primitives, materials, textures, images, animations and cameras, and compares them with a budget. It has no dependencies and runs on current Node.js versions.

The test builds a small GLB in memory, confirms the triangle count (a line primitive is ignored), and checks that a too-low triangle budget, a stray camera and an unwanted animation are all flagged:.

Run the test with node test_glb_budget.mjs, and audit a real file with node glb_budget.mjs chair.glb.

Textures often account for much of a 3D asset's download and memory footprint. Inspect every map and ask whether its resolution matches the size at which the surface will actually appear. A 4K texture may be wasteful if the chair occupies only a few hundred pixels on a phone. Multiple surfaces may be able to share a smaller atlas, and detail that is never visible can be removed.

Do not lower every texture to the same resolution automatically. The seat fabric may need more detail than the underside of the frame. Test reductions on the real page at normal viewing distances.

Material count also deserves attention. A separate material can produce another rendering operation even when it differs only slightly from another surface. Consolidate materials where doing so does not remove required customization.

It has been revealed that A product page should not delay its primary text, price, photographs and purchase controls while downloading a below-the-fold 3D asset. Use an explicit interaction or an IntersectionObserver to begin loading when the viewer approaches the viewport. A simplified pattern looks like this:.

The positive margin starts the request shortly before the viewer becomes visible. The appropriate value depends on page layout, model size and expected network speed. Display a meaningful poster image while loading, so the page stays useful if the asset fails, WebGL is unavailable or the user prefers not to spend bandwidth on the interactive view.

In a recent development, using the device's full pixel ratio can make a canvas unnecessarily expensive on high-density screens. Cap the rendering resolution and evaluate the visual difference on actual devices. Shadows, environment maps, antialiasing and post-processing should also be treated as adjustable costs. A desktop may use the complete presentation, while a lower-powered phone receives simpler lighting and reduced texture resolution.

Recent findings suggest that avoid guessing from a user-agent string. Where possible, choose conservative defaults, observe runtime performance and let the experience degrade gracefully. Pause rendering when the viewer is outside the viewport or the browser tab is hidden, since a product model does not need to consume GPU time while the customer reads specifications farther down the page.

Sources indicate that A model that performs well in isolation may struggle when combined with analytics scripts, image carousels, embedded video and the rest of the production page. Test on real phones, not only through desktop emulation, and include a mid-range device and a throttled network. Measure the time until the poster appears, the time until the model becomes interactive, frame consistency during rotation, and whether the page stays responsive during decoding.

Use browser performance and network tools to separate bottlenecks. A slow download suggests a payload problem. A long main-thread task may point to parsing or scene initialization. Low frame rates after loading may indicate excessive draw calls, shader cost, overdraw or high rendering resolution. Repeat the test after each significant optimization, because a smaller file is useful only if the model still communicates the product accurately.

Interactive content should enhance the product page rather than become its only usable representation. Provide well-composed images, descriptive product text and accessible controls alongside the viewer. Keyboard customers should be able to reach and operate relevant controls, while motion should not begin unexpectedly or continue without purpose. If the 3D experience fails, the customer should still be able to understand the chair and complete the intended task.

It has been revealed that GLB packages everything in one file, which is convenient to deploy. Separate .gltf files let you cache buffers and images independently. Neither guarantees a small payload.

No. A viewer confirms how a model looks, not how it performs. Measure size, textures, draw calls and load time in the real page.

There is no universal number. Set budgets by device class and by how prominent the model is on the page, then test on a mid-range phone.

According to recent reports, shipping 3D on the web is ultimately a delivery problem. The model, textures, loading strategy, renderer, device and surrounding page all contribute to the result. A disciplined preflight process prevents teams from treating a successful desktop preview as proof of production readiness, and gives customers the benefits of interactive 3D without making the rest of the page pay an unreasonable price.

Soaring Eagle Gaming has a newly introduced technology partner in Michigan. The Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe’s online casino and online sports betting operations now run on White Hat Gaming Inc.’s platform. White Hat replaces GAN, which had powered the tribe’s Michigan offer since launch. That launch came under the Eagle Casino and Sports brand.

According to recent reports, platform swaps like this are rare in Michigan. Players keep the same Soaring Eagle brand.

The board reviewed the White Hat platform and the tribe’s branding submission before signing off. The tribe also filed a signed agreement with White Hat. Every supplier and vendor needed for launch had already been approved. Both companies must also fully adopt all internal control amendments the board has approved.

According to recent reports, the board’s list of authorized platform providers now names White Hat as the tribe’s provider for online casino and online sports betting. The tribe already had a content tie to White Hat Studios, the games supplier. In June 2022, White Hat Studios declared it would supply branded games, including Ted, Deal or No Deal and Peaky Blinders, to the tribe’s PlayEagle.com site.

In a recent development, the stakes in Michigan remain sizable. Operators reported $355.7 million in combined online casino and online sports betting gross receipts for September 2026, up 5.4% from August. Online casino accounted for $300.2 million and sports betting for $55.5 million. Adjusted gross receipts came to $313.04 million. Online casino adjusted receipts, however, fell 0.9% from August. The switch comes as GAN works through changes under latest ownership. The program will also move GAN ahead with migrating to a new platform. Adding GAN and Stakelogic raised group sales. It also widened the operating loss compared with the same period a year earlier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities.

Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”.

Industry observers note that the two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different organization” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”.

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”.

HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a major difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure manufacturer.

Clarke mentioned he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

In a recent development, dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”.

“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”.

HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the tech giant’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO remarked HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

In a recent development, dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®.
