💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding.
  • The model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines.
  • Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding. It’s purpose-built for reliable information extraction from complex documents, forms, and structured visuals. Granite 4.0 3B Vision excels on the following capabilities:.

The model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines. It continues to support vision-language tasks such as producing detailed natural-language descriptions from images (e.g., “Describe this image in detail”). The model can be used standalone or in tandem with Docling to enhance document processing pipelines with deep visual understanding capabilities.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.

In a recent development, charts present a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs) because understanding them requires jointly reasoning over visual patterns, numerical data, and natural language, a combination most VLMs cannot handle well, especially when spatial precision matters—such as reading exact values off a line chart. To close this gap, we’ve developed ChartNet: a million-scale multimodal dataset purpose-built for chart interpretation and reasoning, described in detail in our upcoming CVPR 2026 paper.

In a recent development, chartNet uses a code-guided synthesis pipeline to generate 1.7 million diverse chart samples spanning 24 chart types and 6 plotting libraries [see Figure 1]. What makes it so distinctive is that each sample consists of five aligned components—plotting code, rendered image, data table, natural language summary, and QA pairs—providing models a deeply cross-modal view of what a chart means, not just what it looks like. The dataset also includes human-annotated and real-world subsets, filtered for visual fidelity, semantic accuracy, and diversity.

The result is a training resource that moves VLMs from merely describing charts to genuinely understanding the structured information they encode—with consistent gains across model sizes, architectures, and tasks.

Figure 1: ChartNet’s synthetic data generation pipeline.

Most VLMs inject visual information into their language model at a single point, which forces the model to handle both high-level semantics and fine-grained spatial detail simultaneously. Granite 4.0 3B Vision takes a different approach with DeepStack Injection: abstract visual features are routed into earlier layers for semantic understanding, while high-resolution spatial features are fed into later layers to preserve detail. The result is a model that understands both what is in a document and where—which is critical for tasks like table extraction, chart understanding, and KVP parsing where layout matters as much as content. For a full technical breakdown, see the Model Architecture section of the model card.

Recent findings suggest that granite 4.0 3B Vision is packaged as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, rather than as a standalone model. In practice, this means the same deployment can serve both multimodal and text-only workloads, automatically falling back to the base model when vision isn’t required. This keeps enterprise integration straightforward without sacrificing performance.

Charts: Evaluated on the human-verified ChartNet benchmark using LLM-as-a-judge, Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the highest Chart2Summary (86.4%) score among all evaluated models, including significantly larger ones [see Figure 2]. It also ranks second on Chart2CSV (62.1%), behind only Qwen3.5-9B (63.4%), a model more than double its size.

Figure 2: Granite 4.0 3B Vision performance on chart2csv and chart2summary, compared against peer vision-language models using LLM-as-a-judge.

Tables: We evaluate table extraction in two settings: cropped tables (isolated regions) and full-page documents (tables embedded in complex layouts) [see Figure 3]. The benchmark suite includes TableVQA-extract (cropped table images), OmniDocBench-tables (full-page documents), and PubTables-v2 (both cropped and full-page settings). Models are tasked with extracting tables in HTML format and scored using TEDS, a metric that captures both structural and content accuracy. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the strongest performance across benchmarks, leading on PubTablesV2 on both cropped (92.1) and full-page (79.3), OmniDocBench (64.0), and TableVQA (88.1) scores among all evaluated models.

Figure 3: Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s table extraction performance across cropped and full-page benchmarks (TableVQA-extract, PubTables-v2, OmniDocBench-tables), measured by TEDS.

It has been revealed that semantic KVP: VAREX is a benchmark specifically designed to discriminate between small extraction models, comprising 1,777 U.S. government forms spanning simple flat layouts to complex nested and tabular structures. Models are evaluated using exact match (EM), a strict metric that requires the model’s extracted key-value pairs to match the ground truth. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves 85.5% EM accuracy zero-shot.

In a recent development, granite 4.0 3B Vision can operate either as a stand‑alone visual information extraction engine or as part of a fully automated document‑processing pipeline with Docling. The model is designed to support scalable, accurate extraction across diverse document types and visual formats.

Industry observers note that 1. Stand‑Alone Image Understanding Granite 4.0 3B Vision can run directly on individual images, making this option useful for applications with existing workflows that need targeted visual extraction without modifying upstream systems. This offers easy integration into existing automation workflows and is suitable for lightweight, task‑specific tools (e.g., form parsers, chart analyzers, etc.).

Recent findings suggest that 2. Integrated Document Understanding Pipeline With Docling Granite 4.0 3B Vision can also be integrated seamlessly with Docling to support complete end‑to‑end document understanding. This mode can offer:.

Industry observers note that granite 4.0 3B Vision is available now on HuggingFace, released under the Apache 2.0 license. Full technical details, training methodology, and benchmark results are available in the model card. We’d love to hear what you build with it—share your feedback in the community tab.

Rajiv Ramaswami will stay in the chair until new hire lands, then stick around as advisor.

Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the firm’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

Recent findings suggest that in chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew.

According to recent reports, the CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.

Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole fresh set of ecosystems.”.

It has been revealed that ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO mentioned the manufacturer's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”.

According to recent reports, news of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix revealed its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The firm added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami remarked high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the tech giant’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®.

Industry News: Any Custom Frontend with Gradio's Backend

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few weeks ago, we wrote about one-shotting full web apps with gr.HTML: building rich, interactive frontends entirely inside Gradio using custom HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • What if you want to build with your own frontend framework entirely like React, Svelte, or even plain HTML/JS, while still benefiting from Gradio's queuing system, API infrastructure, MCP support, and ZeroGPU on Spaces?
  • It has been revealed that that's exactly the problem gradio.Server solves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few weeks ago, we wrote about one-shotting full web apps with gr.HTML: building rich, interactive frontends entirely inside Gradio using custom HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. That unlocked a lot. But what if that's not enough?

What if you want to build with your own frontend framework entirely like React, Svelte, or even plain HTML/JS, while still benefiting from Gradio's queuing system, API infrastructure, MCP support, and ZeroGPU on Spaces?

It has been revealed that that's exactly the problem gradio.Server solves. And it changes what's possible with Gradio and Hugging Face Spaces.

Text Behind Image : an editor where you upload a photo, the background gets removed using an ML model, and then you place stylized text between the foreground subject and the background. The text appears to sit behind the person or object in the image.

In a recent development, there's no way to express this UI in Gradio components. It's a full web application. But We still wanted the backend power of Gradio: queuing, concurrency management, ZeroGPU support, and hosting on HF Spaces without infrastructure headaches.

gradio.Server extends FastAPI. It gives you the full power of FastAPI (custom routes, middleware, file uploads, any response type) while adding Gradio's API engine on top: queuing, SSE streaming, concurrency control, and gradio_client compatibility.

Here's the entire backend for Text Behind Image:.

That's it. ~50 lines of Python. The model loads at startup, @spaces.GPU handles ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio.Server manages queuing and concurrency. Let's break down what's happening.

If this were a regular FastAPI app, you'd define a @app.post() route for background removal. That works, until two users hit it at once. Without concurrency management, both requests fight for the GPU, and the app crashes or returns garbage.

Recent findings suggest that @app.api() solves this. It wraps your function with Gradio's queuing engine: requests are serialized, concurrency is controlled, and on ZeroGPU Spaces, GPU allocation is handled automatically via @spaces.GPU. As a bonus, any @app.api() endpoint is also callable via gradio_client, so other apps or scripts can use your Space programmatically:.

In a recent development, meanwhile, @app.get("/") is a standard FastAPI route that serves the HTML page. Both coexist naturally because Server is a FastAPI app.

The index.html in this example is a self-contained ~1300-line web application. No React, no build step, no bundler. Just vanilla HTML with:.

The frontend talks to the backend using the Gradio JS Client:.

This is the key part: by using the Gradio JS client rather than a raw fetch() call, the frontend goes through Gradio's queue. That means concurrency is managed, GPU requests don't collide, and you could even show queue position or progress to the user. Everything else, text rendering, layer compositing, export, happens in the browser.

Here's what was not possible before gradio.Server:.

With gradio.Server, Gradio doubles as a backend framework, use its UI system when you want it, bring your own frontend when you don't.

If you want Gradio's UI, you can use gr.Blocks, gr.Interface, gr.ChatInterface. If you want your own UI, use gradio.Server and bring whatever frontend you like. Either way, you get Spaces hosting, API queuing, gradio_client access, the full HF ecosystem, and more.

The app is live on Spaces: ysharma/text-behind-image.

Upload any photo with a clear subject, and start layering text behind it. Try the 3D extrusion, perspective tilt, and stroke effects, they combine nicely.

Sources indicate that this post covered the core idea: gradio.Server lets you pair any frontend with Gradio's backend. There's more to explore, including MCP tool registration with @app.mcp.tool(), SSE streaming for real-time updates, batch processing, and patterns for building multi-page apps with shared state.

In a recent development, we'll dig into those in a follow-up post. Stay tuned.

The beauty of CSS mixins

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Patrickbrosset

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I've been playing with CSS mixins recently, and I'm super excited about what this fresh CSS construct will bring to the way we write CSS.
  • Recent findings suggest that in its simplest form, a mixin is a named piece of CSS code that you define once and can reuse elsewhere in a style sheet.
  • So, instead of just returning the value red, a mixin can return background: red; color: white; border-radius: 2px; all at once.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I've been playing with CSS mixins recently, and I'm super excited about what this fresh CSS construct will bring to the way we write CSS. I think the CSS we'll write when CSS mixins are available will look very different from the CSS we write today.

Recent findings suggest that in its simplest form, a mixin is a named piece of CSS code that you define once and can reuse elsewhere in a style sheet. In that sense, it's very similar to a custom property (also known as a CSS variable) or a CSS function.

The big difference is what mixins can hold:.

So, instead of just returning the value red, a mixin can return background: red; color: white; border-radius: 2px; all at once.

My team at Microsoft is implementing mixins in the Chromium open source project. They've covered a lot of ground, and we're getting ready to ship this in Chromium-based browsers. Native CSS mixins are getting very close!

I can't wait for other browsers to catch up, so that we can all use mixins in earnest.

Recent findings suggest that CSS mixins are experimental. To try the code snippets and demo in this article, use a recent Chromium browser, open about://flags, and enable the Experimental Web Platform features flag.

Sources indicate that you define a mixin with the @mixin rule, and you use it with @apply. Mixin names start with two dashes, like custom properties.

Let's define the --visually-hidden mixin:.

And now, let's use it somewhere else in our code:.

That's all you need to do. The browser will apply the mixin's declarations to the element as if they were written directly in the element's style block, so it's exactly as if you had written:.

Except now, you have a nice little reusable mixin that you can apply wherever you need it.

That's not all, a mixin can take parameters, with optional types and default values too. Consider this --button mixin:.

It applies some colors and spacing to a button-like element, checking that the supplied colors have the right type and falling back to default values if needed. It even handles hover states automatically.

You can use this mixin either with its default values or by passing your own arguments:.

If you pass more arguments than the mixin has parameters, the @apply does nothing.

A mixin can also hold conditional rules, such as @media, @supports and @container.

For example, you can create a mixin that applies styles conditionally to the viewport size:.

Recent findings suggest that this becomes even more powerful when combined with @contents. See the next section.

Arguments are not the only way to customize a mixin. A mixin can also accept an entire block of CSS from the call site. Inside the mixin, @contents marks the spot where that block goes.

For example, here's a --card mixin that defines a couple of declarations and accepts a block of CSS from where the mixin is used:.

When calling the mixin, you can pass other declarations inside a block, which will be inserted at the @contents location within the mixin:.

Here, .note gets the padding and border from the mixin, and then its own background, in the place where @contents appears.

Recent findings suggest that @contents can have a fallback, which applies when the caller passes no block: @contents { background: white; }. If the caller passes an empty block, @apply --card {}, the fallback does not apply.

According to recent reports, the ability to provide your own block of styles when applying a mixin is very useful, for example when using a mixin as a condition. Consider this mixin:.

You can use it to define styles that only apply in dark mode, while keeping the rest of your CSS unaffected. For example:.

Conditional mixins combined with @contents gives us something we've been wanting for a long time: named breakpoints:.

These mixins don't apply any styles of their own, they just conditionally apply styles that are given to them depending on the media query. This is great because we now have a way to give custom names to a series of responsive design breakpoints that can be maintained in one place.

Let's use them here to see how clean our responsive design code can be:.

In a recent development, finally, a mixin can keep private variables to itself, by declaring them in an @private block. The element that applies the mixin can't see these variables:.

Sources indicate that mixins are very versatile. You will find many ways to use them, and I don't think there will be one good way and one bad way to use them. Different teams will work out what works for them.

Sources indicate that in this section, I explored one way in which mixins might be used. I don't know if it will make sense in a real project yet, but I found it interesting to try.

Imagine a white-label website. You own the site and control its markup and default CSS. But you also want your customers to be able to theme the site to match their brand.

In your style sheet, you'd apply mixins like this:.

And your customer could define the mixins something like this:.

Recent findings suggest that you might remember the CSS Zen Garden. It had one HTML page, and anyone could submit a new design by writing a new style sheet for it. It highlighted the power of clean, semantic HTML, with styles, layouts and animations in a separate file. The designs were wildly different from one another and extremely creative.

Industry observers note that but there's a problem when you do this for customers. You expose your entire markup and it becomes a public API. Customers start writing very specific selectors that depend on how your HTML is organized, and you can't change that HTML any more without breaking their customizations. I've done this at a previous job, and I know how painful this can be.

The other option is to expose CSS variables. You keep control of your entire HTML and CSS, and only expose a set of customization variables that are used throughout your code. For example, you define a set of color palette variables, a set of spacing variables, typography variables, etc.

Customers override values only, which is very safe, but can also be limiting. What if they later ask you to have access to the page layout? You now need to expose more variables and make sure they continue working correctly.

Recent findings suggest that mixins sit somewhere in between. You remain in control of your HTML and can change it whenever you want. You expose logically named mixins that correspond to the various areas and surfaces of your page.

As long as you keep applying the same mixins in the right places, customizations continue to work.

But you can also go much further than variables. Each mixin is an entry point where a customer can add any declarations, pseudo-elements, media queries and animations.

I built a small demo, heavily inspired by the CSS Zen Garden, to test this: the Mixin Zen Garden (this will only work with a browser that supports CSS mixins).

Recent findings suggest that it's a simple webpage that has static HTML. The HTML never changes, but you can view the page with different designs that all use CSS mixins as described above:.

(If you write your own design, please share by opening an problem on my repo.).

Here are some things I learned while building it:.

Mixins that do nothing are fine.

A design doesn't need to define every mixin. This makes small designs very short.

One mixin per logical area of the page is more than enough.

A design can put colors, spacing, typography, and decorations in the same mixin.

Choose a mixin by what the role of the element is, such as --sidebar-heading, not by how it should look or what it at the moment is. Every design can decide what that role looks like, and you can change the HTML structure without changing the mixin names.

Well, I've remarked this already, but it bears repeating: mixins are experimental.

They work in Chromium only, behind a flag.

Nested selectors can reach into your markup again.

It has been revealed that A custom design can define a nested selector in a mixin to reach into the HTML markup. For example: @mixin --masthead { & h2 { ... }}.

According to recent reports, doing this exposes your HTML markup again, making it part of the API contract, which we wanted to avoid. Now, if this were to become a real customization mechanism, we could validate custom designs to ensure they only use allowed selectors within mixins.

Sources indicate that theming is only one use of mixins. Other ideas I want to try:.

CSS mixins might change the way we write and organize CSS pretty profoundly. I'm looking forward to seeing what you build with them. If you try the demo, or experiment with mixins on your own projects, let me know!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter.

VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 challenges.

VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the newly introduced advisory includes the following remarks:.

Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs.

This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

Sources indicate that two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

In a recent development, the other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that owners can turn off.

Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

It has been revealed that there’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

According to recent reports, in past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®.

Falcon Perception

📅 01 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts.
  • We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.
  • This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts. The model processes image patches + text in one sequence using a hybrid attention mask, and produces variable numbers of instances with a small, structured token interface and lightweight output heads. On SA-Co, Falcon Perception reaches 68.0 Macro-F1 (vs. 62.3 for SAM 3) with the main remaining gap being presence calibration (MCC 0.64 vs. 0.82). We also introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that breaks down performance by capability (attributes, OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relations) and by dense long-context crowded scenes.

We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.

This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.

According to recent reports, many open-vocabulary perception systems are built as modular pipelines: a (often frozen) vision backbone extracts features, a separate fusion/decoder stage combines them with language, and additional components handle matching and post-processing. This family of designs works well in many settings, but it comes with trade-offs: it can be hard to scale cleanly, hard to attribute improvements to the right component, and easy to accumulate complexity as we add a newly introduced fix for each failure mode.

We asked a simpler question: can a single early-fusion Transformer backbone handle both perception and language modeling, if we choose the right attention pattern, output interface, and training signal?

Industry observers note that in our experiments, the answer is largely yes. The rest of this post describes the main design choices and the evidence behind them.

Recent findings suggest that A single autoregressive Transformer processes a unified sequence of image patches, text, and task tokens. The model predicts object properties in a fixed order: → → . Bounding box coordinates and sizes are decoded via specialized heads and re-injected as Fourier features. High-resolution segmentation masks are generated by a dot product between the token and upsampled image features.

At its core, Falcon Perception is a dense Transformer that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space from the first layer. Instead of a separate vision backbone followed by a late-fusion decoder, we keep a single backbone and rely on masking and a lightweight output interface to make the dense prediction problem tractable.

Sources indicate that images and text have different structure: pixels are 2D and benefit from bidirectional context, while the prediction interface is naturally sequential. We address this with a hybrid attention mask:.

This allows the same backbone to behave like a bidirectional visual encoder on image tokens, while still supporting autoregressive prediction over task tokens.

According to recent reports, dense perception is not a fixed-size prediction problem: an image may contain zero instances or hundreds. Autoregressive generation gives a clean variable-length interface, but fully autoregressive dense generation (e.g., polygons or high-resolution masks token-by-token) rapidly becomes expensive.

We use a small structured interface, Chain-of-Perception, which decomposes each instance into three steps:.

Sources indicate that this ordering is deliberate. Committing to geometry first reduces ambiguity (“which instance?”), and makes the mask prediction step closer to pixel refinement conditioned on the resolved object.

The backbone is shared, while decoding uses lightweight heads tailored to the output type:.

Coordinate & Size Heads use Fourier feature encoding : mapping continuous coordinates through a random Gaussian projection into a high-dimensional sinusoidal space. This overcomes the spectral bias of neural networks, yielding more precise localization than discrete binning alone. Decoded coordinates are re-injected into the sequence as conditioning for subsequent tokens.

According to recent reports, segmentation Head computes a dot product between the token’s hidden state and content-aware upsampled image features. Because the token is produced after geometry and has access to early-fused visual context, we can avoid the separate mask-query machinery and Hungarian matching that often appears in decoder-based instance segmentation training.

Industry observers note that existing referring-expression benchmarks like RefCOCO are saturated — models routinely hit 90%+ — and they conflate what went wrong. Did the model fail because it can't read text? Can't understand spatial relationships? Can't handle a crowd?

We introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that separates samples by the dominant capability required:.

According to recent reports, each sample targets one dominant capability: OCR prompts avoid spatial qualifiers, and spatial prompts avoid in-image text disambiguators. This yields a capability profile rather than a single opaque score, and makes it easier to decide where to invest next (data, training curriculum, or post-training).

According to recent reports, rather than training from random weights (which in our ablations was unstable for segmentation), Falcon Perception initializes via multi-teacher distillation. Two strong vision teachers contribute complementary signals:.

The distilled initialization achieves 74.25% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1k and 85.11% linear-probe mIoU on Pascal VOC, providing a strong visual foundation before perception-specific training.

We build the training set through a multi-stage pipeline:.

We maintain a strict 1:1 ratio of positive to negative samples. This makes presence calibration a first-class target: the model should reliably say “absent,” not only draw masks when confident.

Stage 1 — In-Context Listing (450 GT): The model learns to autoregressively list scene inventories — predicting text expressions and their locations. Full causal attention between queries enables learning of object co-occurrence ("fork, then knife, then plate"). This builds broad scene understanding.

Sources indicate that stage 2 — Task Alignment (225 GT): The attention mask is modified so queries can no longer see each other, simulating independent queries at inference time. Loss on text tokens is masked, focusing gradient signal entirely on presence classification and localization. This stage transitions from "scene understanding" to "answer this specific question.".

Stage 3 — Long-Context Finetuning (10 GT): A short phase with the mask limit raised to 600 per expression and a minimal constant learning rate. This adapts the model for extreme crowd density without forgetting earlier capabilities.

Key design choices validated through ablations:.

On the SA-Co open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark, Falcon Perception (0.6B parameters) achieves 68.0 Macro-F1, compared to 62.3 for SAM 3, with large gains on attribute-heavy (+8.2), food & drink (+12.2), and sports equipment (+4.0) splits. At the same time, Falcon Perception lags SAM 3 on presence calibration (MCC: 0.64 vs 0.82), which is the clearest remaining improvement axis.

Here's an example output — the prompt "Falcon" produces precise instance masks:.

Falcon Perception also performs well for reffering expressions, able to correctly segment the burger with a black bun in each frame of the video:.

This is where the early-fusion design shows the largest differences:.

It has been revealed that on simple objects, the gap is modest. As prompts become more compositional—requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, or relational binding—the gap widens.

In our PBench Dense split, Falcon Perception (0.6B) substantially outperforms generalist VLM baselines (e.g., 72.6 vs 8.9 for Qwen3-VL-30B in our evaluation setup), and matches or exceeds the 8B model on spatial and relational tiers.

As prompts grow more compositional — requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relational binding, or scaling to hundreds of instances — the early-fusion advantage becomes visually clear:.

"168 wine bottles": Falcon Perception identifies the bottles labeled "168", while SAM 3 highlights every bottle. "Honolulu direction sign": Falcon reads the text to find the right sign.

According to recent reports, "Lower meat skewer on left grill," "black car to the right of red car at bottom," "Belgian flag on the left" — Falcon Perception resolves the correct instance from spatial constraints. SAM 3 predicts false positives for multiple candidates.

"Pastry next to brown round bread," "person using phone," "person holding helmet in hand" — Falcon Perception identifies the interacting instance. SAM 3 highlights all instances of the object class, ignoring the relational constraint.

"Snow goose," "pigeon," "colorful canned drinks" — Falcon Perception autoregressively segments hundreds of instances. SAM 3's fixed-size decoder runs out of query tokens beyond ~200 instances.

Modern OCR has moved well beyond extracting text from clean scans. Today's systems must handle multi-column layouts, mathematical formulas, tables, charts, and multilingual content — all in one pass. Most competitive OCR VLMs tackle this with a familiar recipe: a vision encoder feeding a separate text decoder, plus task-specific glue. These systems work, but they tend to be large (1B–3B+ parameters).

We took a different path: reuse the same early-fusion dense Transformer from Falcon Perception, but train a smaller 0.3B-parameter variant from scratch specifically for OCR. The result is Falcon OCR — a single backbone that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space with the same hybrid attention mask (bidirectional for image tokens, causal for text tokens), and switches tasks through prompts rather than additional modules.

Industry observers note that we trained from scratch (no multi-teacher distillation) because the visual features OCR needs — fine-grained glyph recognition, stroke-level discrimination — differ substantially from the object-level features useful for segmentation. Starting fresh lets the backbone develop text-optimized representations from the ground up.

It has been revealed that we train on a curated English-language mixture spanning three core tasks: general document text parsing (digital PDFs, old scans, typewritten documents), mathematical and scientific formula recognition, and table structure recognition. The mixture also includes handwriting, real-world scene text, and synthetic samples generated from rendered LaTeX and HTML sources. The training objective is pure next-token prediction on structured text outputs.

Training proceeds in two phases: a long pre-training phase at constant learning rate where the model learns core OCR capabilities across all element types, followed by a short cosine-decay finetuning phase where the learning rate is annealed to near zero.

We evaluate on olmOCR (binary correctness checks across diverse inputs) and OmniDocBench (continuous metrics over full-page parses). All comparison models are significantly larger and/or use proprietary infrastructure. At 80.3% on olmOCR with only 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is within 1.7 points of the top system and leads all models on Multi-Column (87.1%) and Tables (90.3%). On OmniDocBench it scores 88.64 overall, ahead of DeepSeek OCR v2, GPT 5.2, and Mistral OCR 3.

At 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is roughly 3x smaller than 0.9B-class OCR VLMs, which translates directly into higher serving throughput. Measured on a single A100-80GB with vLLM at high concurrency:.

The compact footprint and vLLM integration (continuous batching, PagedAttention, optimized CUDA kernels) make it practical for large-scale document digitization where millions of pages need processing.

Industry observers note that more broadly, these results suggest that the early-fusion single-stack Transformer is a viable alternative to the "vision encoder plus text decoder" recipe for OCR. One backbone, shared parameter space, one decoding interface, and better data and training signals rather than increasingly complex pipelines. We hope this encourages more work in this direction.

Falcon OCR processes images captured under challenging real-world conditions with varying lighting, diverse text semantics (mathematical formulae, structured tables, handwritten notes), and complex document layouts, to produce structured text output.

Click each category below to expand.

Falcon OCR extracts text from handwritten documents and real-world photographs with variable lighting, orientation, and content complexity.

Falcon OCR accurately reproduces cell entries and structural layout from tables of varying formats and complexity.

Falcon OCR correctly transcribes mathematical expressions ranging from simple equations to multi-line derivations with nested operators.

Falcon OCR preserves reading order and structural fidelity when extracting text from documents with multi-column layouts, figures, and footnotes.

The release includes an inference stack built on PyTorch’s FlexAttention, which makes it practical to express the custom attention patterns and efficiently serve packed variable-length sequences.

In our setup on an H100, typical latencies are on the order of ~100ms prefill, ~200ms upsampling (0ms if cached), and ~50ms decode for a handful of instances. (These numbers depend on resolution, sequence length, and the number of predicted instances.).

For the Falcon-OCR model, we also provide a vLLM docker server for fast deployment and MLX integration for Apple-Silicon.

Please check out the github repo for details.

It has been revealed that falcon Perception is intentionally minimal: one backbone, one objective family, and small heads only where outputs are continuous and dense. The working assumption is that most gains should come from data, compute, and training signals, rather than continually expanding the pipeline with specialized modules.

The architecture doesn't block any obvious scaling path: add more images and harder prompts for better grounding, mix in text-only data for better language, increase context length for denser scenes. It's still just one sequence model.

Falcon Perception is developed by the Falcon Vision Team at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII), Abu Dhabi, UAE.

If you use Falcon-Perception, please cite.

Welcome Gemma 4: Frontier multimodal intelligence on device

📅 02 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗.
  • These models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device.
  • We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗.

These models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device. Gemma 4 builds on advances from previous families and makes them click together. In our tests with pre-release checkpoints we have been impressed by their capabilities, to the extent that we struggled to find good fine-tuning examples because they are so good out of the box.

We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it. This blog post will show you how to build with your favorite tools so let us know what you think!

Similar to Gemma-3n, Gemma 4 supports image, text, and audio inputs, and generates text responses. The text decoder is based on the Gemma model with support for long context windows. The image encoder is similar to the one from Gemma 3 but with two crucial improvements: variable aspect ratios, and configurable number of image token inputs to find your sweet spot between speed, memory, and quality. All models support images (or video) and text inputs, while the small variants (E2B, E4B) and the 12B Unified model support audio as well.

Gemma 4 comes in five sizes, all base and instruction fine-tuned:.

Gemma 4 leverages several architecture components used in previous Gemma versions and other open models, and leaves out complex or inconclusive features such as Altup. The combination is a mix designed to be highly compatible across libraries and devices, that can efficiently support long context and agentic use cases, whilst being ideal for quantization.

As shown in the benchmarks above, this feature mix (combined with the training data and recipe) enables the 31B dense model to achieve an estimated LMArena score (text only) of 1452, while the 26B MoE reaches 1441 with just 4B active parameters 🤯. As we'll see, multimodal operation is comparatively as good as text generation, at least in informal and subjective tests.

These are the main architecture characteristics in Gemma 4:.

One of the most distinctive features in smaller Gemma 4 models is Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which was introduced previously in Gemma-3n. In a standard transformer, each token gets a single embedding vector at input, and the same initial representation is what the residual stream builds on across all layers, forcing the embedding to frontload everything the model might need. PLE adds a parallel, lower-dimensional conditioning pathway alongside the main residual stream. For each token, it produces a small dedicated vector for every layer by combining two signals: a token-identity component (from an embedding lookup) and a context-aware component (from a learned projection of the main embeddings). Each decoder layer then uses its corresponding vector to modulate the hidden states via a lightweight residual block after attention and feed-forward. This gives each layer its own channel to receive token-specific information only when it becomes relevant, rather than requiring everything to be packed into a single upfront embedding. Because the PLE dimension is much smaller than the main hidden size, this adds meaningful per-layer specialization at modest parameter cost. For multimodal inputs (images, audio, video), PLE is computed before soft tokens are merged into the embedding sequence — since PLE relies on token IDs that are lost once multimodal features replace the placeholders. Multimodal positions use the pad token ID, effectively receiving neutral per-layer signals.

Sources indicate that the shared KV cache is an efficiency optimization that reduces both compute and memory during inference. The last num_kv_shared_layers layers of the model don't compute their own key and value projections. Instead, they reuse the K and V tensors from the last non-shared layer of the same attention type (sliding or full).

In practice, this has a minimal impact on quality while being much more efficient (in terms of both memory and compute) for long context generation and on-device use.

The Gemma 4 12B Unified model has no separate vision or audio encoder. Instead, raw image patches and audio waveforms are projected directly into the LLM's embedding space through lightweight linear layers, and all modalities flow into a single decoder-only transformer. This reduces multimodal latency and allows the whole model to be fine-tuned in one pass. The checkpoint size makes it deployment-friendly on consumer hardware.

Sources indicate that we saw in our tests that Gemma 4 supports comprehensive multimodal capabilities out of the box. We don't know what was the training mix, but we had success using it for tasks such as OCR, speech-to-text, object detection, or pointing. It also supports text-only and multimodal function calling, reasoning, code completion and correction.

Recent findings suggest that google has released Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) drafters for the Gemma 4 family: small assistant models that accelerate inference via speculative decoding. The drafter proposes several future tokens at once, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass. You get the same outputs as the target model, just faster — no quality loss, no changes to reasoning behaviour. Reported end-to-end speedups go up to ~3x depending on hardware, batch size, and workload.

Assistants are available for all four Gemma 4 sizes (E2B, E4B, 26B A4B, 31B). They share the KV cache with the target model to avoid recomputing context, and the smaller edge variants additionally use an embedder clustering trick to keep memory and compute low on-device.

Find the checkpoints in the Gemma 4 collection and the mlx-community collection.

Alongside the autoregressive Gemma 4 family, Google DeepMind is releasing DiffusionGemma, a multimodal model that generates text using discrete diffusion instead of token-by-token autoregression. It's built on the same 26B A4B Mixture-of-Experts foundation (25.2B total / 3.8B active parameters, 8 active experts out of 128 plus 1 shared), takes text and image inputs, generates text, and supports up to 256K context — all under the same Apache 2.0 license.

Sources indicate that where a standard causal LM emits one token at a time, DiffusionGemma denoises whole blocks of tokens in parallel. The architecture is encoder-decoder: an autoregressive encoder prefills the prompt and builds the KV cache, while a decoder applies bidirectional attention over a "canvas" of 256 tokens. During multi-canvas sampling, the model iteratively denoises a full canvas with a diffusion sampler; once a canvas is finalized it's encoded and appended to the KV cache, then the next canvas begins. This block-autoregressive approach increases generation speed.

Sources indicate that the headline benefit is throughput: parallel denoising generates roughly 15–20 tokens per forward pass, reaching per-user generation speeds exceeding 1100 tokens/second at low batch sizes (H100, FP8). Inference compute is adaptive too — simpler prompts and structured tasks like code need fewer denoising steps, so tokens-per-second scales with task complexity. It keeps the broader Gemma 4 toolkit: thinking mode, function calling, long context, native system prompts, and image understanding (OCR, document parsing, object detection, pointing) at variable aspect ratios and resolutions.

Industry observers note that benchmarks show an expected trade-off between speed and evaluation metrics — DiffusionGemma trails the autoregressive 26B A4B on most tasks (e.g. MMLU Pro 77.6% vs 82.6%, AIME 2026 69.1% vs 88.3%, GPQA Diamond 73.2% vs 82.3%) in exchange for its large speed advantage, while edging ahead on a few (HLE no tools 11.0% vs 8.7%).

Getting started looks just like the rest of Gemma 4, via the dedicated diffusion class:.

For best results, Google recommends the Entropy-Bounded (EB) sampler with adaptive stopping (up to 48 denoising steps, a temperature schedule decaying from 0.8 → 0.4, and an entropy bound of 0.1 for token selection). As with Gemma 4, place image content before text in your prompt, and toggle reasoning with the <|think|> control token.

Gemma 4 models are ideal for fine-tuning in your favorite tools and platforms and at any budget.

Gemma 4 is fully supported for fine-tuning with TRL. To celebrate, TRL has been upgraded with support for multimodal tool responses when interacting with environments, meaning models can now receive images back from tools during training, not just text.

To showcase this, we've built an example training script where Gemma 4 learns to drive in the CARLA simulator. The model sees the road through a camera, decides what to do and learns from the outcome. After training, it consistently changes lanes to avoid pedestrians. The same approach works for any task where a model needs to see and act: robotics, web browsing, or other interactive environments.

Additionally, we have prepared an example on how to fine-tune Gemma 4 with TRL on Vertex AI using SFT, to showcase how to extend the function calling capabilities, whilst freezing both the vision and audio towers. The examples include how to build a custom Docker container with latest Transformers, TRL, etc. with CUDA support on Google Cloud, and how to run it via Vertex AI Serverless Training Jobs.

You can find the complete example in the "Hugging Face on Google Cloud" docs at https://hf.co/docs/google-cloud/examples/vertex-ai-notebooks-fine-tune-gemma-4.

one gap worth flagging for anyone building on Gemma 4's function calling for real-world deployments: when the model generates a function call, there's right now no verifiable record that a human principal authorized that specific action. a compromised system prompt or injected instruction produces a call that's indistinguishable from legitimate delegation at the tool interface.

i opened a PR on the gemma-cookbook repo today that adds a drop-in HDP middleware layer to address this, sits between Gemma 4's function call output and tool execution, verifies Ed25519-signed delegation tokens, classifies actions by irreversibility (Class 0–3), and blocks unauthorized calls pre-execution.

for edge/robotics deployments (E2B on Jetson Nano / Raspberry Pi directing actuators), there's a companion HDP-P extension covering the physical layer.

This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.

Many of the PDFs have been floating around, but I collected them in one place. Within each set, I tried to group them depending on themes and eras, and highlight the most key ones. Some required more effort to find, I scanned a few myself, plus also created standalone mirrors of various minisites. Some of the mirrors were lightly cleaned up to make their consumption easier â stuff like pixellating images better, inlining images instead of linking to them, or fixing YouTube embeds. Enjoy!

In a recent development, (Commodore) Amiga was a multimedia personal computer particularly popular in the 1980s and 1990s in Europe. Its GUI was called Intuition and/or Workbench.

According to recent reports, android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.

BeOS was an operating system released in the second half of the 1990s. A proper HIG for BeOS never materialized despite numerous promises. These âpreliminary and incompleteâ guidelines have been extracted from the BeOS R4.5 CD.

BlackBerry was a beleagured maker of mobile handsets.

Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.

Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.

Sources indicate that A Unix interface built using X Window System by Digital Equipment Corporation. This style guide was reverse engineered from a proprietary e-book format.

According to recent reports, graphics Environment Manager (GEM) is a 1980s operating system/GUI. It was well-known by users of the Atari ST computers, known in these circles as TOS. Both of the websites mirrored are (obviously) more modern, but seem to contain vintage information, hence the confusing â1980s websiteâ label.

GNOME is a desktop environment for Linux and BSD operating systems. Note that the versioning number of these guidelines is very confusing.

Style guides for Googleâs early VR and AR efforts.

iOS (previously iPhone OS) is Appleâs mobile operating system for iPhone smartphones and their siblings.

Java is a programming language, which comes equipped with JFC (Java Foundation Classes) and Swing GUI components.

KDE originally stood for K Desktop Environment and is a popular Linux GUI.

Style guides for Microsoftâs motion sensing input devices.

These are some historical Apple GUI style guides, starting with Lisa in the 1980, and continuing to the âclassicâ Mac OS, with a brief stop in the Apple II corner.

More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.

An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic.

Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon.

Sources indicate that neXTSTEP was NeXTâs influential operating system and graphical user interface. It eventually morphed into OpenStep on one side, and modern Mac OS X on another.

Apple Newton was Appleâs PDA debuted in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.

Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.

OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.

Palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palmâs mobile devices. Eventually, the company moved toward webOS, covered elsewhere on this page.

PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.

Sources indicate that style guides for various UNIX-based operating systems from SGI, or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.

An early 2000s joint venture between two companies that made mobile phones.

According to recent reports, taligent was a troubled software organization, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I wonder if recycling this same line of "our next model is so amazing, it's unsafe to release it" with every major release still works, or if it's just institutional inertia within those organizations at this point to claim that "the next model is the horribly unsafe one (wink wink. nudge nudge, yes it's really that awesome)".

The thing is, each time the models did have the capabilities in question. GPT-3/ChatGPT *did* pose a threat for bots to plausibly pose as people for malicious activity. Fable *really did* have great ability to find zero-day bugs in software. Etc. They weren't mythical capabilities; we just eventually decided, "fuck it, this is getting out anyway, might as well go for it".

In this case, if there's any issue, it's probably this [openai.com]. For a long time, protein-design models have been considered quite dangerous, for the risk of people making custom bioweapons. But now it appears that generalist models are becoming very good at it as well.

And then, doom saying ended as it usually does.

"We guessed the day of Rapture wrong. We have divined the latest numbers. The new Rapture day is (release date of the next model)".

In a recent development, and then, doom saying ended as it usually does.With multiple companies hacked in high profile ways? With countless critical bugs discovered to the point where dealing with them took down the US banking infrastructure? With attacks on the EC, FBI and CIA? With end user's Claude agents now actively hacking online websites and modifying internal databases in order to make gym appointments? That AI has been trivially used to knock off Taiwan's emergency services network causing the country to run on a fallback?Unlike the rapture, what was being suggested is actually happening right now. Sticking your fingers in your ears, closing your eyes and shouting "LA LA LA LA" won't fix the very real problems with have with AI models.At least you've moved on from global warming to pretend another problem doesn't exist. The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And intruders don't always need to exploit bugs to break in.
  • American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems.
  • In a recent development, the federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And intruders don't always need to exploit bugs to break in.

American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems.

In a recent development, the federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A latest index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23.

It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020.

However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted.

It has been revealed that five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords.

Recent findings suggest that the report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers, targeted more than 100 water systems, with incidents reported across at least 12 states, and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers.

According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique:.

The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [T0883]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22.

These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented.

Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo.

“Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®.

📅 08 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (767 w)

Safetensors is Joining the PyTorch Foundation

📅 08 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.
  • Recent findings suggest that safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code.
  • In a recent development, the format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.

Recent findings suggest that safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code. The pickle-based formats that dominated the ecosystem at the time meant that there was a very real risk you’d be running malicious code. While this was an acceptable risk when ML was still budding, it would become unacceptable as open model sharing became central to how the ML community works.

In a recent development, the format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data. Zero-copy loading that maps tensors directly from disk. Lazy loading so you can read individual weights without deserializing an entire checkpoint.

What we didn't fully anticipate was how broadly it would be adopted. Today, Safetensors is the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub and others, used by tens of thousands of models across all modalities in ML. It has become the preferred way for the open source ML community to share models.

We want Safetensors to truly belong to the community. The project has always been open source, but code contributions are just one part of its evolution. By bringing more companies and contributors into the governance of the project, we make sure that progress reflects the breadth of the community building on top of it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation means Safetensors now has a vendor-neutral home. The trademark, the repository, and the governance of the project sit with the Linux Foundation rather than any single organization. Hugging Face's two core maintainers, Luc and Daniel, remain on the Technical Steering Committee and continue to lead the project day-to-day, but Safetensors now formally belongs to the community that depends on it.

We believe safety is best guaranteed when every contributor can build on what already exists; a principle now embedded in the project's governance itself.

It has been revealed that for the vast majority of users, nothing changes. The format is the same, the APIs are the same, the Hub integration is the same: no breaking changes. Models stored in Safetensors format today will continue to work exactly as they do now.

For contributors, the path to becoming a maintainer is now formally documented and open to anyone in the community. The project's governance lives in GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md in the repository. For organizations building on top of Safetensors, neutral governance under the Linux Foundation provides a stable, long-term foundation, entirely community-driven.

Safetensors is a well-established project, adopted by the ecosystem at large, but we're still convinced we're at the very beginning of the project.

We're working with the PyTorch team so that Safetensors may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models.

Sources indicate that the coming months will see significant growth, and we couldn't think of a better home for that next chapter than the PyTorch Foundation. The roadmap ahead includes device-aware loading and saving, so tensors can load directly onto CUDA, ROCm, and other accelerators without unnecessary CPU staging.

Industry observers note that we're also building first-class APIs for Tensor Parallel and Pipeline Parallel loading, so each rank or pipeline stage loads only the weights it needs. And as the ecosystem's quantization landscape continues to evolve, we'll be formalizing support for FP8, block-quantized formats like GPTQ and AWQ, and sub-byte integer types.

These are problems the whole ecosystem has a stake in solving, and being inside the PyTorch Foundation means we can work on them in collaboration with the other hosted projects rather than in parallel.

Safetensors is open source and contributions are welcome at every level, from bug reports and documentation to upcoming features and participation in governance.

If you're a developer, researcher, or organization that builds on Safetensors and want to be more involved in shaping its direction, open an issue, start a discussion, or reach out to the maintainers directly. The project has always belonged to the community that uses it. The governance now reflects that too.

Sources indicate that will there be a concerted effort now to get newer (and older) LLM models to adopt the more secure safetensors format rather than allowing AI developers to continue with pickle files as they did in the past? And what would some of the objections be, if any, for a developer to not transition to safetensors format?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Approval for ‘Starmind’ granted but it’s a long way from the launchpad, or making sense.

The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s proposal to launch a million datacenter satellites.

The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”.

The order requires SpaceX to ensure its satellites’ radios don’t interfere with US government systems which use the 28.6-29.1 GHz band and requires the firm to stick to operating within the parameters it files with the International Telecommunications Union.

SpaceX asked the FCC to waive its rule requiring the atmospheric disposal of dead satellites orbiting at 2,000 km or less.

Elon Musk’s tech giant asked for “flexibility to dispose satellites operating above 600 km altitude into Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.”.

The FCC found SpaceX did not provide enough information to let it assess if proposed “alternative disposal methods” are compliant with regulations, so deferred its decision on the waiver request.

According to recent reports, “SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules,” the order states. The organization must also file twice-yearly reports about “conjunction events” – moments when its satellites get dangerously close to each other, or other orbiters.

Whether orbiting datacenters are feasible, make sense, or will ever pay for themselves, remain open questions.

Analyst firm Gartner has described the idea as “peak insanity.”.

Sources indicate that google thinks orbiting datacenters become viable if launch costs fall to $200/kg, which would mean SpaceX needs to launch its massive Starship 1,800 times. SpaceX’s assumptions assume near-daily releases, far better than its current cadence of a launch every three days or so.

Fundamental networking research must also come to fruition to handle the amount of traffic large constellations of orbiting datacenters will create.

Terrestrial manufacturing capacity will also need to increase to build all those satellites. Elon Musk’s companies and Intel have planned a giant newly introduced fab to make that possible, without explaining how the supply chains behind chip manufacturing will scale to make it feasible. That's a notable omission given that semiconductor supply chains are already extremely strained.

Approval for SpaceX is therefore nice but in no way a roadmap to a million datacenter satellites.

Google, ironically, is a little further along than SpaceX, having launched a test sat in October and last week announcing it has hired Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch a larger satellite carrying the equivalent of a full datacenter rack in early 2029.

In a recent development, down on Earth, meanwhile, scientists trying to observe the universe continue to bemoan the obstructions caused by mega-constellations of broadband-beaming satellites. Proposals from across the USA, China, Europe and India currently call for around 100,000 satellites. SpaceX’s proposed million orbiters could run workloads which help us to understand the mysteries of the universe while also making them hard to see from down here. ®.

Waypoint-1.5: Higher-Fidelity Interactive Worlds for Everyday GPUs

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.
  • According to recent reports, the first release of Waypoint highlighted that real-time generative worlds were possible.
  • Sources indicate that waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waypoint-1.5 Weights on the Hub.

Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.

According to recent reports, the first release of Waypoint highlighted that real-time generative worlds were possible. It proved that interactive world models could be more than passive video demos, and that locally runnable systems could begin to close the gap between generating a world and actually stepping into one.

Sources indicate that waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation. This release improves visual fidelity, expands the range of hardware that can run the model locally, and takes another step toward interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute.

On desktop hardware including RTX 3090 through 5090, Waypoint-1.5 can generate real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS. This release also introduces a 360p tier designed to run smoothly across a much broader range of consumer hardware, including gaming laptops, and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs.

The biggest change in Waypoint-1.5 is accessibility.

With Waypoint-1, we proved the core experience. With Waypoint-1.5, we wanted to make that experience available on more machines without giving up real-time interactivity. That meant building two model tiers: a 720p model for higher-performance hardware, and a 360p model optimized for broader deployment.

Industry observers note that we also scaled training dramatically. Waypoint-1.5 was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1, which significantly improves the model’s ability to generate more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time.

Sources indicate that under the hood, Waypoint-1.5 also incorporates more efficient video modeling techniques to reduce redundant computation across frames. That matters because real-time world models are not judged only by how a single frame looks. They are judged by whether the world responds instantly, stays coherent as you move through it, and remains usable on local hardware.

In a recent development, A lot of recent progress in generative video and world models has focused on visual fidelity. Those results matter, but fidelity alone is not what makes an interactive world feel real.

What people remember is responsiveness. They remember whether the environment reacts to them, whether motion stays coherent, whether the world holds together as they explore it, and whether the whole experience feels immediate instead of delayed.

That is the gap we care about most: the difference between watching a generated scene and actually being inside one.

Industry observers note that if world models only run on large GPU clusters, they remain impressive demos. If they run locally on consumer hardware, they become something much more useful: a foundation for interactive entertainment, creative tooling, simulation, and AI-native environments people can actually explore.

Waypoint-1.5 is designed around that idea: not just better videos, but more responsive and explorable worlds that remain accessible on consumer hardware.

There are two ways to play Waypoint-1.5.

The first is local execution through Overworld Biome. This release is designed to run across a wide range of hardware configurations, and the updated Biome runtime makes local setup much simpler. With the new installer flow, consumers can go from download to running the model locally in minutes.

The second is Overworld Stream, which lets you try Waypoint-1.5 instantly in the browser with no local setup required.

Whether you want immediate access or full local control, Waypoint-1.5 is built to support both.

Additionally, we provide World Engine, our flexible, easy to use, core inference library powering our official clients, along with nearly a dozen third party clients and libraries.

Waypoint started with a simple question: what would it take for generative worlds to become truly interactive?

Early generative systems showed that models could produce convincing images and videos. But building environments that people can explore, control, and interact with in real time is a different challenge entirely.

Waypoint-1.5 is another step in that direction, improving fidelity and expanding hardware accessibility while continuing to push real-time interactive generation onto local machines.

We think the future of world models will not be defined only by what they can render, but by whether people can actually inhabit and interact with them in real time.

Download Waypoint-1.5, run it locally with Biome, or jump in instantly on Overworld.stream.

And if you build something fun, strange, or unexpectedly immersive with it, we’d love to see it.
