📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Machines of loving grace to turn social media grumps into services, finger painting into career advice.

Indian politicians have proposed that AI could take a major role in citizens’ lives, partly through pervasive surveillance.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week spelled out his vision for an AI-based app that would collect data about children as they grow and analyze it to determine their aptitude for different types of study or careers.

Sources indicate that modi suggested that parents of three-year-old children should enter data about their offspring’s activities and accomplishments into a government-run system that is also accessible to teachers and even a child’s friends. Those records, the PM suggested, will “help identify children's interests and aptitude from an early age and redirect them in the study of their choice in future.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not an entirely creepy idea, because gaining access to India’s top tertiary institutions requires students to pay a hefty fee to sit for entrance exams. Modi pitched recommendations from the AI-powered app as something parents will appreciate as they contemplate whether to fund their offspring’s studies.

India’s most populous state, Uttar Pradesh (UP), has proposed to build an “AI Stack” to serve its 240 million-plus residents.

A 178-page tender seeks bidders to build a system that uses the state’s Family ID – a unique identifier for each household – to link data held by multiple agencies so it can be put to work in a dozen AI use cases.

One of those use cases is a tool for “AI-Enabled Social Media Monitoring and Urban Grievance Detection” that “analyses publicly available social media content including online news channels and connected grievance channels to detect emerging urban concerns, citizen complaints, service interruptions, and recurring service gaps.”.

Recent findings suggest that the government wants that system to autonomously route complaints to relevant agencies, to automate actions like sending crews to patch up damaged roads. Critics have pointed to vague wording in the tender as potentially allowing the UP government to link this system to other agencies – a matter of concern given Indian state and national governments have implemented internet shutdowns to stop protestors from communicating on social media services and messaging apps.

Recent findings suggest that another use case is a knowledge assistant for state police that looks up case histories and other data but can’t use it to assess evidence or provide investigative conclusions. An app for teachers will advise them on how to create custom content to meet students’ needs. Healthcare workers would also get an app to help them make recommendations during patient visits.

Citizens get natural language interfaces to a system that offers advice on how to identify and access government services and schemes.

UP wants to drive these apps with self-hosted open-weight models, and to use only anonymized datasets.

Industry observers note that india’s Internet Freedom Foundation worries that the systems described in the tender aren’t explicitly authorized by any legislation, and that the document doesn’t mention key oversight measures for the AI Stack. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world. And made it directly accessible from your browser. On March 31st, we released Holo3, our most advanced computer-use model to date.

Recent findings suggest that building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another. We’re doing both.

Industry observers note that holoTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would. It automates tasks across any website with zero setup or technical skills required. You describe what you want, and the agent handles it directly inside your browser, navigating interfaces, filling fields, and making decisions the same way you would. The vision models, the action planning, the interface understanding, all of it is running underneath, working for you, and all you ever see is the result.

According to recent reports, some tasks are quick and forgettable, but others are long and repetitive, the kind that reliably eat up your afternoon. You might find yourself cross-referencing competitor pricing across twenty different e-commerce tabs to upgrade a master spreadsheet, or filtering through a dozen job boards and company career pages to find new listings, painstakingly porting the details into a tracking doc to manage your applications.

That's where routines come in. You start a recording, and HoloTab captures what you do in your tab in real time while you click or narrate along the way, demonstrating what you're doing and why. Your screen and your actions give HoloTab everything it needs, enriching the routine with enough context to actually understand the goal.

Industry observers note that once the recording stops, a routine is generated. From then on, you can re-run your routine or schedule it whenever you need to, and HoloTab will handle the rest on its own.

Sources indicate that computer-use AI is going to change how people work, research, and get things done, both in their professional and personal lives, and that shift is already closer than most people realize. But it shouldn't require a technical background to access, and the benefits shouldn't accrue only to teams with engineers who know how to wire these systems together.

HoloTab is free and ready for everyone to use today: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/holotab/hlaoiikljjgcjdhkakedfngifaopbcop.

Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.
  • We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.
  • Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.

We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.

Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.

VAKRA provides an executable environment where agents interact with over 8,000+ locally hosted APIs backed by real databases spanning 62 domains, along with domain-aligned document collections. Tasks can require 3-7 step reasoning chains that combine structured API interaction with unstructured retrieval under natural-language tool-use constraints.

As can be seen below, models perform poorly on VAKRA - in this blog, we include additional dataset details about the tasks in VAKRA and present an analysis of failure modes we observed on different tasks.

As shown below, the VAKRA benchmark comprises of four tasks, each testing a different set of capabilities.

Fig 1: Representative examples of each capability in the VAKRA benchmark.

Sources indicate that this capability includes 2,077 test instances across 54 domains, requiring the use of tools from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD collections (Elder et al., 2026). Compared to the setup in Elder et al., the tool universe in SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD is expanded through the inclusion of a larger number of domains. Each domain is restricted to one tool collection, and tasks involve chaining 1–12 tool calls to arrive at the final answer.

Fig 2: Data sample from SEL-BIRD collection.

Recent findings suggest that as shown above, each instance has an associated JSON data source from which the answer must be derived. The MCP servers supporting this task include a special tool, called get_data(tool_universe_id=id), which must be called at the beginning of each instance. This tool initializes the data source, returns a lightweight preview of the data (see below Figure 3), and stores the full dataset server-side to avoid large data transfers. This prevents the inefficient transfer of large data over the MCP protocol. The call also configures the MCP server to expose the appropriate tool set based on the tool_universe_id and aligns the data source with the domain-specific database for the instance.

The SLOT-BIRD collection provides a global set of 7 tools for generic data manipulation (e.g., filtering, sorting), inspired by systems like Tableau and Google Analytics. The SEL-BIRD collection extends this by introducing more specialized tools: some are shared with SLOT-BIRD, while others are derived by flattening categorical arguments into separate functions (e.g., sort_data with argument ascending: bool = False becomes sort_data_ascending and sort_data_descending). Additionally, the generic (retrieve_data) function from SLOT-BIRD is replaced with query-specific getters. Every key in the data for a given instance has an associated get function (get_KEY_NAME) for an average of 4 get functions per instance.

Fig 3: Data preview obtained from `get_data` function.

Recent findings suggest that this capability includes 1,597 instances across 17 domains, requiring tools from an expanded REST-BIRD collection (Elder et al.). These use endpoint-style interfaces that provide highly specific, query-aligned endpoints that encapsulate most computation. They are served as REST APIs running in a FastAPI server, which is wrapped by the MCP server. This task requires selecting the correct APIs from the domain-specific tool set (as shown in the example in Figure 1). Each domain contains a minimum of 6 to a maximum of 328 tools (with an average of 116 tools). Similar to the previous task, the get_data tool configures the MCP server to expose only the relevant domain-specific APIs.

In a recent development, the OpenAI API Specification restricts the tool list input to a maximum length of 128 tools. This restriction requires an agent builder using this API to manage the length of the tool list directly via a shortlisting mechanism. In the baseline agents in our repository, a simple shortlisting capability handles this challenge.

The Capability 3 segment of the benchmark has 869 test instances drawn from 38 subject domains. These instances rely again on the REST-BIRD API collection, but add multi-hop reasoning to the challenge (refer to example in Figure 1). Multi-hop questions require multiple pieces of supporting evidence to be extracted and combined to reach an answer. The instances in this section require between one and five logical hops to answer a query. The question types distribution for queries within the test dataset is shown below in Figure 4.

Fig 4: API Hop-Type distribution for Capability 3 (MultiHop) and Hybrid Hop-Type distribution for Capability 4 (MultiHop MultiSource Reasoning).

It has been revealed that capability 4 includes 644 instances across 41 domains and is also built on the REST-BIRD API collection. Figure 4 above shows a distribution of hybrid hops for test queries without policies. It contains the most complex queries with the following characteristics:.

Recent findings suggest that multi-Source: This segment adds document indices per domain. Queries in this capability could require information from these document indexes as well as API calls. Similar to Capability 3, this task also has Multi-Hop queries. The required information source applies at the per-hop level, so, for example, a question may entail three logical hops with sources: API - RAG (Document Retrieval) - API. To enforce correct reasoning, sources are decontaminated during data generation, i.e. information required for a given hop is available in only one source. For example, if a hop is to be answered using APIs, the document index is built by removing documents that likely contain the information needed to answer the question.

Multi-Turn: This segment of the dataset also adds multi-turn conversations to the setting. Each instance is a dialog with multiple turns. The data is released as context-response pairs, where the context encodes the current dialog history and the agent is only responsible for answering the current turn.

Tool-usage Policies: A subset of these instances includes tool-use policies that the agent is required to follow. These policies take the form of plain-text instructions about the knowledge sources that the agent is allowed to access and under which circumstances. For example:.

Recent findings suggest that the baseline agent in the project repo imposes adherence to these policies through a simple addition to the prompt: "You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.\n Tool Usage Constraint: {additional_instructions}.". Of course, agent builders are free to choose any constraint enforcement mechanism.

According to recent reports, VAKRA evaluates agents in tool environments where success depends on both the ability to execute coherent, multi-step workflows and answer correctness. We introduce an execution-centric evaluation framework that assesses not only final outputs but also the full tool-execution trajectory that includes tool calls, inputs, and intermediate results.

Sources indicate that the VAKRA Evaluator operates over two key inputs for each sample: a predicted final response and the corresponding tool-call trajectory. The tool calls from the predicted trajectory are executed in the same environment as the ground truth to verify intermediate tool outputs.

The evaluation follows a waterfall-style pipeline (Figure 6), where later stages are conditioned on earlier success:.

Fig 6: Waterfall-style Evaluation Pipeline.

Sources indicate that tool-Sequence Comparison Due to the presence of an executable environment, agents can explore the environment and sometimes return the answer by invoking a different set of APIs than the ones identified by us. In order to support alternative but valid tool invocations and reasoning paths, correctness is assessed by executing each predicted tool and comparing the set of tool responses against those from the ground truth (rather than enforcing strict step-level matching).

In a recent development, specifically, we first perform a programmatic check, verifying whether all information present in the ground-truth tool responses is recovered by the predicted tool responses. This check may be inconclusive in cases involving partial matches, semantic equivalence, or differences in representation (e.g., ordering, aggregation, or formatting). In such cases, we apply a secondary LLM-based evaluation, adapted from the CRAG framework Yang et al., 2024, to determine whether the predicted trajectory retrieves all required information despite structural differences. This step uses an adapted prompt to determine whether the predicted trajectory captures all required information, even if obtained through a different sequence of tool calls.

Final Response Evaluation For trajectories that pass the previous check, the final response is evaluated using an LLM-based judge. This step ensures that the response is (i) grounded in the predicted tool outputs, and (ii) factually consistent with the ground truth answer, accounting for potential variations in phrasing or structure.

This design ensures that agents are rewarded not only for producing correct answers, but for obtaining them through valid and complete reasoning processes.

Every capability is equally weighted to obtain a final leaderboard score.

To obtain a capability score, every sample within a capability is equally weighted for capabilities 1 through 3.

For capability 4, we weight heterogeneous queries higher:.

We now present detailed error analysis across the four VAKRA capabilities. To facilitate our analysis, we adopt stage-wise error categorization to assign each failure to the first point of breakdown. Specifically, we evaluate, in order: (i) whether the correct tool(s) were selected, (ii) whether the required arguments were provided without omissions or hallucinations, (iii) whether argument values were correct, and (iv) whether the final response is both accurate and grounded in the tool outputs.

Since a single sample may exhibit multiple errors across different steps, we sequentially classify each instance to the earliest failing stage (e.g., tool selection errors take precedence over argument errors). This avoids double-counting and allows error categories to be interpreted as disjoint fractions of the dataset. While more granular metrics (e.g., precision/recall over tool usage) are possible (Elder et al., 2026), we find this formulation provides a simple and interpretable breakdown of agent failures.

The instances in this part of the benchmark required selecting and sequencing multiple tools to solve a single task. We have 2077 samples in this capability. This was challenging for all models, but GPT-OSS-120B performed best on this segment of the benchmark.

Fig 7: SEL-BIRD vs SLOT-BIRD Error Types Analysis.

Recent findings suggest that the Business Intelligence (BI) API capability contains two sets of APIs, from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD tool collections. The SEL part of this benchmark had 600 samples, while the SLOT part of the benchmark had 1477 samples. These two collections are grouped under the BI API capability, but have slightly different characteristics. The SLOT-BIRD collection has a smaller number of generic tools with a large number of parameter values to fill, while the SEL-BIRD collection has a larger set of tools and fewer parameters per tool. This focus is reflected in the relative errors made by models using these two tool collections.

Fig 8: Comparison of Accuracy Across Models by Hop Depth.

It has been revealed that multi-hop reasoning increases the difficulty of the original task by requiring models to successfully answer multiple implicitly coupled questions, each of which requires selecting and calling the correct API. As expected, all models performed best on the questions with only a single logical hop, and saw performance degradations on 2-hop and again on 3+ hop questions.

Fig 9: Model Accuracy Rates by Interaction Type (API, Document-Retriever, Hybrid).

Recent findings suggest that the final segment of the dataset includes document sources in addition to the tool/API sources in the other segments. This leads to instances that require single or multiple API calls, single or multiple document searches, or some combination of API calls and document searches.

Fig 10: Model Accuracy Rates by Policy Type.

Policies introduce an additional layer of difficulty on top of multi-hop, multi-source reasoning. When policies align with the required source for answering i.e. they do not affect the tool list required for models to answer the question, we refer to it as "No Updates to Answer" -- as shown in Figure 10, all models except for Granite-4.0-h-Small-32B experience a clear drop in performance under policy constraints that restrict access to the most relevant information source (i.e. "Policy updates the answer").

In general, we find that models either violate constraints or fail to retrieve sufficient information, where they sometimes understood the policy but could not answer the question correctly, or they exhibit one of the previously analyzed failure modes.

Overall, tool-use policy-constrained settings suggest that while models can reason over tools and sources, they struggle to incorporate external constraints into that reasoning - often a key requirement for reliable real-world deployment.

VAKRA exposes a critical gap between surface-level tool competence and robust, end‑to‑end agent reliability. Although modern models can increasingly select APIs and execute isolated tool calls, VAKRA reveals that these abilities alone are insufficient for real‑world deployment. In practice, models often break down when required to perform compositional reasoning under execution constraints—spanning APIs, documents, dialog context, and policy requirements.

It has been revealed that think your agent is solid? Put it to the test.

Run it on VAKRA and see where it falls apart—tool selection, multi-hop reasoning, or policy constraints.

Breaking: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • According to recent reports, as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query.
  • If you're latest to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. In my previous blogpost, I introduced the fresh multimodal capabilities, showing how to use embedding and reranker models that handle text, images, audio, and video. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to train or finetune these multimodal models on your own data.

According to recent reports, as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query. The resulting tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr demonstrates how much performance you can gain by finetuning on your own domain. On my evaluation data, the finetuned model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 compared to the base model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models I tested against, including models up to 4x its size.

If you're latest to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first. For training text-only embedding, reranker, or sparse embedding models, see the Prior Blogposts section at the end.

It has been revealed that general-purpose multimodal embedding models like Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B are trained on diverse data to perform well across a wide range of languages and tasks: image-text matching, visual question answering, document understanding, and more. But this generality means the model is rarely the best choice for any specific task.

Consider Visual Document Retrieval: given a text query like "What was the tech giant's Q3 revenue?", the model must find the most relevant document screenshot from a corpus of thousands. This requires understanding document layouts, charts, tables, and text, which is a very different skill from e.g. matching pictures of shoes with product descriptions.

Industry observers note that by finetuning on domain-specific data, the model can learn these specialized patterns. In my experiment, finetuning improved NDCG@10 from 0.888 to 0.947, ahead of every recent multimodal model I tested, including ones up to 4x larger.

Training multimodal Sentence Transformer models involves the same components as training text-only models:.

According to recent reports, the multimodal training pipeline uses the same SentenceTransformerTrainer as text-only training. The key difference is that your datasets contain images (or other modalities) alongside text, and the model's processor handles the image preprocessing automatically.

Let's walk through each component, using Visual Document Retrieval (matching text queries to document screenshots) as a running example.

The most common approach is to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model, or to start from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) checkpoint. The Transformer module automatically detects supported modalities from the model's processor.

Industry observers note that to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model (e.g. one that already has a modules.json file), you can pass processor_kwargs and model_kwargs to control preprocessing and model loading respectively. processor_kwargs are passed directly to AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(...) (e.g., image resolution bounds: higher max_pixels means higher quality but more memory), while model_kwargs are passed to the appropriate AutoModel.from_pretrained(...) call (e.g., precision, attention implementation):.

It has been revealed that you can also start from a fresh VLM checkpoint that hasn't been trained for embeddings yet. Sentence Transformers will attempt to recognize the architecture, infer the supported modalities from the processor, and set up the appropriate forward method and pooling. If the automatic detection doesn't work perfectly for a particular model, the configuration in the saved sentence_bert_config.json can be edited to adjust modality settings, forward methods, and output handling:.

Sources indicate that in both cases, the Transformer module inspects the processor to determine which modalities are available, and Pooling is added automatically if needed. You can verify the supported modalities:.

According to recent reports, instead of using a single VLM backbone, you can compose separate encoders for different modalities using the Router module. This lets you combine any existing encoders and route inputs to the appropriate one based on detected modality:.

In a recent development, since Router-based multimodal models use separate encoders per modality, their embedding spaces are initially unaligned. Training is required to align the spaces for meaningful cross-modal similarity. The Dense projection layer shown above helps map embeddings from different encoders into a shared space.

This approach is useful when you want to use lightweight, specialized encoders rather than a large VLM. You can also combine Router-based multimodality with task-based routing (e.g. different encoders for queries vs. documents) using route_mappings. See the Router documentation for advanced routing scenarios.

According to recent reports, for this example, I use the tomaarsen/llamaindex-vdr-en-train-preprocessed dataset, a preprocessed English subset of llamaindex/vdr-multilingual-train. The source dataset was released alongside the Visual Document Retrieval Goes Multilingual blogpost by LlamaIndex, and consists of ~500k multilingual query-image samples collected from public internet PDFs, with queries synthetically generated using VLMs (gemini-1.5-pro and Qwen2-VL-72B). My preprocessed version filters to the 53,512 English samples and resolves 4 of the 16 ID-based hard negatives per sample into actual document screenshot images, so it can be used directly for training without further preprocessing:.

Sources indicate that the train config contains the first 10,000 samples, and the eval config contains the next 300 samples (a full config with all 53,512 samples is also available). For training, I select query, image, and negative_0 to form (anchor, positive, hard negative) triplets. Including additional hard negatives would likely improve the training signal, but each extra negative also increases memory usage and training time, so I stick with one. For evaluation, I keep all four hard negatives per query to build a more challenging retrieval corpus (more on that in the Evaluator section).

Recent findings suggest that just like text-only training, the dataset format must match your chosen loss function. The rules are the same:.

For multimodal datasets, the inputs can contain:.

Industry observers note that the data collator automatically calls model.preprocess(), which detects the modality of each input and applies the appropriate preprocessing. No manual tokenization or image processing is needed.

Many Hugging Face datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers, allowing you to easily find them at https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers.

Industry observers note that for this training, I use CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, a common choice for retrieval tasks. It accepts (query, positive) pairs with any number of additional hard negative columns, from 0 up to n, as long as each sample has the same number of negatives. During training, the loss pushes each query's similarity to its positive up and its similarity to every negative down. The negatives come from two sources:.

More negatives per query means a stronger training signal, so a larger batch size directly improves training quality. Beyond that, the "cached" variant of the loss uses gradient caching to make large effective batch sizes feasible even when GPU memory is limited.

The mini_batch_size parameter controls how many samples are processed at once during the cached forward passes. For large multimodal models, setting this to a small value (e.g., 1) is crucial to avoid out-of-memory errors without sacrificing the benefits of large effective batch sizes:.

To produce embeddings that work well at multiple dimensionalities, I wrap the base loss with MatryoshkaLoss. This trains the model so that truncating the embedding to a smaller number of dimensions still yields good performance:.

Industry observers note that this is especially useful for multimodal models, where embeddings can be large (2048 dimensions for Qwen3-VL). With Matryoshka training, you can use truncated embeddings (e.g., 256 or 128 dimensions) at deployment time for faster search with minimal quality loss. As I'll show in the Results section, the finetuned model achieves near-peak performance even at 512 dimensions.

Recent findings suggest that the SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments class lets you control training hyperparameters. Here's the configuration used for the VDR finetuning:.

A few things to note for (multimodal) training:.

It has been revealed that to track retrieval performance before, during, and after training, I use the InformationRetrievalEvaluator. It computes standard retrieval metrics like NDCG@10, MAP, and Recall@k:.

The evaluator takes text queries, a corpus of images (including hard negatives), and a mapping of which documents are relevant to which queries. Note that the corpus contains a mix of positive and hard negative document screenshots, making this a challenging evaluation. Using batch_size=1 prevents out-of-memory issues during evaluation of the large VLM.

Recent findings suggest that the SentenceTransformerTrainer brings everything together. Here's the complete training script:.

It has been revealed that the training script is nearly identical to a text-only training script. The only differences are:.

Everything else (the trainer, training arguments, dataset loading) works exactly the same as text-only training.

According to recent reports, after training for just 1 epoch, the finetuned tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 on the evaluation set (300 queries, 1500 corpus documents, cosine similarity). This is a significant improvement over the base Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models:.

The finetuned 2B model outperforms even the 8B Qwen3-VL-Embedding model, demonstrating the power of task-specific finetuning. Finetuning on your own domain is often worth considering, even when a larger general-purpose model is available!

The comparison above uses full-size 2048-dim embeddings. Thanks to the Matryoshka training, the finetuned model also holds up well when truncated to fewer dimensions, letting you trade off embedding size and retrieval quality at deployment time:.

The finetuned model's peak is at the full 2048 dimensions (0.948), but it stays within 0.3% of peak all the way down to 512 (4x smaller), and retains over 92% of peak even at 64 (32x smaller). Matryoshka training concentrates the most crucial information in the earlier dimensions, so moderate truncation costs very little performance.

The gap between 1024 and 2048 dimensions is small (0.946 vs. 0.948), so I've saved the model with truncate_dim=1024 set in its configuration. This means that SentenceTransformer("tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr") produces 1024-dimensional embeddings by default, halving the storage footprint compared to the full 2048. If you want a different dimensionality, pass truncate_dim=N when loading to override it.

You can also finetune multimodal Cross Encoder (reranker) models using the same training infrastructure. The key difference is using CrossEncoderTrainer and Cross Encoder-specific loss functions. This section provides a brief overview; see the full training examples for complete, runnable scripts with dataset preparation and evaluation.

Here's a simplified example based on the doodles training script, which trains a reranker to match images with text captions:.

There are multiple valid architectural choices for multimodal rerankers, including:.

Both approaches are demonstrated in the multimodal cross encoder training examples.

In a recent development, the two scripts linked above split the training data into two datasets, one per direction (image-to-text and text-to-image), with a task-specific prompt for each that tells the model how to score in that direction. Each positive pair is then expanded with randomly sampled negatives so the loss sees a balanced mix of matches and non-matches.

The Sentence Transformers repository includes several multimodal training examples:.

The direct prerequisite and the prior training guides are listed first, followed by related technique posts that stack with multimodal training:.

Industry News: The token factory never sleeps

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that SPONSORED FEATURE: Agentic AI turns inference into a round-the-clock production job.
  • Agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure.
  • Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that SPONSORED FEATURE: Agentic AI turns inference into a round-the-clock production job. Here's what it takes to keep the tokens flowing in the datacenter you already have.

Agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure. According to Goldman Sachs, token consumption is set to jump 24-fold to 120 quadrillion tokens per month between this year and 2030. Enterprises, wary of frontier model sticker shock, are now building their own GPU estates to cope.

Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production. The indicators of success for such companies are different than those for a frontier model provider, and so are the constraints. DIY AI infrastructure at the enterprise level has to earn ROI promptly, meaning that enterprises must focus on sustained operation. That makes engineering criteria such as uptime, heat and power, service windows, and deployment times doubly important. The performance benchmarks that hyperscalers focus on won't matter nearly as much to the average bank or retailer.

ASUS is presenting the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, built on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, as a worked example of sustained AI inference infrastructure. It announced two models at NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October: the 3U hybrid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BHFS and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BLFS.

In a recent development, agents represent a hockey stick curve for token consumption because an agent isn't a single prompt. It loops until the job's done, often spawning other versions of itself in the process. This is how it breaks a goal into steps and works through them iteratively.

While training is a batch workload, agent inference is a production service that runs around the clock and only gets bigger. NVIDIA is making each generation of systems more powerful than the last to keep up with the demands of both.

In a recent development, running at scale, day after day, is another matter. A useful way to think about the infrastructure that does it is as a token factory: it takes in power, data and GPU compute and turns out tokens. What counts is throughput, meaning how many tokens, and how many owners, the same power and floor space can serve, hour after hour.

It has been revealed that enterprises are moving ahead promptly with their AI factory projects. According to Deloitte's AI infrastructure survey, published in March, 64 percent of respondents have started limited or at-scale AI factory deployments, while 88 percent expect to do so by 2028. They are spending more on AI infrastructure to do it: 86 percent expect their budgets to increase over the next three years.

Enterprises have different problems from hyperscalers and frontier model companies, though. Model builders often get to design greenfield campuses around their GPUs. Conversely, enterprises are often working with small operations teams in existing datacenters that may not have been built with AI in mind. That means they need to think harder about maintenance windows, existing management tooling and predictable deployment. And they'll often be retrofitting halls whose racks rarely draw more than 30 kW.

Sources indicate that in token factory terms, the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System is the core compute engine. Each system puts eight NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPUs on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, linked by sixth-generation NVLink. ASUS has designed its equipment to support the constraints above. Its customers can choose between the hybrid and fully liquid-cooled models, and they can opt for partial or full rack configurations by buying multiple trays. This enables them to match their facilities' needs.

The other difference between model providers and enterprises lies in which numbers they care about. Peak performance is different from sustained performance. The first is a specification sheet number, while the second is what the GPU actually delivers hours into a heavy workload.

Industry observers note that production inference tends to run continuously, especially when it uses agents, as opposed to training, which is a sporadic job. So the sustained figure is the one that buyers pay for. Heat becomes a real glitch here because when cooling can't keep up, GPUs throttle their clocks to protect themselves. In a token factory, a throttled GPU is a slower production line.

The more advanced the architecture becomes, the higher the stakes get. NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU has raised them to their highest point, delivering up to 400 petaflops of NVFP4 inference per eight-GPU board, according to NVIDIA's sparse specification. This is screamingly fast, but the increased heat per board means less margin before throttling.

ASUS designed both models to put direct-to-chip liquid cooling on every GPU. Only the 3U unit leaves the CPUs on air cooling. ASUS also says it puts every configuration through a 168-hour stress test.

As boards increase their compute density, pushing up the power and heat requirements, planning naturally has to move out of the server room and into the facility. That's the case whether you're talking about an entire NVL72 rack or a stack of eight-GPU servers like the ASUS systems.

It has been revealed that there are other things to consider beyond heat. Few datacenters run racks drawing more than 30 kilowatts, states the Uptime Institute. Yet a single liquid-cooled tray of the ASUS systems draws up to 23.9 kilowatts, and a full rack of nine has a power budget of about 216 kilowatts.

Floor loading and power distribution matter as much as cooling.

It has been revealed that NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU raises the stakes again. The eight-GPU format enables organizations to buy their computing power in more granular steps. That's where the two ASUS systems come into their own. With few enterprises needing a training cluster at NVL72 scale, the advantage is that an HGX box lets them buy AI compute in digestible pieces.

The ASUS systems also come with a 54V busbar and cable-free board-to-board design. ASUS says this simplifies assembly and improves reliability.

In a recent development, so that's space, power and heat. But a GPU board won't produce many tokens if the network, storage or operational tooling can't feed it properly. Agent workloads move context and data all the time, so east-west bandwidth and local storage are key to effective utilization. Any new equipment should ideally slot straight into the enterprise's existing management and monitoring tooling.

In a recent development, ASUS ships the whole rack, including servers, networking, power and storage, as a single blueprint. ASUS pre-validates this AI Factory reference architecture at rack scale so that organizations can plan for future growth. That includes dedicated management nodes and a management switch.

Inside each tray, ASUS has sized the data paths to keep the GPUs fed. Eight OSFP ports on NVIDIA ConnectX-9 give every GPU 800Gb/s of east-west bandwidth to the rest of the cluster, and an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU adds two 400GbE ports. Within the board, the eight GPUs talk to each other over NVLink at 3,600GB/s, ASUS notes. The 2U tray takes up to 4TB of DDR5 system memory and has eight E1.S NVMe bays for fast local data access, while the 3U model offers a choice of U.2 or E1.S drives.

In a recent development, the other glitch for enterprises putting AI inference into production is service and maintenance. In a liquid-cooled box, routine fixes can mean draining a coolant loop, which is downtime, and lost token output, that most enterprises can't afford, especially when dealing with non-batch workloads such as inferencing. So ASUS set out to make components quicker to swap.

On the 2U fully liquid-cooled model, ASUS did it with independent, tool-less CPU and GPU sleds, each with its own direct-to-chip cooling. On the 3U hybrid, ASUS states the air-cooled CPU sled cuts maintenance time by up to 50 percent.

Services aren't just about server maintenance. They're also about decreasing the time to value for AI. Most enterprises won't have in-house rack-scale GPU integration skills, which is why pre-validation and design services are so key.

Sources indicate that ASUS notes its services run from early facility assessment through to operations. Its professional services cover five offerings: infrastructure design, deployment, performance optimization, AI platform development and lifecycle management. For rapid deployment, ASUS uses its own automation platform, the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center (AIDC).

So, with an enterprise token factory judged on how reliably it keeps producing rather than on peak FLOPS, in-house AI deployment teams will be back to focusing on the basics, albeit while dealing with an innovative technology. That means they'll be asking questions about sustained performance, heat and power in existing facilities. They'll be looking at integration at the rack level and with management software, along with service windows and deployment time. ASUS is positioning itself as a partner that can answer those questions with the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, which it's making available this quarter.

Find out more about the liquid-cooled ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens.
  • Industry observers note that the platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

India’s Digital Infrastructure for Governance Impact and Transformation tool can leak data.

India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens.

Industry observers note that the platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants.

DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities.

In a recent development, india also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka.

India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.”.

In a recent development, “An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.”.

eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an patch that fixes the problem.

While local government consumers of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities.

Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®.

Pimalaya goes stable

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pimalaya

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once, at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard.
  • Industry observers note that most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody.
  • In Another year with NLnet I said this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once, at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard. Here the list:.

Industry observers note that most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody. This post explains why, how, and where it goes from here. It is long, feel free to jump to the tool you care about.

In Another year with NLnet I said this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk. This release is the result of both.

The thing is, every piece is now connected:.

According to recent reports, releasing them one by one meant releasing tools that disagree with each other: one version of the store here, another version of the output there. So I decided to bring every tool to release level first, then to release them all together. It took way longer than I wanted, but this way what you install today is one coherent family.

Recent findings suggest that the other reason is the contract. The CLIs are not only used by humans anymore: they are used by scripts, by frontends (the Vim plugin, the TUI, the Android app), and by AI agents through MCP. All of them need a stable, versioned contract: the same JSON shapes, the same error codes, the same exit codes. Majors are the right moment to fix it, and from now on it should not move anymore without a new major.

Few things made this release possible.

Sources indicate that specs before code. Every repository has a cairn/ folder holding its living spec, its change proposals and a dated log. Every behaviour change goes through a proposal, then gets folded into the spec. This way the truth is written somewhere, and not only in my head.

One shared kit. The pimalaya-cli and pimalaya-config libs hold everything the CLIs have in common: the output contract, the error codes, the REPL, the MCP server, the configuration loading. In fact most of the work of this release was moving code from the CLIs into this kit, and deleting the copies.

Recent findings suggest that one unified API, as a union. Before, the commands shared by every backend were the intersection of what the backends could do: if one backend could not do it, nobody could. Now it is the union: each backend registers the capabilities it really serves, with the same observable result as the others, and a command an account cannot serve fails before even connecting, with a clear capability-missing code.

Measured gates for pimdir. Audits always find something, so "no new finding" never ends. Instead, I built a test generator that produces stores, remote states and an oracle from a seed, and ran campaigns of 4,180 jobs against io-pimdir: crashes injected at every step, the search index checked against a full rebuild after each event, the sync engine replayed against scripted servers. The rule was simple: 2 campaigns in a row without any spec break, then freeze. Campaign 1 found one, campaigns 2 and 3 were clean, a late fix restarted the count, then campaigns 4 and 5 were clean. Freeze.

In a recent development, live tests on real providers. Every CLI was tested against real accounts: Google, Microsoft, Fastmail and iCloud, plus few Chinese providers for Himalaya (QQ, 163, 139). A last "live night" just before the release found few bugs that went straight into the libs.

Sources indicate that libs first, apps after. The libs were released between the 13th and the 25th of November, the apps then moved to them without any patch or git pin. Everything you install comes from crates.io.

It has been revealed that pimdir is a local-first standard for personal information: mails, contacts, calendars, tasks and files in one portable store, kept as a replica of every source, and searchable with one query language. A store is one SQLite file plus a content-addressed blob directory, the same on every OS and architecture. I already explained why such a standard is needed in Another year with NLnet, and how the Android app became its first full implementation in Pimalaya for Android enters closed alpha.

It comes in 3 parts, versioned separately:.

They are released together because a store holds sync state that follows the sync part, and the query language binds every program that offers search.

In a recent development, what v1 means: schema version 1 never changes, every schema change is a migration, and a minor version only adds test cases. You can implement it in any language that speaks SQLite, use the I/O-free core of io-pimdir (like the Android app does, on the platform SQLite), or use its std client.

In a recent development, few days before the freeze, I compared it with notmuch, which is the reference in this area. They do not do the same job (notmuch indexes mail files it does not own, pimdir owns the bodies, syncs them and holds other domains), but the search can be compared. On a store of 1 million messages from the Enron corpus, pimdir was ahead of notmuch on 50 of the 51 query measures and tied the last one, imported the million faster, and used a third of the memory. Stemming, regex and per-thread queries are still missing, they are on the list.

One warning for the early adopters: a store written by a draft version is refused, never migrated. Sync it till nothing is pending with the last draft binary, move its directory aside, then let a release create and sync a new one.

This is the change many of you will not like, so let me explain it properly.

Industry observers note that every CLI had a configuration wizard: you typed your email address, it discovered the servers, asked for the password, stored it in your keyring, and wrote the TOML for you. It is gone, from every CLI.

It has been revealed that the direction. The CLIs are now low-level tools: plain text to glance at, JSON for scripts, frontends and agents. Comfort (tables, colours, relative dates, guided setups, rich composition) belongs to frontends. In fact this is not new: it is the same split that started the whole project, back when the logic left the Vim plugin. The CLI was always supposed to be the backend a frontend needs. This release just goes all the way.

According to recent reports, I know some of you used the wizard to get started, and that copying a sample feels like a step back. If the welcome or the samples are not clear enough, it is a bug: please open an glitch, I would rather fix the docs than bring back a second setup system per CLI.

Himalaya is now a low-level CLI over a unified mail API: the same commands on every backend, the protocol-specific ones next to them, plain text for a glance and --json for the rest.

Backends: IMAP, SMTP, ManageSieve, JMAP, the Gmail API, Microsoft Graph, Maildir (with a upcoming maildir++ layout for Dovecot and Courier stores), mbox, and pimdir. The README has recipes for Proton Mail (through Bridge), Fastmail, Gmail, Outlook, Posteo and iCloud.

It has been revealed that what is gone: the wizard, the m2dir backend (superseded by pimdir), the table and colour options, HIMALAYA_CONFIG. Unknown configuration keys are now refused, JSON keys are camelCase, and the v2 search syntax needs to be rewritten. The migration guide lists everything, with a full table for the queries.

According to recent reports, neverest is rebuilt around the pimdir store: every account syncs into one shared store, which the other CLIs read, search and queue their writes into. It syncs mails, contacts and calendars over IMAP, Gmail, Microsoft Graph, Google Calendar, Google People, CalDAV and CardDAV.

According to recent reports, JMAP sources are not supported yet (it is a draft), so Fastmail syncs over IMAP, CardDAV and CalDAV for now. Coming from v0.x? Your configuration and state are not carried over: start from the config.sample.toml, then run neverest sync --init.

The first stable release of Cardamum: a low-level CLI over a unified contacts API, with the same commands on CardDAV, JMAP, Microsoft Graph, Google People, vdir and pimdir.

card search speaks the pimdir query language on every backend, account capability reveals what an account serves without connecting, and you get the REPL and the MCP server like the others. Editing a card is left to a composer such as tcard. The wizard and the discover route are gone.

Same story for calendars: the same commands on CalDAV, JMAP (fresh), Google Calendar, Microsoft Graph, vdir and pimdir.

New: event search, recurrence expansion, attendees and alarms, online meetings (--online-meeting), invitation replies through pimdir, and an agenda that draws a month or a year like cal(1) does. Editing an event is left to a composer such as tcal. The wizard, the tables and colours, and the todo and journal commands are gone: tasks and journals will move to dedicated tools (Unfog and Journal), not released yet.

Carillon is a local watcher that fires hooks on what changes in your mailboxes, address books and calendars, over IMAP, JMAP, Maildir, CalDAV, CardDAV, Microsoft Graph, the Google APIs and the pimdir store. It uses push where the server offers it (IMAP IDLE, the JMAP event stream) and polls elsewhere. A hook runs a command, shows a desktop notification, or both.

Fresh in v1: a pimdir backend, on-alarm-trigger for the alarms of events and tasks, on-birthday-trigger for birthdays and anniversaries, a per-hook timeout, and a report of what moved while an IMAP or Gmail session was lost. Hooks now take the same shape as Comodoro's.

Ortie manages OAuth tokens for the other tools. v3 aligns it on the rest of the family: ready-made Google, Microsoft and Fastmail accounts to paste, token revocation, an auth listen to catch a redirection handed off from another machine, account checks, a REPL, and an MCP server that never hands the token to the agent. The wizard and the hooks are gone (the storage write command does what a hook did).

According to recent reports, comodoro manages timers: one server owns a timer, any number of clients drive it, over a local socket or TCP. v3 joins the same standard: comodoro watch feeds a status bar without polling, hooks get the cycle name and duration, plus the welcome, account checks, a REPL and an MCP server. Comodoro is now a binary only: the library is gone, and the open JSON-RPC protocol is the contract for third parties.

None of the above would exist without the libs below, all released in November on crates.io:.

They are all I/O-free, as usual: feel free to build your own tools at the top of them.

In a recent development, each README lists the ways to install: prebuilt binaries from the GitHub releases (or the install.sh script), cargo install --locked, Nix, and the APT, DNF and Homebrew repositories at pkg.pimalaya.org. The packages are landing there over the coming days, and the nixpkgs and home-manager updates are on their way.

Special thanks to the NLnet foundation and the European Commission's NGI initiative, for the financial support through NGI Zero Core and now the NGI Zero Commons Fund. This kind of slow, deep work is only possible thanks to them.

And thank you to everyone who reported bugs, tested betas, or simply waited patiently while everything was being rebuilt. Any feedback is welcomed, on GitHub, on Matrix or on Mastodon. Let me know how it goes!

Breaking: The PR you would have opened yourself

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness.
  • Sources indicate that we provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers.
  • In 2026, code agents started to actually work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness.

Sources indicate that we provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers. The Skill is designed to support contributors and reviewers as an aide, not an automation. We explain why we did it, how, and comment about how to meaningfully contribute to open source in the age of agents.

In 2026, code agents started to actually work. What used to be auto-completion at the side of your editor turned into a system that one-shots reasonable solutions from brief specifications. The generated code usually works out of the box, covers what you asked for, and makes reasonable assumptions about details you didn't specify. This is great. As Jensen Huang puts it, we've instantly gone from 30 million to one billion coders in the world. Creative minds are unleashed.

But it forces us to rethink open source.

Take the transformers library as an example. It has hundreds of contributors, is used in thousands of projects, has been downloaded over a billion times. Suddenly, anyone with an agent can instruct it to find some open matter, fix it, and submit a PR. And that's exactly what's happening. Those people feel happy because they are contributing to a great library, but the sad reality is that, most of the time, they don't realize they are not.

Why not? There are two assumptions that agent-generated PRs usually miss.

Industry observers note that codebases like transformers care deeply about the code. It's cool to build projects where it doesn't matter what the code looks like, but transformers is not one of them. Being used by thousands of people, transformers is primarily built as a human-to-human communication method, through code. Model files read top to bottom, because we want practitioners to understand them without jumping through complex abstractions. This permeates throughout the library design and is the reason why, for example, we favor flat hierarchies.

Agents don't have that context. Because design decisions are not explicit, agents suggest refactors to "improve" the codebase by following "best practices", without realizing they are breaking implicit contracts between the library and its users. They are verbose, generalize too early, don't notice when a change affects other areas, introduce subtle bugs, break performance. They are also sycophantic, and accept any idea as good and follow it through diligently, including ones a maintainer would have pushed back early on with a terse comment.

Recent findings suggest that A small number of maintainers still has to read every PR, understand it, decide if the design direction is right, identify side effects, and write feedback. PR volume has gone up tenfold, but the amount of maintainers has not (and cannot, because team coordination does not scale).

Sources indicate that transformers is one of the first projects to feel this pressure because of sheer volume, but the same dynamic is happening everywhere. As an example from a different domain, App Store reviewers are swamped because anyone can now build and submit an app, so many do.

According to recent reports, the same logic applies to MLX: their maintainers care deeply about the code and read every PR carefully. We wanted to see whether agents could help contributors land high-quality model ports fast, and at the same time support reviewers in their work. Not only do we aspire to produce PRs that could have come from a careful human submission, but we also provide additional artifacts to increase the signal: generation examples, numerical comparisons, and a separate non-agentic test harness for reproducibility.

Industry observers note that another connection between transformers and MLX is that, most times, mlx-lm models are ported from transformers implementations. Because transformers focuses on clarity and readability, it has become the source of truth for model definitions. Downstream contributors wait until the transformers implementations are ready before they port to other frameworks. As a side effect, this is an excellent environment for an agent because it naturally limits the scope: rather than creating an implementation from scratch, the agent relies on transformers code as the source of truth.

This approach supports our goal: when a model lands in transformers, it should be available on MLX shortly after.

We built a Skill that mlx-lm contributors can use to port a model from transformers to MLX. Given a prompt like "convert the olmo_hybrid architecture to MLX", the Skill sets up a virtual environment to work on, discovers and downloads the relevant models from the Hub, reads the transformers modeling code, writes the MLX implementation, and runs a battery of tests. If results don't look right, it debugs and iterates, and does not declare success until it's satisfied.

We designed it to be useful to reviewers as much as contributors.

In a recent development, for the contributor, the Skill of course handles all the scaffolding: finding model variants on the Hub, diffing their configs to spot parameters that vary across model variants, downloading checkpoints, setting up editable installs of both mlx-lm and transformers. But it also handles the more difficult modeling tasks. It pays attention to salient architecture details and verifies sensitive areas, like RoPE configurations, that may result in hard-to-find bugs. It detects when the config doesn't declare a dtype and infers it from the safetensors metadata header. It runs per-layer comparisons between transformers and MLX to pinpoint exactly where divergence occurs. These are the kinds of checks that only someone with porting experience would think to run.

According to recent reports, for the reviewer, the Skill produces a PR that is upfront about being agent-assisted, but does look like a careful human submission. Reviewers will see that the code follows mlx-lm conventions: idiomatic solutions, no unnecessary comments, no speculative abstractions, no modifications to shared utilities without explicit approval. Given that the code is agent-assisted, we try to include more data than the median PR, to provide as much signal as possible. The PR body includes a report with a summary of the variants and their architectural differences, generation examples, numerical comparisons, dtype verification, per-layer comparisons against the transformers baseline. The PR always discloses that it was agent-assisted, and the Skill will not open it until the contributor has accepted the results.

For verification, the Skill generates a test manifest for a separate, non-agentic test harness that is, by design, easily reproducible and not subject to LLM hallucinations or complacency (more on this below).

Skills are recipes for agents: simple text files with guidelines that steer the model through a complex task. They are not magic; you can achieve the same results via prompting and iteration. But they provide consistency (every run follows the same process, whereas different people would prompt differently), minimize ambiguity and serve as documentation: anyone can read the Skill to understand what it does, identify missing cases and suggest improvements.

We bootstrapped the Skill by porting a model ourselves, in conversation with Claude. I asked it to port GLM 4.7 from transformers to mlx-lm, giving instructions as I would during a normal session. One trick: I pointed Claude at a checkout of mlx-lm from which I had deleted the already-existing implementation, so I could compare the output against the ground truth. After a few iterations I had a working implementation, a conversation that revealed how Claude approached the problem, and the first draft of the Skill, which Claude created as a summary of the process. I edited it heavily, and incorporated the learnings from @gabegoodhart, who kindly shared their own porting conversation for a different model 🙌.

We repeated this loop several times and the Skill grew. On the technical side, we covered stuff such as RoPE bugs that may produce plausible output that degrades with long sequences, float32 precision contamination that silently kills inference speed (you'd be surprised how frequently these things happen!), config fields that vary across model variants in ways the implementation must handle, distributed inference for super large models that don't fit on a single machine. We taught it how to invoke the hf CLI to discover and download models. Most importantly, we instructed it to run the tests that experienced porters would, and to not declare success until they pass.

Sources indicate that on the cultural side, we covered softer characteristics and explained the conventions that make a PR easy to review: don't use comments to explain code (the reviewer has to parse the comment and the code 🤦‍♂️), never propose refactors, don't touch shared utilities without asking. These rules cost the agent nothing but save the reviewer lots of time.

The end result: the contributor types a prompt, and the Skill produces a PR like this one, plus a test manifest for the external test harness.

The Skill shares a comprehensive results report as part of the PR. All these come from tests the agent runs during conversion, but we didn't want the reviewer to take a leap of faith to accept them. To go a step forward, we created a separate, non-agentic test harness that runs systematic tests on the converted code. This brings a couple of benefits:.

The test harness is not a CI gate. Some checks are straightforward (is the output dtype correct?), but most are qualitative. Is it normal that a pre-trained model repeats itself in long sequences? Is a 4% relative logits difference against the transformers baseline acceptable? These are judgement calls based on experience with similar architectures. The harness provides useful signal, but it's the reviewer and contributor who still have to make the call.

The Skill is designed for the people who are already opening mlx-lm model PRs, or who would do it manually on their own. It's not meant for mass consumption, because PRs to mlx-lm are rarely accepted on sight. The typical cycle is: contributor opens a PR, reviewers point out improvements, both sides iterate until the quality bar is met. If this is true for expert submissions, it will remain true for agent-assisted ones.

In a recent development, if you're not prepared to engage in that cycle, you probably shouldn't be opening a PR. The reviewers will make an effort to understand your code (even knowing it was agent-assisted), so you should do the same. Own the code, and be ready to incorporate their feedback. In particular, don't hand reviewer comments back to an agent and post whatever it produces. LLMs double down on their decisions, go on tangents, and don't push back effectively. Once you engage with the reviewer, this becomes a person-to-person conversation, so it's your turn to discuss and be respectful of the time they put in.

Sources indicate that you can also use the Skill to learn; you don't need to submit anything until your confidence and experience build. Read the Skill to identify problem areas you weren't aware of: it contains nearly 15 thousand words among the skill file, reference docs and utility scripts. Point it to your own fork of mlx-lm, try a conversion, and compare your output against the accepted implementation once it lands in the official repo. If you do this a few times, you'll learn a lot about transformers, MLX, and language model architectures.

According to recent reports, we developed and tested the Skill using Claude Code. The same approach would work with Codex or other coding agents, but we haven't tested them. If you try the Skill in a different environment, please let us know how it goes!

The Skill works well for LLMs in mlx-lm, but there's plenty of room to grow.

The bottleneck in open source is not typing speed: it's understaning the codebase to change it without breaking the implicit and explicit contracts with users. Agents can help in this process, if we teach them what matters. We explored what this looks like in the context of mlx-lm, and hope it's useful for contributors and reviewers to land high-quality model conversions faster!

Thanks a lot to Ben, Shaun, Aritra for reading previous versions of this post and making it so much better 🙌.

We are incredibly indebted to Apple for making MLX an open-source project, and to the community for instantly recognizing its value and contributing enthusiastically 🙏.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Automating Spark Upgrades with Codex Agents at OpenAI.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, engineering manager for data infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks. OpenAI’s platform runs at exabyte scale, with hundreds of thousands of datasets and a Spark fleet on millions of cores, and Mukherjee showed how Codex-driven agents can take on that kind of work when the right systems sit underneath them.

Sources indicate that mukherjee clearly distinguished between deterministic systems and agents. She stated that anything requiring consistent outputs for the same inputs, such as access control, configuration resolution, and data correctness guarantees, should remain within the realm of proper systems. Agents utilize these systems as tools and do not attempt to reimplement them. As she expressed:.

We should definitely build the systems where we want guarantees and guardrails.

Agents earn their place where failure modes and remediations cannot be fully enumerated in advance, such as debugging: follow the evidence, decide what to try next, and stay inside the tools’ guarantees.

The Spark upgrade outlines steps taken to ensure safety. The team first built a shadow-run service for testing, which reused production inputs and operated on a low-priority queue to avoid impacting live operations. They also implemented a configuration override service to prevent experiments from changing global settings and developed a validation skill to compare production and shadow runs. After these safeguards were in place, agents claimed jobs, debuted shadow runs, reviewed validation reports, classified errors, and transitioned jobs to the latest Spark version.

Recent findings suggest that mukherjee reported that the same primitives now cover more of routine platform operations. Agents can tune job efficiency continuously by inspecting query plans, trying a config change, comparing runs, and iterating. For lower-risk incremental library releases, the team sometimes skips the shadow step and promotes directly, trading capacity for higher rollback risk. Jobs that pass shadow validation but later fail in production can auto-roll back to the previous Spark version so pipelines keep running without manual intervention. On the support side, agents can search past incident reports, suggest runbook updates, trace why a table is stale through orchestrator and scheduler logs, and help owners understand access-control denials, while permissions still enforce the user’s own credentials.

Mukherjee recommended starting with the repetitive, open-ended tasks where judgment matters and failure modes are too numerous to hard-code, building the safety mechanisms first, and only then letting agents operate inside those bounds so experimentation stays repeatable, observable, and reversible.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.
  • Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts revealed almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results indicated that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Sources indicate that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.
