📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client token support provided by AWS. Implementing this required making some fairly substantial changes to the generator, the bespoke Haskell program that turns the service definitions in botocore into cabal packages. amazonka is over a decade old, and the generator has evolved as AWS have added fresh styles of APIs for their different services. Some services return XML, some return JSON, some return raw bytes, some return additional information in HTTP response headers, and so on. As a result, the generatorâs logic had been extended each time and had grown gnarly.

Recent findings suggest that to untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, âmake the plan a valueâ or âdecide what to do, and then do itâ. This move decouples two parts of a program by introducing an intermediate data structure (a âplanâ, or a value of a âplan typeâ) describing what is to be done before any action is taken.

Sources indicate that I really like this pattern because the âdeciding what to doâ part of a program is often more complicated than the âdoingâ part. Separating the two often turns the âdecidingâ part into a pure function that produces a plan, making test cases simpler to write. And then if the âdoingâ phase is also complicated (because of remote API calls, rollbacks, parallel execution, or whatever else), itâs more manageable because those complications are not entangled with the planning logic. You also get to add a --dry-run flag almost for free, which is really useful for testing. (Henrik observes that testing for a dryRun variable everywhere pollutes the code somewhat. I think if he split his code into a planning phase and consumed that plan with either a âdry runâ printer or a ârealâ executor, the inline checks that he dislikes would disappear.).

Industry observers note that this technique isnât subtle or obscure. Iâve seen it called the proposal-execute pattern, and the ârouting slipâ enterprise integration pattern is literally about centralising the decision logic before execution. Iâve previously called it a âtiny DSLâ, and Matt Parsons sells its benefits in his Three Layer Haskell Cake article:.

Having resolved to introduce a initiative type, how do we work it into a venerable program like the Amazonka generator? For this part of the generator, it means separating the analysis of the loaded service definitions from the generation of the instance AWSRequest declarations. I did this by introducing a Config record of simple data and a function instanceD :: Config -> Decl () that builds Haskell code from that config record.

Industry observers note that I found the generatorâs logic too difficult to understand and replace in a single change, so I replaced it incrementally using the strangler fig pattern. The most complicated part of this change was response parsing, so I added to the Config record an enumeration of ported response parsers, and a fall back to âdo things the old wayâ for everything else:.

One thing that makes Amazonkaâs generator rewarding to hack on is that the service bindings act as an extensive and automatic golden test suite. Any changes to the generated bindings show up in diffs, and so if there are no diffs and the generator doesnât crash, the change probably didnât break anything. This makes the process of replacing the entangled code relatively simple (not easy):.

It has been revealed that the end result worked well and kept the individual commits readable (example: factoring out status code parsing). Adding the idempotency machinery was then straightforward.

Industry observers note that the data types in the Amazonka example represent parameters to a Haskell code template, but this refactoring also works for more expressive plan types, such as âtiny DSLsâ, âlists of commandsâ, or âfree structuresâ. The trick is to keep a âdo it the old wayâ constructor in your plan type until the âold wayâ has been refactored away.

In a recent development, A well-chosen strategy type introduces a narrow waist that decouples producers and consumers of your plan type, and the most obvious wins come from introducing alternate consumers of the plan: things like testability, --dry-run, and simpler executors all follow from that. A less obvious benefit is that you can also analyse and transform the plan itself. This is a great place to add pre-execution sanity checks or access controls. I regret that my tiny DSLs post inverted a transformation by interpreting it as matrix multiplications and inverting the result; it would have been simpler to provide an invert :: [Transform] -> [Transform] function.

Introducing alternate producers of the blueprint type can also pay off, but needs a bit more imagination:.

âMaking the plan a valueâ works well in any language, but Haskellâs laziness makes it especially nice. Lazy evaluation can avoid materialising the whole plan in memory if it is consumed right away. Even in strict languages, the decoupling benefits are great enough that the extra memory use is often worth it.

For those who never heard of con artists, "circular financing" is the idea that I give you one dollar, on condition that you give it straight back to me.Not quite. It's more like this, in simple terms. Suppose I'm the "you" mentioned in your illustration.(1) You invest $1 in my tech giant, on condition in (2) below.(2) I use that dollar to buy something from you, as a condition on the investment you gave me in (1) above. Note that I don't just give the dollar back to you: I use it to buy your merch.(3) You remain with $1 invested in my company, and you can claim $1 in revenue from the sale, but you are out $1 worth of inventory. So your effective "net" is $1 i.

Ecom-RLVE: Adaptive Verifiable Environments for E-Commerce Conversational Agents

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations.
  • This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥.
  • Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations. EcomRLVE-GYM provides 8 verifiable environments — product discovery, substitution, cart building, returns, order tracking, policy QA, bundle planning, and multi-intent journeys — each with procedural problem generation, a 12-axis difficulty curriculum, and algorithmically verifiable rewards. We train a Qwen 3 8B model with DAPO over 300 steps and present early results demonstrating that environment scaling and adaptive difficulty transfer to agentic, real-world task completion.

This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥.

Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion. A customer who asks "find me a USB-C charger under $25 that ships in two days" needs an agent that invokes the right catalog search, filters on three hard constraints, avoids hallucinating product IDs it never retrieved, and handles follow-ups when the top result goes out of stock.

Supervised fine-tuning can teach surface-level tool use from demonstrations, but it cannot scale to the combinatorial space of constraint configurations, partial-information dialogues, and multi-step transactional workflows that real e-commerce demands.

In a recent development, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers an alternative: the agent optimises for outcomes — did the products satisfy the constraints? Was the cart correct? Was the return initiated for the right order line? The challenge is constructing reward functions that are both verifiable (no LLM-as-a-judge subjectivity) and adaptive (difficulty that grows with the policy's capability).

RLVE-Gym provides 400 environments for sorting, multiplication, Sudoku, and other algorithmic-reasoning tasks; however, those are all single-turn, text-in / text-out puzzles — extending to agentic domains was left as future work.

EcomRLVE-GYM fills that gap: we stay in the verifiable regime (e-commerce outcomes can be checked algorithmically) while extending to multi-turn, tool-augmented, agentic conversations — environments where the agent must act (call tools, modify world state) rather than merely reason (produce a text answer) and compensates for the deficiency of the search system.

EcomRLVE-GYM transforms customer-service outcomes structurally verifiable:.

Every signal above can be evaluated by a program with access to the hidden ground-truth goal. No human annotation or LLM-as-a-judge is needed.

In a recent development, before we explain the framework, here is what a single EcomRLVE episode looks like at difficulty d = 4. The environment generates a hidden goal, a simulated user opens the chat, and the agent must use tools to satisfy the request. Every action is verified algorithmically — no LLM judge required.

According to recent reports, the reward is fully computed by code: F1 over (product, variant, qty) tuples, an efficiency bonus for finishing in fewer turns, and a hallucination check that every recommended product ID was actually retrieved. If the agent had picked the Lightning variant instead of USB-C, the simulated user would have corrected it mid-dialogue — and the F1 would have dropped.

Each environment covers a distinct real-world shopping scenario. The agent must complete the task using tools (catalog search, cart operations, order lookups, policy queries) and is scored by a program — not a human or another LLM.

Every environment uses the same three-part reward signal:.

Invalid outputs (malformed JSON, illegal tool calls) trigger an immediate failure score, creating a strong incentive for well-formed responses from step one.

Sources indicate that A single difficulty number d controls 12 independent aspects of a task simultaneously. This is important because e-commerce conversations are hard in many different ways at once — not just along one dimension.

Here are four representative difficulty axes:.

Sources indicate that the other eight axes cover turn budget, input noise (typos, slang), context switches, retrieval depth, order-history size, policy complexity, and tool budget. The full breakdown is in the technical report.

Adaptive scheduling. Each environment tracks the agent's success rate independently and only advances to harder problems once the agent is passing the current level reliably. This keeps every environment training at the agent's capability frontier — avoiding both "too easy to learn from" and "too hard to make progress on".

Cart building is a good showcase because it requires the full search → inspect → clarify → act loop, has a binary ground truth, and introduces a challenge absent from most recommendation benchmarks: variant selection.

To succeed, the agent must develop five distinct skills:.

The agent uses six tools to accomplish this:.

Industry observers note that the generator samples 1–5 target products (scaling in difficulty with d), each potentially requiring a specific variant (USB-C vs Lightning, Matte vs Glossy) and a quantity > 1. The agent must:.

Real product catalogs have sparse variant data — many products have none, and those that do typically vary only by colour or size. To create a richer discrimination task, we synthesize variants at episode initialization:.

At d = 0 the agent adds a single product with no variant complexity — learning the basic catalog.search → cart.add workflow. At d = 6 it juggles 3 items, nearly all requiring a specific variant, with half needing qty > 1.

The cart must be exactly right — correct product, correct variant, correct quantity. Partial credit is given for partially correct carts, but a perfect score requires every item to match. If the agent adds the wrong variant, the simulated user corrects it mid-dialogue ("that's the Lightning version, but I need USB-C"), giving the agent a chance to self-correct before the episode ends.

In a recent development, two real E_CART episodes from a Qwen 3 8B agent. Same environment, same agent — difficulty alone changes the game.

At d=1 the agent solves the task in 3 clean turns. At d=8 it spirals — picking Bamboo instead of Charcoal, XL instead of XS, never fixing the air fryer despite two user corrections, then hallucinating that the variant doesn't exist. This is exactly the kind of multi-step error cascade that the difficulty curriculum surfaces, and that adaptive training should teach the agent to recover from.

Sources indicate that A verifiable environment needs a user simulator that behaves realistically. We use Qwen3.5 (9.7B) to generate natural, varied user messages rather than canned templates — covering everything from typo-filled requests to mid-conversation topic switches.

Two design choices matter for training quality:.

Preferences match stated constraints. Each simulated user has a hidden set of preferences (price sensitivity, brand loyalty, shipping speed, etc.). These are deliberately biased toward whatever constraints the user communicated — so if the user remarked "under $25", the reward function actually cares about price. Without this, an agent could be penalised for correctly following the user's instructions.

Strategic omission. The LLM deliberately withholds some constraints from the opening message to force the agent to ask clarifying questions. The system tracks exactly what was and wasn't mentioned, so the agent is never penalised for information it was never given.

Following RLVE's methodology, we define nested environment collections:.

We hypothesise — consistent with RLVE's findings — that C8 agents outperform single-environment specialists, even on the specialist's own task.

We trained Qwen 3 8B with DAPO on C1 (Cart Building) for 300 steps as an initial viability study.

We saw progressive growth in difficulty reached, confirming that adaptive scheduling produces a steady learning signal rather than the saturation (static-low) or starvation (static-high) patterns predicted by the RLVE paper.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emulating Android, too, but offers just two handsets and one tablet.
  • AWS now offers two fresh types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.
  • Recent findings suggest that the cloudy colossus revealed both virtual offerings on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emulating Android, too, but offers just two handsets and one tablet.

AWS now offers two fresh types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.

Recent findings suggest that the cloudy colossus revealed both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS.

AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices.

“With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement.

Industry observers note that AWS also indicates developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues.

That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland.

It has been revealed that when The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu.

At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0.

Analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10th place.

iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list.

AWS might excite more developers if it adds emulators for the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy A07 4G, A17 5G, A17 4G, and Galaxy S26, as they occupy the fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth and ninth places on Counterpoint’s list.

Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors.

Recent findings suggest that amazon does offer physical Galaxy A17 devices and three versions of the iPhone 17. But Device Farm doesn’t offer any foldable devices, meaning developers struggling to wrap their heads around the iPhone Duo will need either ask Apple for a loaner or shell out $2,000 to acquire one.

At least developers don’t have to change behavior to access the few virtual devices AWS offers, as existing Device Farm APIs and test frameworks will work on real or notional machines. ®.

  • Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes after Eight Years at 15.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes. The latest limit applies to synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and without an opt-in. The 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018, after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015.

Raising the limit is a configuration change per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds with a validation error:.

The change covers one of the three shapes Lambda took this year. Web Functions keep 15 minutes, and Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, while on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations now get 30 minutes and asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September. AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations, and report generation as the workloads that outgrew 15 minutes.

According to Tarun Rai Madan, Dan Slusariuc, and Snehil Ameta, the authors of the announcement, the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity:.

Concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. At the same request rate, a function that runs for 30 minutes instead of 15 needs twice the concurrency. For example, 1 request per second at 30 minutes each needs 1,800 concurrent executions.

Recent findings suggest that the rest of the post is about what sits around the function. An SQS queue's visibility timeout has to be at least six times the function timeout, which means three hours. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams read one batch per shard at a time, so a slow function slows the shard. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes. A NAT gateway still drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and the Init phase keeps its 10-second limit.

Wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner, tested the SQS rule in eu-west-1 by raising a function to 1,800 seconds behind a queue with a 90-minute visibility timeout and then lowering the queue to 60 seconds. Both changes were accepted with the mapping still enabled, while a new mapping from the same queue was refused:.

So the check exists, but only at creation. One more thing the test revealed: at creation, Lambda compared the queue with the function timeout itself, not with six times it. I did not test where exactly that line sits, so treat the six times as guidance you enforce yourself.

He adds that an asynchronous function which times out three times has run for 90 minutes before the event reaches a dead-letter queue, and concludes that 30 minutes is the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.

Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS and AWS Serverless Hero, writes:.

Industry observers note that hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.

Sources indicate that the comments under the post took two directions. Magnus Eriksson, architect and former AWS employee, notes that Lambda "is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2" and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads. Matthew Bonig, AWS DevTools Hero and co-author of The CDK Book, looked further ahead: "Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs.".

On Reddit, the most-upvoted reply welcomed the change because it avoids Fargate and ECS for hour-long batch jobs. The answer under it was that Fargate is beautifully simple. One commenter sets out where the longer limit fits:.

A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory, so check the cost per invocation before moving batch style work here, and keep the handler idempotent with a dead letter queue, because a failure or timeout partway through a long run can leave partial work behind. For multi step work, long running jobs, or anything that needs clear state and retries, Step Functions with Fargate or ECS is still usually cleaner.

Sources indicate that joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance, reads the move as Lambda team recognizing that Cloud Run is its most compelling competitor. Cloud Run services allow 60 minutes per request, and Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption and Premium plans enforce no maximum, with a 60-minute grace period during scale-in. AWS has not said whether the Lambda limit will move again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tempus AI entered a senior secured credit agreement on November 25, 2026, providing $385 million of term-loan commitments and $115 million of revolving commitments to help finance its pending Personalis acquisition, according to its Form 8-K.

In a recent development, in a separate November 24, 2026 decision, Tempus elected to pay approximately $600 million in cash and issue approximately $900 million in Tempus Class A common stock to Personalis shareholders. These are financing commitments, not evidence that the full amounts have already been drawn. Initial funding requires the acquisition to have closed or be reasonably expected to close within one business day after funding.

Industry observers note that tempus expects borrowings to fund part of the acquisition consideration and related transaction costs, as well as working capital and general corporate purposes. Ares Capital Corporation is the administrative and collateral agent, Ares Capital Management LLC the lead arranger and bookrunner, and ACF Finco I LP the revolving agent.

Term loans bear interest at either the agreement’s Base Rate benchmark plus 4.50% or its Term SOFR benchmark plus 5.50%; revolving loans use Base Rate plus 2.75% or Term SOFR plus 3.75%. Term SOFR has a 1.00% floor, the Base Rate a 2.00% floor, and interest on the loans is payable solely in cash.

In a recent development, both facilities mature on the fifth anniversary of the effective date. A springing provision can move maturity to 91 days before Tempus’s 0.75% convertible senior notes due 2030 unless those notes are repaid or converted first or specified liquidity requirements are met.

Sources indicate that certain Tempus subsidiaries will guarantee the obligations, which are secured by substantially all assets of Tempus and those subsidiaries. The agreement includes minimum-liquidity and minimum-revenue covenants. Revolving availability depends on eligible accounts receivable and certain qualified cash, subject to reserves and other limitations, and revolving interest can be charged on a minimum balance even when actual borrowings are lower.

Sources indicate that the cash election uses flexibility described in Tempus’s July 20, 2026 acquisition announcement. The merger agreement priced Personalis at $16.25 per common share, representing approximately $1.5 billion in enterprise value net of Tempus’s existing ownership. Consideration was originally structured as all stock, with Tempus holding an option to pay cash capped at 50% of the consideration and a floating exchange ratio capped at 0.3356 Tempus shares per Personalis share.

The cash estimate assumes 108,740,631 Personalis shares outstanding immediately before closing and no perfected appraisal demands. The number of shares designated for cash can automatically decrease, with a corresponding increase in the stock portion, to satisfy the merger agreement’s reorganization threshold, determined using Tempus’s closing-date trading price.

Tempus says the acquisition pairs its multimodal data, AI capabilities and commercial infrastructure with Personalis’s tumor-informed molecular residual disease (MRD) technology, including the NeXT Personal test, which detects small traces of circulating tumor DNA to monitor treatment response, residual cancer and recurrence.

The transaction builds on a partnership established in November 2023, through which Tempus invested in Personalis and commercialized NeXT Personal. Tempus CEO Eric Lefkofsky called MRD “a large and rapidly growing market” and said the collaboration had demonstrated the strength of combining Personalis’s technology with his tech giant’s commercial infrastructure.

According to recent reports, tempus originally expected the acquisition to close in late 2026 or early 2027. Closing remains subject to Personalis stockholder adoption of the merger agreement and other customary conditions. Tempus has now aligned the debt package with its cash-and-stock election, but the borrowing timetable and the proposed AI-supported MRD expansion both remain tied to completion of the acquisition.

AI and the Future of Cybersecurity: Why Openness Matters

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following the announcement of Mythos and Project Glasswing, institutions throughout the world are grappling with the potential dawn of a new era of cybersecurity.
  • Mythos is a “frontier AI model”, a large language model (LLM) that can be used to process software code (among many other things).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the announcement of Mythos and Project Glasswing, institutions throughout the world are grappling with the potential dawn of a new era of cybersecurity. In this post, we break down the current situation, discuss the role of openness, and situate the future of cybersecurity within the larger AI ecosystem.

Mythos is a “frontier AI model”, a large language model (LLM) that can be used to process software code (among many other things). This follows a general trend in LLM development, where LLM performance on code-related tasks has recently skyrocketed. What’s particularly significant about Mythos is the system it’s embedded within: It's the system, not the model alone, that has enabled Mythos to rapidly find and patch software vulnerabilities. Understanding this distinction is key to understanding the current landscape of AI cybersecurity.

What Mythos demonstrates is that the following system recipe is powerful:.

It has been revealed that together, these ingredients can uncover software vulnerabilities, find exploits, and build patches. It’s in this recipe — not in any one model — that both the benefits and the risks come in.

This matters because others can build comparable systems. Smaller models embedded in systems built with deep security expertise could potentially produce similar outcomes more cheaply, which is particularly promising for defense. AI cybersecurity capability is jagged: It doesn’t scale smoothly with model size or general benchmark performance. The system the model is embedded within matters a lot.

It has been revealed that so what Mythos has demonstrated is that it’s possible to build an AI system that finds and addresses software vulnerabilities. We already knew this was possible and there has been increasing work on this, but we’re just beginning to explore what it means in the context of agentic AI: Systems that can rapidly and autonomously take action.

According to recent reports, as autonomous systems that identify software vulnerabilities proliferate (and they will), open code and tooling can help level the playing field. Software security has become a speed race across four stages: detection, verification, coordination, and patch propagation. Open ecosystems distribute these across a community, where more closed-source projects centralize knowledge and action across all four stages inside a single vendor, representing a single point of failure where only one organization can see and fix the code. The distributed nature of open development is robust to such constraints, and can be especially powerful in communities with dedicated security professionals, like the Linux kernel security team, the Open Source Security Foundation, and the team at Hugging Face working on model and supply-chain security.

A common argument for more closed systems is proprietary obscurity, where the code underlying a system is inaccessible. Unfortunately, this provides less protection than it used to. AI systems are increasingly able to assist with reverse engineering of stripped binaries, which matters because most legacy firmware and embedded code is closed, binary-only, and no longer maintained. That code represents a huge attack surface, and it’s becoming more legible and accessible as AI tools improve.

There’s also a risk created by how AI is being used inside closed codebases. When companies adopt AI coding tools under the wrong incentives (for instance, evaluating engineers by the volume of features shipped rather than code quality) AI-accelerated development can introduce more vulnerabilities into proprietary code than traditional development would. Those vulnerabilities then sit inside a closed codebase where only one organization can find and fix them, while AI-enabled attackers are increasingly capable of discovering them from the outside. The combination of more vulnerabilities produced more quickly, behind a single-organization firewall, is exactly the kind of imbalance that open ecosystems are positioned to avoid.

Sources indicate that underlying all of this is capability asymmetry between attackers and defenders. Open models and open tooling narrow that gap by giving defenders access to the same class of capabilities attackers can reach for — capabilities that would otherwise be concentrated within a small number of well-resourced entities.

Cybersecurity defense is where open source and AI agents can play a key role together. Based on the System Card, it appears that Mythos is capable of operating with close to full autonomy, something we’ve advised against due to the potential loss of control. AI agents that are instead semi-autonomous, where the types of actions they can take are prespecified and certain steps require human approval, hit a sweet spot of benefit and risk. In semi-autonomous systems, people remain in control, and the AI agent is responsible for specific subtasks. This is possible to do with open code that organizations can run privately within their own institutions, specifying allowable tools, skills, and system access privileges. With this setup, AI agents can be deployed defensively, finding vulnerabilities and assisting with patching under an organization’s own controls.

The semi-autonomous approach depends on humans being able to actually understand what an AI agent did and why. That’s much more possible when the system is built on open components, such as open agent scaffolding, open rule engines, and auditable decision logs and traces, than when it’s a black box. The “human in the loop” is only meaningful if the human can see into the loop.

According to recent reports, companies don’t have to build these capabilities entirely from scratch. There’s a rich open-source ecosystem of security tooling, including vulnerability scanners, intrusion detection systems, log analyzers, and fuzzing frameworks, that AI agents can be integrated with.

Industry observers note that for high-stakes organizations, starting from open, auditable foundations means security teams can actually inspect how their monitoring works, rather than trusting a single vendor’s claims. This is particularly important where sensitive data and processes are involved, and where sensitive material should generally not be flowing through external AI providers. Open systems can be rigorously analyzed by in-house security professionals, fine-tuned on an organizations’s own secure data, modified to produce organization-specific oversight mechanisms, and run entirely within an organization’s own infrastructure, keeping everything behind appropriate firewalls.

Attackers will develop models that take advantage of vulnerabilities. A significant part of the answer is leaning into transparent practices: open security reviews, published threat models, shared vulnerability databases, and open tooling that any team can adopt. The alternative of each organization trying to secure itself in isolation with proprietary tools doesn’t scale against attackers who are coordinating and sharing techniques in their own communities.

According to recent reports, the future of AI cybersecurity will be shaped less by any single model and more by the ecosystems that surround them. Openness provides defenders with the visibility, the control, the community, and the shared infrastructure to stay ahead.

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.

Among the qualities that make up conscientiousness, being hardworking and organised stood out.

For extraversion, which includes both sociability and energy, the clearest result was for people who described themselves as active.

These patterns matter because inflammation that stays elevated over time is linked to both physical and psychological health.

Lower levels of long-term inflammation are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, stroke and premature death.

They have also been associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

The researchers pooled data from six studies involving more than 19,000 adults in the United States, England and Japan.

Participants rated how well words such as ‘organised’, ‘hardworking’ and ‘active’ described them.

The researchers then looked at how those answers related to two markers of inflammation in blood samples, C-reactive protein and interleukin-6.

Earlier research had already linked higher conscientiousness with lower levels of both inflammatory markers (Luchetti et al., 2014).

In this study, people who described themselves as organised or hardworking tended to have lower levels of both markers.

Being hardworking showed the strongest association within conscientiousness, even stronger than the association for the overall trait score.

People who scored higher on extraversion tended to have lower C-reactive protein, and much of that association came from how active they said they were.

In fact, being active was more strongly associated with lower C-reactive protein than any other characteristic the researchers examined.

Being talkative highlighted a small association in the opposite direction, while being lively was associated with lower levels of both inflammatory markers.

In several of the studies, the association with being active held up even after the researchers took other aspects of extraversion into account.

Being active and hardworking may both reflect how much energy people have for everyday tasks.

In earlier research, people who scored higher on the activity aspect of extraversion or the achievement-striving aspect of conscientiousness tended to have better aerobic capacity during a brisk walking test (Terracciano et al., 2013).

Regular physical activity could help explain part of the association with inflammation.

The relationship could run in the other direction, too, if people with higher inflammation feel less energetic and come to see themselves as less active or lively.

The study was published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology (Stephan et al., 2026).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some clean-up jobs need powerful stuff.

Sources indicate that the end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.

"We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio indicates depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.

It has been revealed that the PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away.

In a recent development, "We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore.".

Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air.

Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down.

One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea.

And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs.

When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and revealed that the computer room had flooded.

Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs.

"Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register.

"After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol.".

As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka.

"Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote.

Industry observers note that by this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again.

"We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote.

The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen.

"It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs.

In a recent development, have you had to clean up hardware in a hurry, perhaps with odd substances or implements? If so, click here to send On Call your story. We'll raise a glass to each one of you who sends a story and do it again if we share it on a future Friday. ®.

Browser tabs as a container runtime

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fzakaria

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tl;dr tabc is a container runtime, like runc, that runs each container in a Chromium tab.
  • Despite my zealot love for Nix, there is no denying the convenience and ubiquity of Docker.
  • Despite all the footguns you can get yourself into by writing a non-reproducible Dockerfile, it was a still a remarkable step forward in making software deployment more predictable and portable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tl;dr tabc is a container runtime, like runc, that runs each container in a Chromium tab. docker run --runtime tabc alpine works and starts in under a second. On a Mac it needs no hypervisor and no Linux VM; Linux for everyone!

Despite my zealot love for Nix, there is no denying the convenience and ubiquity of Docker. Containers have become the standard unit of software deployment, providing a consistent environment across different machines and simplifying the management of dependencies.11Containers are not even a “real” thing within the Linux kernel although there are recent attempts to formalize them as a kernel-level abstraction.

Despite all the footguns you can get yourself into by writing a non-reproducible Dockerfile, it was a still a remarkable step forward in making software deployment more predictable and portable.

Recent findings suggest that nothing has really challenged Docker’s dominance in the container space and it’s reliance on Linux as the underlying platform. The absurdity of the situation has become that developers on MacOS end up running a Linux virtual machine to simply run containers.

People, even the creator of Docker, believed a common runtime for software isolation would have been a game-changer and that WebAssembly could have played that role if it had existed earlier.

Recent findings suggest that “If WASM+WASI existed in 2008, we wouldn’t have needed to created Docker. That’s how vital it is.” - Solomon Hykes, 2019.

Here we are, 7 years later, we still have Docker, and WebAssembly is mostly used for speeding up web applications.

Is there another way to achieve the same level of isolation and portability without relying on the host being Linux?

What if though Docker ran its containers on WebAssembly instead of directly on the Linux kernel?

What if the isolation provided by the browser could replace the kernel-level isolation that containers rely on?

This idea, the holy grail of running Linux in a browser is not new. JSLinux did it in 2011, and v86, WebVM and qemu-wasm are also attempts in the same direction. They all have their share of limitations: 32-bit only, performance complications, incomplete hardware emulation, that make them impractical for general-purpose use.

Recent findings suggest that unkernel is a newly developed project by Pooya Parsa that changes the economics of what is possible. unknernel compiles the Linux kernel to WebAssembly, allowing it to run directly in the browser without relying on traditional hardware emulation. Only your container’s own code goes through an emulator, and everything else the kernel does runs at near native speed.

It is now practical to run Linux containers directly in the browser, leveraging the isolation provided by WebAssembly and the browser environment with acceptable performance.

Sources indicate that that is a real docker run, on a real Docker daemon, starting a real Alpine image. This works even on a Mac with no Docker installed and no Linux virtual machine running. 🤯.

In my last post I was inspired from Gary Bernhardt’s The Birth & Death of JavaScript and its discussion of the evolution of software isolation.

In the talk, Bernhardt imagines a project called METAL that moves the JavaScript VM into the kernel. The VM already keeps programs apart, so the hardware no longer has to. Process isolation becomes the VM’s job.

According to recent reports, we did not need to move the VM into the kernel. A browser tab is the VM Bernhardt imagined.

tabc is a OCI container runtime that runs each container in its own browser tab. That means you can use it with Docker just like any other runtime.

Whereas the default Docker runtime, runc, starts your program as a process on the host’s kernel, tabc leverages the browser as its execution environment, running each container in a separate tab with its own instance of the Linux kernel compiled to WebAssembly.22The tab boots unkernel, and the “container” runs within it.

This is the part that I’m most excited about: at no point does your container ever touch the host’s kernel and require Linux. All tabc asks of the host is a browser, nothing needs Linux underneath.

According to recent reports, this is a complete rethinking of the container stack on macOS. Docker on a Mac is a Linux virtual machine with a nice installer. Docker Desktop, Colima, OrbStack and Podman Machine all boot a Linux VM first. Even Apple’s own container tool boots a VM per container.

Isn’t WebAssembly a virtual machine? Technically yes, in the same way the JVM is: it runs code for a made-up CPU. The difference is that it is all software. Nothing asks macOS for a hypervisor.

On Linux, Docker pulls the image and hands it to tabc. A Mac with no Linux VM has no Docker daemon to do that, so tabc run pulls the image itself.

Without Linux and namespaces, what is giving the container its isolation?

Industry observers note that browsers such as Chromium are an incredibly battle-tested sandbox, and we only use them for web pages. 🤦 Rather than simply relying on the host kernel’s isolation mechanisms, tabc leverages the browser’s sandbox to create an additional layer of security.33Every container may also get a browser of its own, with its own profile, so two containers share no process and no storage.

According to recent reports, starting a container in a browser tab is surprisingly fast, and most of the time is spent starting the browser itself. On my Linux laptop44I ran fifteen runs of echo hi from an Alpine bundle on a Ryzen 7 7840U. a container takes roughly 0.87 seconds from command to exit. This startup cost can be eliminated by using your browser’s already running instance via --open or --link, more on that later.

Unkernel has drastically improved the performance of running Linux in the browser but since the processes themselves are still emulated, there can be some noticeable delay for larger compute-heavy workloads.

According to recent reports, aside You can get a sense of the performance impact on a lot of packages by visiting https://trynix.dev. You have access to over 300,000 packages from Nixpkgs that run directly in your browser using Unkernel.

Although some of these slowdowns seem excessive, many workloads are still well within acceptable limits for interactive use that let this go beyond trivial examples and novelty.

Depending on whether you have every container running in its own browser instance or sharing tabs within a single browser, the memory overhead can be more dramatic. An idle container costs ~540 MiB of host memory split between the tab that holds the guest, the browser process, and helper processes.55For scale, Firecracker quotes under 5 MiB of overhead per microVM and 125 ms to boot.

Nevertheless, this overhead is acceptable for many interactive use cases where the convenience of running containers in browser tabs outweighs the memory cost.

Did you remember when I noted you can run this on MacOS without a Linux VM !?

Video: the trading floor in The Wolf of Wall Street. Matthew McConaughey's character stands up and shouts "holy fucking shit".

Industry observers note that aside The idea of a container in WebAssembly was attempted before with container2wasm. It however emulated the entire machine, including the kernel, rather than just the program so it was way heavier and slower than what tabc does.

By default the browser is hidden. It does not have to be. Ready to cook ? 🧑‍🍳.

This is where the idea kind of comes together and becomes borderline magical: the browser tab itself becomes the container, and you can interact with it just like any other tab.

Sources indicate that with --open, tabc leverages the desktop environment to open the container’s page in the default browser. Even crazier is that the page itself is a pty, so you have cross-terminal interaction between the browser tab and the terminal you started it from.

Video: a terminal at the top runs tabc with --open, and a tab in the Chromium window under it boots Linux and shows a shell prompt. A command typed into the tab appears in the terminal, and one typed into the terminal appears in the tab. nginx is started in the container, and a second tab at localhost:8123 shows the page it serves.

You then can visit the container’s web server at the port exposed, in this case localhost:8123, in you guessed it: another browser tab in the same browser.

Once you have containers you can start, they then can become composed: docker compose. Nothing beyond the runtime: tabc key in the Compose file changes. Everything else from compose continues to work: network, volumes, and all.66The --dashboard flag opens the tabc dashboard, where the tabs are panes in a single browser page.

Tip Since MacOS has no Docker daemon for compose, tabc brings its own lightweight one to handle it: tocker.

We just started two containers in the browser: a web server and a Redis instance, each running in its own tab pane and communicating with each other by service name.

Unix’s major bet was that everything is a file. In the browser, everything is a tab. Our mail, our editors and our terminals already moved there. We can now add containers to the list.

That works on Linux and on an Apple Silicon Mac on any recent browser.77On Linux the Nix package brings its own Chromium unless you pass --open. The README has more details on setup and usage.

Solomon Hykes was half right. WebAssembly became the runtime, and Docker stayed anyway.

🏆 Leaderboard · 🔧 GitHub · 📄 Paper.

If you've been tracking Arabic LLM evaluation, you've probably noticed a growing tension: the number of benchmarks and leaderboards is expanding rapidly, but are we actually measuring what we think we're measuring?

We built QIMMA قمّة (Arabic for "summit"), to answer that question systematically. Instead of aggregating existing Arabic benchmarks as-is and running models on them, we applied a rigorous quality validation pipeline before any evaluation took place. What we found was sobering: even widely-used, well-regarded Arabic benchmarks contain systematic quality challenges that can quietly corrupt evaluation results.

This post walks through what QIMMA is, how we built it, what problems we found, and what the model rankings look like once you clean things up.

Sources indicate that arabic is spoken by over 400 million people across diverse dialects and cultural contexts, yet the Arabic NLP evaluation landscape remains fragmented. A few key pain points have motivated this work:.

Translation challenges. Many Arabic benchmarks are translations from English. This introduces distributional shifts. Questions that feel natural in English become awkward or culturally misaligned in Arabic, making benchmark data less representative of how Arabic is naturally used.

It has been revealed that absent quality validation. Even native Arabic benchmarks are often released without rigorous quality checks. Annotation inconsistencies, incorrect gold answers, encoding errors, and cultural bias in ground-truth labels have all been documented in established resources.

Industry observers note that reproducibility gaps. Evaluation scripts and per-sample outputs are rarely released publicly, making it hard to audit results or build on prior work.

Coverage fragmentation. Existing leaderboards cover isolated tasks and narrow domains, making holistic model assessment difficult.

To illustrate where QIMMA sits relative to existing platforms:.

QIMMA is the only platform combining all five properties: open source, predominantly native Arabic content, systematic quality validation, code evaluation, and public per-sample inference outputs.

QIMMA consolidates 109 subsets from 14 source benchmarks into a unified evaluation suite of over 52,000 samples, spanning 7 domains:.

A few things stand out about this design:.

Industry observers note that this is the methodological heart of QIMMA. Before running a single model, we applied a multi-stage validation pipeline to every sample in every benchmark.

Each sample was independently evaluated by two state-of-the-art LLMs:.

We chose two models with strong Arabic capability but different training data compositions, so that their combined judgment is more robust than either alone.

Each model scores a sample against a 10-point rubric, with binary scores (0 or 1) per criterion:.

A sample is eliminated if either model scores it below 7/10. Samples where both models agree on elimination are dropped immediately. However, where only one model flags a sample, it proceeds to human review in Stage 2.

It has been revealed that flagged samples are reviewed by native Arabic speakers with cultural and dialectal familiarity. Human annotators make final calls on:.

For culturally sensitive content, multiple perspectives are considered, since "correctness" can genuinely vary across Arab regions.

The pipeline revealed recurring quality issues across benchmarks; not isolated errors, but systematic patterns reflecting gaps in how benchmarks were originally constructed.

False or mismatched gold indices, factually wrong answers, missing or raw text answers.

Corrupt or illegible text, spelling and grammar errors, and duplicate samples.

Stereotype reinforcement and monolithic generalizations about diverse communities.

Misalignment of gold answers with evaluation protocols.

Code benchmarks required a different intervention. Rather than discarding samples, we refined the Arabic problem statements in 3LM's Arabic adaptations of HumanEval+ and MBPP+, leaving task identifiers, reference solutions, and test suites completely unchanged.

The modification rates were striking:.

Modifications fell into five categories:.

QIMMA uses LightEval, EvalPlus and FannOrFlop as its evaluation framework, chosen for consistency, multilingual community adoption, and reproducibility.

QIMMA standardizes prompting by question format, with six template types:.

All prompts are in Arabic. For MizanQA and ArabCulture, benchmark-specific system prompts from the original papers are preserved.

Sources indicate that results as of April 2026; covering top 10 evaluated models. Visit the live leaderboard for current rankings.

Sources indicate that across the full leaderboard (46 models), a clear but imperfect size-performance correlation emerges. However, there are interesting exceptions:.

InfoQ Homepage News Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type after Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

Recent findings suggest that the Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Confirmed on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.

Industry observers note that the headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result to describe an operation that cannot fail, it took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.

To make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting concerns on upgrade are advised to revision dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.

Sources indicate that the core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the new Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.

On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:.

This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:.

The upcoming global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:.

On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:.

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,.

you should immediately patch security advisories.

One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

According to recent reports, importStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an patch could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.

Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.

Upgrading uses rustup revision stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

Recent findings suggest that fireworks AI made Tencent’s open-weight Hy4 Flash available on its serverless API on November 25, 2026, pricing the Standard tier at $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens. The announcement adds benchmark tests that position the model as a low-cost option for professional and agentic work.

Industry observers note that cached input costs $0.003 per million tokens. A Priority tier is also available, and the service is served globally. Developers can instead use on-demand dedicated GPUs; the Hy4 Flash model page lists function calling as supported and fine-tuning and embeddings as unsupported.

Hy4 Flash uses a mixture-of-experts design, in which only about 12 billion of its roughly 220 billion parameters are active for each token. It accepts text and image input. The native context window is 1M tokens, while Fireworks is serving 512K at launch, a material constraint for applications built around very long documents or extended agent sessions.

Tencent introduced Hy4 Flash on November 16, 2026, as its most cost-effective Hy model for everyday productivity and released the weights on GitHub, Hugging Face, ModelScope, and AtomGit. Tencent says reinforcement learning reduced average end-to-end output tokens by 50%, while megakernels, 4-bit quantization, and DFly lifted decoding speed beyond 150 tokens per second.

Fireworks reports testing the model on seven professional benchmarks with the same harness used for other models on each leaderboard, at high reasoning. Costs are based on recorded tokens at Fireworks’ serverless prices, and the results are dated November 22, 2026. Hy4 Flash reached the score-cost Pareto frontier on every board where cost was recorded, meaning no listed model delivered a higher score at a lower cost.

Industry observers note that fireworks’ run of Epiq’s CorporateBench, which tests questions across thousands of internal firm emails and meeting notes, produced a 75.9% score for Hy4 Flash: sixth of 14 models and slightly above Claude Opus 5.5’s 75.4%. The respective costs were $0.013 and $2.80 per task.

Rogo’s Substantial Finance Benchmark produced a 49.2% tie with Claude Opus 5 in Fireworks’ tests, at $0.0065 per task for Hy4 Flash versus $1.83 for Opus 5. Hy4 Flash also placed above Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro, which each scored 48.2%. GPT-6 Luna was the only cheaper model on that board, but scored 35.3%.

Industry observers note that on Sierra’s τ³-Banking agent benchmark, Fireworks reports a 49.2% score for Hy4 Flash against 49.1% for Claude Opus 5. The cost was $0.012 per trial versus $2.59. Across all boards where it recorded cost, Fireworks found Hy4 Flash was the lowest-cost model except on Massive Finance.

Fireworks’ rankings were weaker elsewhere: Hy4 Flash placed 16th of 18 models on HealthBench Professional and 19th of 22 on DeepSWE. Tencent recommends the larger Hy4 for long-horizon software engineering because of its higher intelligence ceiling, reinforcing that the cost results do not establish uniform superiority across professional work.

Before opening the endpoint, Fireworks ran Hy4 Flash through its launch-validation suite on FireAttention, its inference engine, and compared the results with Tencent’s official endpoint. The tech giant reports that every score came within one point of Tencent’s. The Fireworks results were:.

The deployment’s appeal is therefore workload-specific: Fireworks’ tests pair near-parity with Claude Opus on selected professional tasks with much lower recorded costs, while the reduced hosted context and weaker health and software results set clear limits. Validation against Tencent’s endpoint gives developers a direct reference point for assessing whether Fireworks’ serving configuration preserves the model’s expected behavior.

We recently released a Transformers.js demo browser extension powered by Gemma 4 E2B to help users navigate the web.

While building it, we ran into several practical observations about Manifest V3 runtimes, model loading, and messaging that are worth sharing.

This guide is for developers who want to run local AI features in a Chrome extension with Transformers.js under Manifest V3 constraints.

By the end, you will have the same architecture used in this project: a background service worker that hosts models, a side panel chat UI, and a content script for page-level actions.

In this guide, we will recreate the core architecture of Transformers.js Gemma 4 Browser Assistant, using the published extension as a reference and the open-source codebase as the implementation map.

Before diving in, a quick scope note: I will not go deep on the React UI layer or Vite build configuration. The focus here is the high-level architecture decisions: what runs in each Chrome runtime and how those pieces are orchestrated.

If Manifest V3 is newly introduced to you, read this short overview first: What is Manifest V3?.

In MV3, your architecture starts in public/manifest.json. This project defines three entry points:.

Sources indicate that the background service worker also handles chrome.action.onClicked to open the side panel for the active tab. Related entry point to know: a popup can be defined with action.default_popup and works well for quick actions. This project uses a side panel for persistent chat, but the orchestration pattern is the same.

The key design decision is to keep heavy orchestration in the background and keep UI/page logic thin.

One practical consequence of this division is that the conversation history also lives in background (Agent.chatMessages): the UI sends events like AGENT_GENERATE_TEXT, background appends the message, runs inference, then emits MESSAGES_UPDATE back to the side panel.

This split avoids duplicate model loads, keeps the UI responsive, and respects Chrome's security boundaries around DOM access.

It has been revealed that once runtimes are separated, messaging becomes the backbone. In this project, all messages are typed through enums in src/shared/types.ts.

The orchestration rule is simple: the background is the single coordinator; side panel and content script are specialized workers that request actions and render results.

In src/shared/constants.ts, this extension uses two model roles:.

The split is intentional: Gemma 4 handles reasoning/tool decisions, while MiniLM generates vector embeddings for the semantic similarity search in ask_website and find_history.

All inference runs in background (src/background/background.ts):.

This gives a single model host for all tabs/sessions, avoids duplicate memory usage, and keeps the side panel UI responsive. Because models are loaded from the background service worker, artifacts are cached under the extension origin (chrome-extension://) rather than per-website origins, which gives one shared cache for the whole extension install.

MV3 lifecycle note: service workers can be suspended and restarted, so model runtime state should be treated as recoverable and re-initialized when needed.

The model lifecycle is explicit:.

In a recent development, permissions and privacy are part of the architecture, not a checkbox at the end. In this project, public/manifest.json asks for sidePanel, storage, scripting, and tabs, plus host_permissions for http(s)://*/*:.

According to recent reports, why keep this narrow: permissions define user trust and Chrome Web Store review risk. Request only what your features actually need, and state clearly that inference runs locally in the extension runtime so owners understand where their data is processed.

Sources indicate that before the execution loop, it helps to understand how model tool calling works (the basis for any agentic workflow). You pass messages plus a tool schema (name, description, and parameters), and Transformers.js formats the actual prompt from those inputs using the model's chat template. Because chat templates are model-specific, the exact tool-call format depends on the model you use. With Gemma-4-style templates, the model emits a special tool-call token block when it decides to call one.

At generation time, the model can emit output like:.

That is exactly why this project has a normalization layer (webMcp) and a parser (extractToolCalls): model output must be converted into deterministic tool executions.

src/background/agent/webMcp.tsx normalizes extension tools into a model-friendly shape:.

Example tools include get_open_tabs, go_to_tab, open_url, close_tab, find_history, ask_website, and highlight_website_element.

The core design choice here is to separate internal model messages from UI-facing chat messages:.

This keeps user communication clean while preserving a deterministic tool loop in the background.

Sources indicate that state placement is another architectural decision that matters a lot in MV3. In this implementation, state is split by lifecycle and access pattern:.

As described in section 1.2, keeping conversation history in background gives one canonical state across UI updates. This keeps short-lived state in memory, durable settings in extension storage, and heavy retrieval data in a local database.

You do not need a complex build setup, but MV3 does require predictable outputs for each runtime.

The goal is simple: one artifact per Chrome entry point, in the exact place public/manifest.json expects.

The architecture choice that unlocks this whole project is clear separation of concerns: background owns orchestration and model execution, UI surfaces stay thin, and content scripts handle page access.

This project uses a side panel, but the same approach works for other setups:.

The practical rule is simple: decide where state lives (global, tabId, or site-scoped), keep that state and the model inference in background (basically as background services), and let UI/content runtimes act as focused clients.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

S&P Global Ratings placed NVIDIA’s AA issuer credit rating and AA senior unsecured debt rating on CreditWatch with negative implications on November 25, 2026, citing concerns about board independence, executive oversight and succession planning. The agency said it could downgrade NVIDIA within 90 days if further due diligence finds that governance deficiencies remain.

Industry observers note that the ratings were affirmed, with CreditWatch marking a review for a possible downgrade. The issuer rating moved from AA/Stable/A-1+ to AA/Watch Neg/A-1+, while the senior unsecured rating moved from AA to AA/Watch Neg. NVIDIA’s A-1+ commercial paper rating was affirmed separately.

In a recent development, the concerns center on the board’s structure, composition and effectiveness. S&P mentioned events involving the CEO and questions about potential export-control violations exposed those weaknesses; the CEO’s departure and later reinstatement did not resolve its questions about oversight of the executive code of conduct. Weak executive oversight and a lack of succession planning also sharpened key-person concerns.

In S&P’s assessment, long director tenures may have compromised independence, while governance practices may have lagged NVIDIA’s rapid expansion and growing importance in global technology infrastructure. The agency revised the management-and-governance modifier used in its credit analysis to neutral from positive and was unaware of any remedial board action addressing the potential deficiencies.

In a recent development, S&P intends to meet NVIDIA’s board and management to discuss board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession proposal. It expects any downgrade to be limited to one notch unless investigations or disclosures indicate harm to NVIDIA’s reputation or future business prospects.

Export controls form a separate part of the assessment. NVIDIA’s China exposure raises questions about geopolitical risk management and internal controls, in S&P’s view. A conclusion that export-control rules were circumvented or violated, or that past disclosures about exposure to China and nearby regions were misleading or understated, would weigh on overall credit quality.

Recent findings suggest that for now, S&P’s assessments of NVIDIA’s competitive position, technology leadership and financial profile remain unchanged. S&P mentioned stricter export controls could reduce future growth prospects, while its published scores still classify business risk as strong, competitive position as excellent, financial risk as minimal and liquidity as exceptional, with an aa stand-alone credit profile.

The credit profile rests on a business S&P describes as data-center-scale AI infrastructure. Its platform covers chips, networking, systems and software for model training and inference, data analytics, scientific computing, robotics and 3D graphics. Compute and networking generated 90% of revenue in the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, while graphics generated 10%. Its core end markets are data center, gaming, professional visualization and automotive.

In a recent development, the review therefore separates NVIDIA’s operating and financial strength from the governance controls around it. S&P is testing whether board oversight and succession planning have kept pace with the company’s role in AI infrastructure; adverse export-control or disclosure findings could broaden the concern to its reputation and business prospects.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.
  • The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me.
  • According to recent reports, in practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.

The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call @backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me.

According to recent reports, in practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type.

In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming.

Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes:.

We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes.

In a recent development, its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example.

It has been revealed that our spreadsheet has now several fields: a title, and row and column properties. When iterating over them, we have two kinds of indexes: row indexes and column indexes. Adding typed indexes is attractive to prevent callers from mixing them up.

Recent findings suggest that this enum gives us a way of referencing all the struct fields for which we will construct a typed indexed. If all fields were to be indexed, we would have used std.meta.FieldEnum(Sheet), but our spreadsheet has a title.

It has been revealed that this checks at compile time that each Field enum variant name is indeed a field inside Sheet. As we’ll see later, we will have to access Sheet’s fields by name, so it’s good to check the names of Field variants match the names of Sheet fields.

It has been revealed that this defines the kind of type indexes we’ll construct: one for row data slices and one for columns data slices. Each indexed field of Sheet has one correct typed index kind. We match them with an exhaustive switch over Field.

Recent findings suggest that we now have all we need to construct the two typed indexes of kinds .row and .col. A generic function returning a type at comptime is how to do it.

Recent findings suggest that the typed index type for row is Sheet.Index(.row), and for colum it is Sheet.Index(.col). Note the title case of the Index function, matching Zig’s convention for types.

Remains to give a way of making use of these types.

Recent findings suggest that this part may look complex if you are not familiar with comptime-enabled generics in Zig, so let’s be precise. This defines a method on Sheet that requires f to be a Field instance known at compile time. This allow to infer at compile time both the type of i and the return type.

Sources indicate that index(kindOf(f)) is just a chain of function calls on a known value. So it is comptime known. And most importantly, the type of i is bound to the one of f at compile time. Given the body of Sheet.kindOf, it’s easy to see that s.at(.row_width, i) will compile only if i has type Index(.row)!

The return type of Zig function must be comptime known, and it is the case here by using some reflection. @FieldType(Sheet, name) returns the type of the field of Sheet named name (given as a []const u8). @tagName(f) gives just that for the input enum variant. std.meta.Elem returns the element type for a collection type (here a slice). Finally, we return a pointer to allow the caller to mutate, but a value would work just fine for a read-only case.

This gives us a clear usage at call site.

The Sheet.Index(.row) syntax is particularly lovely: a method call feeling like a qualified concrete type.

It has been revealed that still, as I hinted earlier, this design it not completely hermetic to bugs. Nothing prevents you from forging a Sheet.Index(.row) from any integer with @fromBackingInt. And opaque types are really just for interaction with C.

Also, any caller can access Sheet fields directly (Zig has no notion of private fields.).

As for all Zig code, one must follow documented usage (“Direct access is discouraged. Use Sheet.at.”) and make good use of the public methods by proactively inspecting types.
