DeepSeek-V4: a million-token context that agents can actually use

📅 24 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active.
  • Focusing on long running agentic workloads.
  • This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DeepSeek released V4 today. Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active. Both have a 1M-token context window. The benchmark numbers are competitive, but not SOTA. It doesn't matter. The real innovation is how DeepSeek v4 is designed for efficient large context length support, and hence as one of the best candidates for agentic tasks.

Focusing on long running agentic workloads. Running a frontier open model as an agent today breaks in predictable ways. The model stops. You reprompt. The trace blows past the context budget, or the KV cache fills the GPU, or tool-call round trips degrade halfway through a long task. V4 is built to fix these known failures, and point the way for the community to follow.

This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.

According to recent reports, A 1M context window is just capacity, not performance. Whether you can use it depends on the cost of every forward pass at that depth. For an agent running a long tool-use trajectory (a SWE-bench task, a multi-step browse session, a terminal session with hundreds of commands), every tool result is appended to the context, and every subsequent token pays the full attention cost against everything that came before.

Sources indicate that two numbers matter: single-token inference FLOPs and KV cache size. Both grow with sequence length. At 1M tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires 27% of single-token inference FLOPs compared with DeepSeek-V3.2, so it runs faster on the same hardware. It also uses 10% of the KV cache memory. V4-Flash drops these numbers even further: 10% of the FLOPs and 7% of the KV cache.

If we compare the KV cache memory against a established architecture like grouped query attention with 8 heads, stored in the usual bfloat16 format, DeepSeek v4 requires roughly 2% the cache size. This makes it much easier to deploy for very large context handling.

Figure 1: benchmark comparison (left), per-token FLOPs and accumulated KV cache against sequence length (right).

The efficiency gain comes from splitting attention into two mechanisms and interleaving them across layers.

Recent findings suggest that compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) compresses KV entries by 4x along the sequence dimension using softmax-gated pooling with a learned positional bias. A lightning indexer (FP4, ReLU-scored multi-head dot product) picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. It inherits the sparse-selection idea from DeepSeek Sparse Attention in V3.2, but runs it over blocks that are already 4x shorter than the original sequence. The indexer's search space shrinks with it.

It has been revealed that figure 3: CSA. The compressor collapses every 4 tokens into one compressed KV entry. The lightning indexer picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. A sliding-window branch handles the most recent uncompressed tokens.

Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) compresses KV entries by 128x and drops the sparse selection. Every query attends densely to every compressed block. The compressed sequence is short enough that dense attention is cheap.

Sources indicate that figure 4: HCA. A heavier compressor (128x vs. 4x) followed by dense attention over the compressed stream, with the same sliding-window branch for recency.

In a recent development, the layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Different layers carry different attention patterns, and forcing one mechanism across all of them wastes capacity. In V4-Pro's 61-layer stack, layers 0–1 are HCA, layers 2–60 alternate CSA and HCA, and the MTP block at the end runs sliding-window only.

Recent findings suggest that both paths use FP8 storage for most KV entries and BF16 only for the RoPE dimensions. The lightning indexer inside CSA runs in FP4. These storage choices compound with the compression ratios to produce the 2% KV cache figure.

Figure 2: overall architecture. Attention layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Feed-forward layers use DeepSeekMoE. Residual connections are replaced with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC).

Industry observers note that efficient long-context attention is necessary for agent workflows but not sufficient. The paper describes three post-training and infrastructure choices that target agent use cases directly.

Sources indicate that V3.2 kept reasoning traces across tool-result rounds but discarded them whenever a upcoming user message arrived. For an agent handling a single user turn, this was fine. For multi-turn agentic workflows, where the user sends a follow-up after the agent has already chained several tool calls, the model lost its accumulated reasoning and had to reconstruct state.

V4 preserves reasoning content across user message boundaries when the conversation contains tool calls. The model retains the complete reasoning history across all rounds, including across user turns. This allows a coherent, cumulative chain of thought over long-horizon agent tasks. For conversational use without tools, the old behavior is preserved: reasoning is flushed on each turn to keep context concise.

Figure 7: thinking with tools (top) preserves reasoning across all turns. Thinking without tools (bottom) discards reasoning at each upcoming user message.

V4 introduces a |DSML| special token and an XML-based tool-call format. The XML format reduces escaping failures compared to JSON-in-string tool calls, a common failure mode when models emit nested quoted content.

The schema separates string parameters (passed as-is with string="true") from structured parameters (passed as JSON with string="false"). This removes a class of parsing errors around numbers and booleans that JSON tool-call formats routinely hit.

In a recent development, the agent behavior was trained with RL against real tool environments. The paper describes the sandbox infrastructure built for that purpose. DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) is a Rust platform that exposes four execution substrates behind one Python SDK: function calls, containers, microVMs (Firecracker), and full VMs (QEMU). A single cluster runs hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandboxes.

According to recent reports, three DSec features matter for agent training: fast image loading via layered 3FS storage (so RL rollouts do not wait on container startup), preemption-safe trajectory replay (so interrupted training steps resume without re-running tool calls), and a uniform API across substrates (so training harnesses target function calls or full VMs without rewriting). These infrastructure decisions underpin the agent benchmark scores.

In a recent development, the knowledge and reasoning numbers are competitive but not leading. The agent numbers are where V4-Pro-Max separates from the field.

Specific numbers from the agent section of Table 6:.

In the paper's internal R&D coding benchmark, 30 curated tasks across PyTorch, CUDA, Rust, and C++, V4-Pro-Max hits 67% pass rate, versus 47% for Sonnet 4.5 and 70% for Opus 4.5. In a survey of 85 DeepSeek developers using V4-Pro as their daily driver, 52% stated it was ready to replace their current primary coding model and 39% leaned toward yes.

Recent findings suggest that the long-context retrieval numbers are in Figure 9. MRCR 8-needle accuracy stays above 0.82 through 256K tokens and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

According to recent reports, figure 9: MRCR 8-needle retrieval. V4-Pro-Max stays above 0.82 through 256K and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Four checkpoints are on the Hub. The instruct models use FP4 for MoE expert weights and FP8 for everything else. The base models are FP8 throughout.

In a recent development, both instruct models support three reasoning modes: Non-think (fast, no chain of thought), Think High (explicit reasoning in blocks), and Think Max (maximum reasoning effort with a dedicated system prompt). Think Max requires a context window of at least 384K tokens. The recommended sampling parameters across all modes are temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0.

Recent findings suggest that the V4-Pro numbers on SWE Verified, MCPAtlas, and the internal R&D benchmark put it at parity with frontier closed models on agent tasks. The open question is how the community's tool harnesses adapt to the |DSML| schema and whether the interleaved thinking gains transfer to out-of-domain agent frameworks.

Figures in this blog post are from the technical report at DeepSeek_V4.pdf.

Sources indicate that according to my personal tests DeepSeek V4 Flash (Non-thinking mode) passed the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval test on both 32k and 435k actual prompt tokens with a 100% result across depths of 0-100%. In no-needle negative control with the NOT_FOUND instruction, the model also returned 100% correct failures, reducing the risk of contamination and false positives.

So thinking mode may degrade behaviour in some tests.

Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance.
  • Nov 26, 2026 10 min read.
  • Microsoft Ignite 2026, held in San Francisco and online from November 17 to 20, centered on running AI agents in production, with Microsoft positioning Copilot as the operating system for work and extending agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance.

Nov 26, 2026 10 min read.

Microsoft Ignite 2026, held in San Francisco and online from November 17 to 20, centered on running AI agents in production, with Microsoft positioning Copilot as the operating system for work and extending agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender.

Sources indicate that CEO Satya Nadella opened the keynote by acknowledging the November 12 Microsoft 365 outage, then positioned Copilot as the operating system for work, combining chat, coding, and autonomous agents in one experience. In his edited keynote remarks, Nadella argued that customers must be able to examine and independently verify what AI does, revealed an AI Transparency Initiative aligned with NIST's Agent Standards Initiative, and rejected setups where models audit other models:.

These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable.

The Book of News groups the announcements by product area, and many of them ship as previews rather than in general availability.

Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines are now generally available, a year after InfoQ reported on Microsoft introducing the chip at Ignite 2025 and two and a half years after the preview of Cobalt 100 VMs. According to the Azure announcement, the processor combines 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores on TSMC's 3nm process, and the VMs run in 14 regions today, with 23 planned by the end of 2026. Microsoft claims up to 50% better CPU performance than Cobalt 100, plus up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS through Azure Boost. Customers can run cores at a fixed 3.2 GHz in Deterministic Mode or let them boost up to 3.6 GHz in Opportunistic Mode, and the lineup adds Mpsv4 VMs for high-memory workloads and storage-optimized Lpsv5 VMs. Amadeus reported more than 30% higher flight-search throughput than on Cobalt 100, and OpenAI's Vadim Filanovsky described a similar result:.

We saw higher throughput and lower latency on Cobalt 200.

Confidential computing gains three previews: multi-GPU confidential computing on VR72 for models larger than a single GPU, Azure Confidential Enclaves with AKS Kata CoCo containers, and Azure Confidential Clean Room for multiparty analytics without exposing raw data.

In a recent development, customers can now deploy Foundry open-weight models and agents to their own AKS clusters. At the same time, an Agent Sandbox extension provides VM-level isolation for agent-written code, and Agent Grid applies central policy to agent, model, tool, and service interactions. Flex nodes extend AKS clusters to servers outside Azure. According to the AKS team's Ignite post, managed GPU node pools, which handle GPU drivers, device plugins, and Azure Monitor metrics, are generally available, with NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 support and mixed multi-instance GPU in preview. Confidential VM node pools on Azure Container Linux are also generally available on both Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP VM sizes.

On the operations side, Azure Monitor health models are generally available and build a real-time health graph from telemetry, ranking incidents by business impact. The Azure Copilot deployment agent, also generally available, turns natural-language requirements into deployed workloads, and Azure SRE Agent picks up previews for customer-managed keys, Entra Agent ID integration, cross-agent communication, and multicloud investigations. For migration projects, Azure Catalyst is now generally available, with its agent (formerly the Azure Copilot migration agent) handling discovery, assessment, and planning. Separately, GitHub Copilot modernization adds a preview of BizTalk-to-Logic Apps migration.

Industry observers note that microsoft now pitches Sovereign Private Cloud as a full stack on Azure Local, with VMs and AKS at the base, followed by data services, Foundry Local, GitHub Enterprise Local, and Microsoft 365 Local. Darryl van der Peijl, a Microsoft MVP for Azure Local, Hyper-V, and Azure Arc, listed what shipped in his Azure Local Insider newsletter: Foundry Local on Azure Local and GitHub Enterprise Local are generally available, while a Sovereign control panel, Blob Storage and DocumentDB on Azure Local, multi-tenancy, and rehoming are in preview. The control panel assesses data residency, encryption, network exposure, and business continuity for Azure resources without enforcing any controls, and during the preview it runs in European regions only, with the service hosted in Sweden.

Van der Peijl singled out rehoming, which moves an Azure Local instance from Azure management to local management while VMs, AKS clusters, and data stay in place:.

Until now, going from connected to disconnected meant a migration project. Microsoft showed a script that does the rehoming in one run.

It has been revealed that azure Local also runs on arm64 for the first time, in public preview on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Development Kit, which hosts containers on bare metal without a hypervisor. Windows Server 2028 entered preview through the Windows Server Insider Program, bringing a hardened Server Core, post-quantum cryptography, native NVMe enabled by default, NVMe over Fabrics, and boot from ReFS. According to van der Peijl, Microsoft added inference as a new pillar for the release, calling on-premises inference servers token factories, and is moving network drivers from kernel mode to user mode as part of its Windows resiliency work. Windows Admin Center vMode is now generally available at no extra cost and manages up to 1,000 Hyper-V hosts and 25,000 VMs, which Microsoft described on stage as "kind of a replacement for SCVMM.".

Foundry's main theme was continuous improvement. Multi-turn evaluation and production insights that group recurring failures and rank fixes are now generally available, while the agent optimizer, human annotation, rubric evaluators, Managed Training, and Programmed Training for custom SFT and reinforcement learning loops on open-weight models are in preview. The optimizer adjusts an agent's instructions, skills, and model choice, with a human approving each change before it ships.

In a separate engineering post, the Microsoft team behind the optimizer described how the loop works. They reported that the reflector, a separate model that reads failing traces and diagnoses why an agent scored poorly, influenced results more than switching the agent's own model, for example between gpt-4o and gpt-4.1-mini. Developers drive the loop from the Azure Developer CLI:.

Writing on DEV Community, Hector Flores advised readers to treat Microsoft's claim that the model router saves up to 65% compared with a frontier model as a ceiling rather than a forecast, and he welcomed the human approval step in the optimizer loop:.

Self-modifying agents with no review gate are an incident waiting to happen.

On the model front, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is generally available in Foundry, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Built on Gemma 4 26B A4B with added image input, it scores 68 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 and runs more than twice as fast as its predecessor, and Copilot uses it to route requests. MAI-Code-2 and MAI-Code-2-Flash are generally available on GitHub, MAI-Image-2.7 is in preview, and the model router now covers the top 50 models in a catalog of more than 11,000. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol became generally available in Foundry, with Global Standard deployments covering 28 regions. On Standard deployments with short context, Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while Astra costs $8 and $40. Foundry IQ added knowledge graphs and an iterative retrieval model, Microsoft-Retriever-1, both in preview.

Microsoft also made Azure AI Gateway generally available as a standalone product, split out of the API Management AI tier, to govern, route, and monitor access to AI models and MCP tools across providers. It includes 10,000 free requests per gateway per month, with paid billing starting January 1, 2027, across 17 regions.

Microsoft IQ, which Nadella described as an externalization of the context system behind Copilot, is now generally available without a newly introduced SKU. It exposes Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ context to Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Foundry, and MCP-compatible harnesses, and Web IQ is now available to all Azure customers at a lower price. Business plugins, which package reusable context, skills, and tools with hierarchical inheritance and governance, are available through the Frontier program.

Sources indicate that postgreSQL got most of the attention on the data side. Azure HorizonDB is now generally available as a managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database with built-in vector indexing, and teams can lock it down with Entra ID, private endpoints, and their own encryption keys. Calling models from SQL through AI Functions and AI Pipelines is still in preview. The same holds for Fabric HorizonDB, a serverless variant inside Fabric that provisions in seconds and pauses when nobody uses it, and for a DMS path that moves existing Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers onto HorizonDB.

It has been revealed that teams moving off Oracle can test a upcoming Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration in Azure DMS, also in preview. Cosmos DB developers now have a generally available Rust SDK and semantic reranker, and Cosmos DB Shell lets them query from VS Code or the portal with MCP support built in. On Azure Managed Redis, the Redis 8 preview folds JSON, search, time-series, and vector search into a single version. Anyone who wants to develop against Azure SQL Database on a laptop can pull a preview container that needs no Azure subscription.

The Microsoft Copilot SDK 2.0 is generally available, built on a native Rust runtime, supported in six languages, and using the same agent harness Microsoft and GitHub run internally. The GitHub Copilot app now takes Azure DevOps repositories from clone to merge and runs tests in a real, signed-in browser. Copilot code review adds local reviews in the CLI and app, secret detection, adaptive review effort, and cross-repository context. Copilot Code, a natural-language app builder with cloud and local sandboxes, is in the Frontier program, with general availability planned for December and a macOS local sandbox still to come.

The Copilot app now brings Chat, Cowork, Code, and Autopilot into one experience, and Office in Copilot puts Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside it as a generally available feature. Autopilot, a long-running personal agent with its own identity, memory, and tool access, is rolling out to Frontier customers. Salesforce in Copilot entered preview with more than 38 prebuilt sales skills, and zero-copy data federation between Salesforce Data 360 and Fabric OneLake is generally available. For spend control, Agent 365 FinOps previews cost visibility, policies, alerts, and Fabric-based chargeback.

According to recent reports, cost tracking also featured in practitioner reactions. In his newsletter, Microsoft principal AI apps architect Anurag Karuparti wrote that tokenomics is among the top challenges his customers raise, and he proposed a different unit for agent ROI:.

The metric that matters isn't just tokens consumed. It's cost per successful business outcome. That's how I think enterprises should start measuring agent ROI.

Writing for business leaders, Aaron Reich, CTO of the Accenture and Microsoft joint venture Avanade, built his Ignite analysis around trust rather than speed:.

It has been revealed that speed isn't the bottleneck anymore, trust is. As AI drives the cost of knowledge toward zero with apps being easier to build, agents doing more work, and abundant intelligence, the scarce things are hard and need more attention: institutional knowledge, judgment, accountability and trust.

At the Microsoft Hub, where he spent the week answering customer questions, Microsoft MVP Muhammad Atif noticed a change in what customers wanted to know:.

In a recent development, how do we actually put this into production? How do we scale AI and agents across the organisation? How do we govern and secure them? How do we control the cost as adoption grows?

According to recent reports, entra now assigns Agent IDs automatically to discovered local agents, starting with GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, and previews an MCP Firewall that controls access to MCP servers, tools, prompts, and transports. The Microsoft MCP Server for Enterprise, which gives agents permission-controlled access to Entra data, is generally available. Defender's runtime protection for local AI agents on Windows is generally available to Defender for Endpoint P2 customers, while Intune previews local agent governance that marks devices with unapproved agents as noncompliant. Agent 365 now has a generally available tools registry that lists the plugins, skills, MCP servers, and connectors agents use; MCP governance is in preview through Azure AI Gateway and LiteLLM; and Dynamic Agent Risk combines runtime, posture, and blast-radius signals into risk levels for each agent. Microsoft Perception, formerly Project Perception, is now generally available, with its Triage Agent covering about 80% of alerts in a typical Defender queue.

(Source: Microsoft Tech Community, Agent 365 blog).

In her Ignite recap, cloud and identity consultant Shannon Kuehn warned against handling agents as ordinary applications:.

Treat agents like apps and you'll spend 2027 cleaning up after them.

The complete list of announcements is available in the Microsoft Ignite 2026 Book of News, and Microsoft has made keynote and breakout session recordings available on demand on the Ignite website.

December 15–16, 2026. Examine how senior practitioners run agents, evals, model serving, and AI-assisted engineering in production, including what failed and what changed. Register Now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, roboSense reported on November 25, 2026 that unaudited third-quarter 2026 revenue rose 65.2% year over year to RMB672.7 million, while LiDAR sales volume climbed 210.1% to approximately 575,500 units. Space Camera also entered the supply chains of several global AI companies, a separate sensing development alongside the LiDAR shipment growth.

RoboSense reported approximately 427,800 LiDAR units for robotics and other applications in the first nine months of 2026, up 423.0% year over year. Its digital LiDAR is being used across commercial cleaning, autonomous delivery, embodied AI and 3D spatial data collection. The range of applications ties the increase to several end uses rather than a single robotics category.

Integration of E2 and EM4 with NVIDIA Holoscan Sensor Bridge expands the development ecosystem around those sensors. The tech giant’s reliability and integration work is aimed at customers moving robots into practical deployments, with its existing robotics customer base providing a route to commercialize newer products.

ADAS remains the larger disclosed category by units: RoboSense reported approximately 866,900 LiDAR sales for advanced driver-assistance systems in the nine-month period. As of September 30, 2026, its design wins covered 197 vehicle models with 36 automotive OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers, and 91 of those models had reached start of production. The automotive base therefore remains important to the company’s scale even as robotics volumes expand rapidly.

  • In a recent development, energy, mood or sleep lost to worry?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

In a recent development, energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI released Privacy Filter on the Hub this week: an open-source personally-identifiable information (PII) detector that labels text across eight categories in a single forward pass over a 128k context. Model card. We spent a few hours building with it and landed on three apps that each reveals a different slice of what it can do.

All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK. In all these apps, gradio.Server plays the same backend role, and that consistency is exactly what makes it really powerful.

It has been revealed that privacy Filter is a 1.5B-parameter model with 50M active parameters, permissively licensed under Apache 2.0. PII categories are private_person, private_address, private_email, private_phone, private_url, private_date, account_number, secret. Context is 128,000 tokens. Achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PII-Masking-300k benchmark. Full numbers and methodology are in the official release blog.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Document-PII-Explorer.

It has been revealed that user problem. You want to read a PII-heavy document (a contract, a resume, an exported chat log) with every detected span highlighted by category, a filter in the sidebar, and a summary dashboard up top. The reading experience should feel like a normal document, not a form.

Recent findings suggest that what Privacy Filter does here. The whole file goes through in a single 128k-context forward pass, so there's no chunking, no stitching, and span offsets line up directly with the rendered text. BIOES decoding keeps span boundaries clean through long ambiguous runs.

Recent findings suggest that what gr.Server does here. You could wire this up in Blocks with gr.HighlightedText and a sidebar, and it would work. The reading experience we wanted (serif body, category filters that toggle CSS classes client-side instead of re-running the model, a summary dashboard that doesn't force a page re-render) was easier to hand-author than to compose. gr.Server lets us serve the reader view as a single HTML file and expose the model behind one queued endpoint:.

Industry observers note that note the decorator: @server.api(name="analyze_document"), not a plain @server.post. That's the piece that plugs the handler into Gradio's queue, so concurrent uploads are serialized, @spaces.GPU composes correctly on ZeroGPU, and the same endpoint is reachable from both the browser and gradio_client with no duplicated code. The browser calls it with the Gradio JS client:.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Image-Anonymizer.

User problem. You want to share an image or any screenshot (a Slack thread, a receipt, a Stripe dashboard) with black bars over the PII. You want to toggle bars on and off, drag them to reposition, or draw one by hand for anything the model missed, then export the result.

Industry observers note that what Privacy Filter does here. Tesseract runs OCR and returns per-word bounding boxes. The backend reconstructs the full text with a char-offset to box map, then runs Privacy Filter once over the whole text. Detected character spans are looked up against the word map and joined into pixel rectangles per line.

Recent findings suggest that what gr.Server does here. gr.ImageEditor supports layered annotation and is a reasonable starting point for image redaction. The workflow we wanted (per-bar category metadata, toggle all bars in a category at once, client-side PNG export at natural resolution with no server round-trip) was cleaner to build on a custom frontend. gr.Server hands back pixel rectangles from one queued endpoint and lets the canvas own everything else:.

Industry observers note that the frontend invokes it with client.predict("/anonymize_screenshot", { image: handle_file(file) }), the same pattern as above. Toggles, drags, new-bar drawing, and PNG export all happen in the browser; edits never round-trip to the server.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-SmartRedact-Paste.

User problem. You want a pastebin that redacts before sharing. You paste a log line, an email, a support ticket. You get two URLs back. The public one serves the redacted version with , , placeholders, following the redaction convention from the official blog examples. The private one is gated by a token you keep and shows the original with spans highlighted.

It has been revealed that what Privacy Filter does here. Swap each detected span with a placeholder on the stored paste. That's the entire redaction step. Multilingual text (Spanish, French, Chinese, Hindi, and others in the model-card examples) routes through the same call with no change.

What gr.Server does here. This app needs two distinct GET routes for the same paste ID, one public and one token-gated, and the URL shape matters because the reveal URL is the thing you keep. gr.Server works here because it's a FastAPI app underneath — which is also why @server.api and plain @server.get can sit side by side in the same process. Note: this can also be built with gr.Blocks() by mounting custom routes with FastAPI :.

A daemon thread evicts expired pastes every 30 seconds. The whole service, including storage, is about 200 lines of application code because everything lives in one process.

The split across all three apps is the same — anything that touches the model goes through @server.api, everything else stays on plain FastAPI routes:.

@server.api gives you Gradio's queue (serialized requests, correct @spaces.GPU composition on ZeroGPU, progress events) and it's what the browser hits through @gradio/client. The same endpoint is also what gradio_client users hit from Python — one function, two SDKs, no duplicated code. Plain @server.get/@server.post are reserved for the static surfaces: HTML pages, file lookups, cheap dict reads. That's the rule of thumb from the gradio.Server intro post, and it's what makes these three apps feel consistent even though their UIs are very different.

Industry observers note that drop in a resume, a screenshot of a Slack thread, a log line with a token in it. The fun part is seeing what Privacy Filter catches (and occasionally misses) on text you actually care about.

Nice demos — the 8-category Privacy Filter taxonomy is a strong EN consumer/sanitization baseline for pastebins and screenshots.

One gap I keep hitting for clinical notes outside EN: taxonomy coverage ≠ “run the same 8 labels on another language/domain.” Locale clinical text needs entity classes and distractors that the EN consumer schema doesn’t encode; otherwise you measure a different product than the one you deploy. Synthetic labeled notes help for that coverage test before anyone claims compliance.

Curious whether you’ve tried feeding clinical-style notes (even synthetic) through the same 8 labels and where the misses concentrate.

Introducing NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni: Long-Context Multimodal Intelligence for Documents, Audio and Video Agents

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benchmark highlightsBuilding on Nemotron Nano V2 VL, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers substantial visual gains and adds entirely upcoming audio and video+audio capabilities - while also leading another open-weights omni model, Qwen3-Omni, in many domains.

In a recent development, efficiency highlightsCompared to other open omni models with the same interactivity, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers 7.4x higher system efficiency for multi-document use cases and 9.2x higher system efficiency for video use cases Figure 1. Total system throughput for multi-document and video use cases sustained by each model at a fixed per‑user interactivity threshold (tokens/sec/user).

At a high level, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is aimed at five classes of workloads:.

This is not only about OCR. The model is positioned for long, messy, high-value documents where understanding depends on layout, tables, figures, formulas, section structure, and cross-page references. Think contracts, technical papers, reports, manuals, multi-page forms, or compliance packets. The model can handle 100+ page documents.

According to recent reports, nemotron 3 Nano Omni includes strong speech understanding capabilities that enable high-quality transcription across diverse audio conditions. It handles long-form audio with varying speakers, accents, and background noise. These capabilities can be integrated into broader workflows, allowing spoken content to be transcribed, analyzed, and combined with other modalities for tasks like summarization, question answering, and cross-modal reasoning.

Sources indicate that many enterprise and developer workflows depend on mixed audio and visual evidence: screen recordings with narration, training videos, meetings with slides, tutorials, product demos, customer support captures, and long-form video archives. Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is built to reason over those inputs jointly.

The Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model is specifically trained for agentic computer use, enabling it to assist with tasks in graphical user interface (GUI) environments. Its capabilities include interpreting screenshots, monitoring the state of the user interface, grounding its reasoning in on-screen visuals, and helping with action selection or workflow automation.

Sources indicate that the model is designed for more than perception. It excels at reasoning-intensive tasks that require synthesizing information across long context windows, multiple modalities, and structured or semi-structured evidence. It can carry out multi-step reasoning, perform calculations, and connect signals from text, images, tables, and other inputs to arrive at coherent, well-supported answers.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a unified encoder-projector-decoder design. The language backbone is Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, paired with the C-RADIOv4-H vision encoder and the Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2 audio encoder. The modality-specific encoders connect into the LLM backbone through lightweight projectors.

Figure 2. Model architecture of NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni 30B-A3B.

The model backbone interleaves three key components: 23 Mamba selective state-space layers for efficient long-context processing; 23 MoE layers with 128 experts, top-6 routing, and a shared expert for conditional capacity; and 6 grouped-query attention layers to preserve strong global interaction and expressivity.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni combines state-space models, attention, and MoE in a unified design that maintains strong reasoning performance while remaining practical for long, multimodal contexts.

Industry observers note that on the vision side, the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni replaces the tiling strategy used in the v2 model with dynamic resolution processing at native aspect ratio. Each image can be represented using a variable number of 16 x 16 patches, with a minimum of 1,024 to a maximum of 13,312 visual patches per image. For square images, this is equivalent to 512 x 512 and 1840 x 1840, respectively.

That flexibility is critical for handling high-resolution, complex visual inputs such as OCR-heavy documents, financial tables, slides, research figures, screenshots, and GUI layouts—especially when both fine details and overall structure need to be understood together.

Sources indicate that for video, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a dedicated Conv3D tubelet embedding path. Instead of embedding each frame independently, every pair of consecutive frames is fused into a single "tubelet" before the ViT, halving the number of vision tokens the language model has to attend to. This allows us to either double the number of frames with the same token budget, or halve the number of tokens with the same number of frames.

Sources indicate that EVS is an important feature, enabled during inference time, that drops redundant video tokens after the vision encoder. This reduces latency and improves throughput while maintaining accuracy. The first frame of the video is kept entirely, then for each subsequent frame, EVS keeps the “dynamic” tokens where the video is changing and drops the “static” ones where nothing has changed from the previous frame. We combine this with Conv3D to enable superior compression: Conv3D fuses tokens from pairs of frames into one, and then EVS prunes redundant static information.

The audio side is powered by Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2, connected to the backbone through its own 2-layer MLP projector. Audio is sampled at 16 kHz, and the model is trained with inputs up to 1,200 seconds (20 minutes), while the LLM max context length supports 5+ hours.

Industry observers note that this represents a shift from traditional VLM pipelines by enabling native audio processing within a shared multimodal sequence, allowing audio, visual, and text tokens to be jointly modeled. This is crucial for scenarios like narrated screen recordings, video Q&A where speech alters visual meaning, long-form instructional or meeting content, and tasks requiring temporally grounded multimodal reasoning.

Each encoder is connected to the LLM with a lightweight 2-layer MLP projector that maps encoder features into the shared embedding space. Once projected, vision, audio, and text tokens are interleaved and processed jointly.

This design keeps the overall system modular while still enabling genuine cross-modal reasoning inside the backbone itself.

The SFT stages are trained on NVIDIA H100, scaling from 32 to 128 nodes depending on the stage. The stack uses Megatron-LM, Transformer Engine, and Megatron Energon, with tensor parallelism, expert parallelism, sequence parallelism, context parallelism for the long context stages, online sequence packing, and selective activation recomputation.

Post-SFT reinforcement learning uses NeMo-RL and NeMo Gym with a Megatron backend. The RL infrastructure used a Ray-based distributed setup across B200 and H100 clusters, plus multimodal deduplication, so repeated rollouts do not multiply image, video, and audio memory.

We open-source substantial parts of our training code.

In a recent development, we introduce multi-environment text and omni training in Nemotron 3 Nano Omni. Our text RL training stage happens across diverse environments in Nemo-Gym, which evaluates the model’s ability to perform sequences of actions such as tool calling, writing code, and multi-part planning that satisfy the verifiable criteria.

Omni RL trains the model to reason across images, video, audio, and text within a unified framework, covering tasks from single-modality to fully multimodal scenarios. A diverse verifier suite evaluates outputs across formats like multiple-choice, math, GUI grounding, and ASR, while intentionally including unanswerable cases to teach the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient rather than hallucinate.

In a recent development, nemotron 3 Nano Omni is trained on an enhanced dataset that emphasizes high-quality reasoning across multiple modalities. We significantly expand task coverage and introduce synthetic data for complex reasoning scenarios where public datasets are limited. To support this, we build task-specific, multi-stage pipelines for scalable synthetic data generation.

InfoQ Homepage News Mock Service Worker Releases v3.0 with ESM-Only Build, Socket-Based Interception and GraphQL Subs.

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read.

Recent findings suggest that mock Service Worker, the API mocking library maintained by Artem Zakharchenko, has released version 3.0, nearly three years after the Fetch-based v2.0 rewrite. The release ships as ESM-only, completes the library's GraphQL story with subscription support, and introduces a socket-based interception algorithm in Node.js that Zakharchenko describes as going as deep into the runtime as JavaScript will allow without recompiling Node.

According to recent reports, the headline breaking change is that MSW is now distributed natively as ECMAScript Modules only, with support for Node.js v18 and v20 dropped in favour of v22, v24, and v26. TypeScript 5.9 is now the minimum supported version. Several transitive dependencies have been removed, including graphql (now a proper optional peer), path-to-regexp, picocolors, and statuses. The result is a library tarball that drops from 416KB to 234KB, with type definitions shrinking by half, from 190KB to 90KB.

Alongside ESM, v3.0 introduces granular entrypoints that replace the single msw import with designated paths for each protocol:.

GraphQL subscription support, a long-standing community request on the project's tracker, lands in this release. Building on the WebSocket interception shipped previously, subscription handlers can now be defined against a graphql.link() and publish events on demand, closing the gap between MSW's HTTP, WebSocket, and GraphQL coverage.

According to recent reports, an experimental defineNetwork API is introduced as the eventual replacement for setupServer and setupWorker. The newly introduced primitive splits interception into sources (where traffic comes from) and handlers (how it is answered), allowing teams to replay HAR files, combine custom interceptors, or hand control of request timing to a test runner. The first ecosystem package to expose it directly is @msw/cloudflare, which wraps the API for Workers environments.

In a recent development, the most technically significant change sits in the underlying Interceptors library. Zakharchenko writes that after seven attempts at the problem, the team has moved network interception in Node.js down to the TCP and TLS wraps, the JavaScript bindings for Node's C-level network code. Moving any lower, he notes, would require recompiling Node.js itself. The upcoming architecture supports arbitrary socket-based protocols, with SMTP cited as an early example. Nock already relies on the Interceptors library for its Node.js support.

Recent findings suggest that A GitHub discussion reports failing tests after upgrading, traced to MSW now intercepting the browser-issued OPTIONS preflight requests that previous versions quietly ignored. Separately, a developer in discussion #2771 challenged the earlier decision to deprioritise Jest and JSDOM, arguing that a runner with 46 million weekly downloads warrants a formal breaking-change note rather than a quiet docs change.

In the Node-only space, MSW continues to compete with Nock, fetch-mock, and undici's built-in MockAgent, though as a recent comparison notes, none of those cover both browser and server with a single handler definition.

Teams on v2 should consult the official 2.x to 3.x migration guide before upgrading. Full release notes are available on GitHub.

Mock Service Worker is an open-source, MIT-licensed JavaScript library for mocking network traffic using Service Workers in the browser and runtime-level interception in Node.js. It is used widely for frontend and full-stack testing, and now covers HTTP, WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and GraphQL including subscriptions.

Recent findings suggest that deepL released Aure v2 on November 26, 2026, at its inaugural Unmute Summit in Tokyo, reporting a 50% reduction in median translation delay from the original Aure. The model is available across DeepL Voice for Online Meetings, DeepL Voice for In-Person Conversations and the DeepL API for Voice.

Sources indicate that instead of passing audio through separate transcription, text translation and speech-generation stages, Aure v2 translates directly from speech to speech in one architecture. DeepL’s internal benchmarks also gave it higher translation quality than six competing systems in every tested language pair, including 32% fewer English–Japanese translation errors than Google Gemini 3.5 Live Translate.

Those results come from a November 2026 study of one-minute real-speech recordings across 10 language pairs with human-validated transcripts. All models were accessed through public APIs without app overhead, and DeepL said results may differ in real conversations.

According to recent reports, speed also depends on deciding when to begin the translated audio. Starting too early can sacrifice context and accuracy; waiting too long can produce a better translation while slowing the conversation. DeepL identifies German and Japanese as especially difficult because essential information can appear at the end of a sentence.

High-quality recordings that demonstrate well-timed, expressive real-time translation are scarce, so DeepL used reinforcement learning rather than relying on large volumes of such examples. Aure v2 was rewarded during training for accurate translations that started quickly, gradually learning when it had heard enough context to begin.

Recent findings suggest that deepL introduced the original Aure model on November 11, 2026. It continuously adapted translated speech to changes in tone, emotion, emphasis and pace, moving beyond an earlier system that derived vocal delivery from a static sample at the start of a conversation. The latest model extends that work by targeting delay and accuracy as well as expressiveness.

Aure v2 supports six languages at launch: English, German, French, Spanish, Japanese and Korean. The original model’s launch list additionally included Italian and Portuguese, and DeepL said other languages would remain available through existing voice models. The fresh model is enabled automatically for supported languages without additional setup.

Recent findings suggest that for enterprise customers, DeepL indicates audio, transcriptions and translations are not used to train its models, and meeting data is deleted when calls end, subject to customer-controlled retention settings. DeepL holds ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certifications and supports GDPR compliance.

DeepL reports that total Voice minutes grew more than eightfold year over year in Q3 2026, while translated meeting minutes increased approximately sevenfold. As of October 2026, the number of active Voice subscriptions with meeting usage had grown approximately 12-fold year over year in Japan and South Korea combined, eightfold in the US and ninefold in Germany.

Aure v2’s significance for DeepL Voice therefore rests on a practical tradeoff: faster output can keep multilingual meetings and customer-support conversations moving, but only if the model starts speaking without losing the sentence context and vocal expression the original Aure was designed to preserve.

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Sources indicate that building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Sources indicate that building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Industry observers note that figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

Recent findings suggest that the LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically notable—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing challenges when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model claims, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

It has been revealed that we employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

According to recent reports, to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

Recent findings suggest that after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

In a recent development, after SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient update therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

To further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

In this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Industry observers note that granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

It has been revealed that figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

We also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Recent findings suggest that granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

How WinHelp files work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Quin

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them.
  • Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco.
  • A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.

Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco. Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.

A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: |SYSTEM holds the title and settings, |TOPIC holds the text, |FONT holds the fonts, |CONTEXT holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like |bm0.

The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.

All the text lives in |TOPIC, which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.

Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a new topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.

WinHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, says whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:.

The length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, x followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes xxxxxx.

Recent findings suggest that one fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.

On top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.

In a recent development, winHelp 3.1 keeps the table in |Phrases. In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:.

Recent findings suggest that the lowest bit of the code says whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.

The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across |PhrIndex and |PhrImage. Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in 01 starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, 011 starts a run of literal bytes, 0111 means a run of spaces, and 1111 means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte.

|PhrIndex doesn't store where each phrase starts. It stores how long each one is, packed into as few bits as it can get away with. Each length is a unary count in steps of some power of two, followed by the remaining low bits to add on top. The step size is set once for the whole file.

Recent findings suggest that my first version always read at least one remainder bit. That works until a file uses a step of one, where there's no remainder to store. Then every length reads one bit too many, and everything after the first phrase is garbage. The fix was a single bits > 0 check.

When a help author wrote a topic, they gave it a context string, a name like SaveFile. You'd expect a link to store the position of the topic it points to, but it actually stores a hash of the target's name. To follow a link, you hash its target name the way WinHelp does and look the result up in |CONTEXT, which maps hashes to positions.

Each byte goes through a lookup table that gives uppercase and lowercase letters the same values, so links are case insensitive. The table's entries are signed, so anything at or above 0x80 subtracts instead of adding. Get that wrong and almost every hash still comes out right, so it's really easy to miss. Oh, and an empty name hashes to 1, not 0, because that's what WinHelp does.

Text doesn't store its own formatting. A paragraph says "switch to font 4", and |FONT says font 4 is the bold one. Links are drawn the same way. WinHelp underlines a link by switching to an underlined font, so libhlp has to tell that underline apart from underlining the author actually asked for.

WinHelp is older than Unicode, so text is stored in whatever Windows code page the author used, which might be a double-byte one for East Asian languages. Sometimes the file's language ID says which one. When it doesn't and the text is mostly non-ASCII, libhlp guesses the code page from the text itself.

According to recent reports, then there's WinHelp 3.0, the version from Windows 3.0, which is different enough to almost be its own format. Its topic blocks are 2 KB and never compressed, its records give the distance to the next record instead of its position, its topic headers are 12 bytes instead of 28, and its links point at topic numbers instead of hashes. libhlp reads it, but it took its own commit.

Recent findings suggest that and then there are the files that only share the extension. Borland's help compiler and MS-DOS QuickHelp both made .hlp files that have nothing else in common with WinHelp, so libhlp just turns those away.

It reads the text, titles, tables, emphasis, links and pictures of every WinHelp version I know of, from 3.0 to the Windows 95 compiler, and it bounds checks everything. Paperback uses it to open .hlp files, so if you've got an old one sitting around, now you can read it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Mozilla Partners with Mistral to Bring Open-Weight AI Models to Firefox Smart Window.

Nov 27, 2026 2 min read.

Mozilla, the non-profit organisation behind the Firefox browser, has announced a partnership with Paris-based Mistral AI to bring the French tech giant's open-weight models into Firefox Smart Window, Mozilla's AI browsing assistant presently in beta.

The deal introduces Mistral Small 4 as a recommended model for Smart Window people in France, the United States and Canada, with rollouts planned for the United Kingdom and Germany later this year. It coincides with Smart Window's first expansion beyond North America and marks a deliberate attempt by Mozilla to resist the pattern of browser makers coupling tightly to a single American AI provider.

Sources indicate that smart Window, originally declared in November 2025 as "AI Window", operates as an optional window separate from regular browsing. It helps users make sense of complex searches, group related tabs, revisit pages they have seen before and carry work across sessions. Users decide when to use it, which model to use and what browsing context to share. Conversations are not stored on Mozilla's servers by default, and Mistral has agreed to zero data retention for the partnership.

Mistral Small 4 is a 119-billion-parameter model distributed on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence. Mozilla selected it after evaluating performance in the beta, with multilingual quality as a central criterion. According to Cybernews, the partnership expands Mistral's reach by approximately 200,000 active monthly Firefox owners, giving the French manufacturer its first large consumer distribution channel outside its own Le Chat app.

Mozilla Corporation CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo framed the deal as a bet on openness: "A browser shouldn't be a one-way funnel. It should preserve what made the internet powerful to begin with: the freedom to explore, discover different ideas and tech, and decide for ourselves where to go next." Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch described the collaboration as "two open source advocates working together.".

The move puts Firefox alongside, but distinct from, Chrome's Gemini integration, Edge's Copilot sidebar and Opera's Aria. Where those tightly couple the browser to one vendor's stack, Smart Window's picker lets users switch between Gemini, Qwen, Mistral Small 4 and others. Golem.de highlighted this multi-model approach as Mozilla's strategic differentiator against the single-provider lock-in of its larger rivals.

It has been revealed that reception on Mozilla Connect, where the project gathers beta feedback, has been mixed. Some testers have praised the privacy controls, while others question whether Mozilla should be investing in AI at all. One commenter argued that remaining "AI-free would set you apart and draw in a demographic desperate to be catered to." Others reported practical frustrations, including theming inconsistencies with vertical tabs, bookmarks that fail to carry over from Classic Windows and a mandatory Mozilla account login that erodes trust from the outset.

For Firefox customers wanting to try Smart Window, access is handled through the waitlist at firefox.com/smart-window. Once invited, the feature can also be toggled through the browser.smartwindow.enabled preference, with configuration guidance in Mozilla's about:config documentation. Firefox 155 introduced French-language support, and Mistral Small 4 appears under the Personalised category in Smart Window's model picker.

Industry observers note that firefox is Mozilla's open-source browser, maintained since 2004 by Mozilla Corporation. Mistral AI, founded in 2023 in Paris, publishes open-weight language models with a focus on European languages and regulatory contexts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GeoIntelX announced on November 26, 2026, a collaboration with the Instituto Geológico de Angola and Ivanhoe Mines’ exploration team to apply artificial intelligence to more than a century of Angola’s historical geological records.

Sources indicate that ivanhoe Mines is funding the platform’s implementation in Angola, including digitization of historical geological maps, reports and other physical records held in the country’s geological archives. IGEO is the government institution responsible for managing those national archives, so the work combines a company-funded exploration tool with digitization of a public collection.

Industry observers note that ivanhoe is conducting its Angolan work through Cuando-Recursos, its wholly owned subsidiary. The copper exploration program covers more than 22,000 square kilometres in the Moxico and Cuando provinces. GeoIntelX describes the package as one of the region’s largest greenfield programs targeting sediment-hosted copper deposits.

Tim Williams, Ivanhoe Mines’ vice president of geosciences, stated the collaboration should accelerate evaluation of prospective targets, letting his team concentrate on the most promising areas and surfacing geological insights that could otherwise take years to uncover. The expected results are more efficient exploration and a better chance of discoveries, alongside local geological and technical skills development.

Sources indicate that geoIntelX states its GIX platform digitizes and structures historical reports, georeferences geological maps and integrates the information through geospatial search. For maps and reports created separately, that location-based structure allows them to be searched as one body of evidence. The process is intended to turn physical material into accessible data for identifying and evaluating prospective mineral targets.

Industry observers note that the platform also provides chat-based access to AI agents trained for geological work, which GeoIntelX says lets geoscientists, executives and operations leads assess geological potential, economic constraints and infrastructure needs from available information. Exploration teams internationally already use the technology.

Co-founder and CEO Gilad Hoshen said making historical data accessible again could help exploration teams “avoid unnecessary data re-acquisition, assess opportunities faster and make better-informed decisions.”.

Industry observers note that IGEO’s mandate includes promoting and coordinating geological research and mapping, studying Angola’s mineral resources and rocks, and managing information produced by geological and mining studies authorized in the country. The archive work therefore affects more than Ivanhoe’s workflow: it concerns how Angola preserves and accesses geological knowledge gathered by companies and institutions.

Sources indicate that josé Manuel, IGEO’s chairman and CEO, noted the initiative could improve access to information, support the identification of prospective areas and contribute to better-informed decisions. Its institutional objectives include stronger national expertise in geosciences and digital technologies and expanded cooperation between Angolan institutions and sector partners. Manuel stressed technical rigor, coordination with national institutions, and preservation and responsible use of Angola’s geological information.

It has been revealed that the collaboration ties an active copper exploration program to the creation of a structured national archive. Its lasting significance will depend on whether the same records improve target evaluation and expand Angola’s own capacity to manage and apply its geological information.

Industry observers note that asa Korr is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence in mining, resource extraction, and heavy industrial operations. His work focuses on how AI-driven automation, sensing, and predictive analytics are transforming extraction efficiency, worker safety, and environmental management across the mining sector.

Industry observers note that with an industrial and engineering-oriented perspective, Asa examines how machine learning is applied to equipment monitoring, geological modeling, autonomous haulage, and risk detection in some of the world’s most demanding operating environments. He pays particular attention to safety analytics, operational resilience, and how AI supports more sustainable resource extraction while reducing human exposure to hazardous conditions.
